US singer D4vd's celebrity lawyers withdraw from murder case

BBC News Mon, 31 Aug 2026 17:54:23 GMT

The celebrity lawyers hired to represent US musician D4vd in his upcoming murder trial have withdrawn from the case.

The star, whose legal name is David Anthony Burke, has been appointed a public defender to mount his defence against the charge of murdering Celeste Rivas Hernandez, 14, whose remains were found in September 2025 in a Tesla registered to his address.

Burke, 21, pleaded not guilty to the murder charges in a Los Angeles court on Monday.

A judge determined last month that he will stand trial for murder. Prosecutors have alleged he stabbed the teen after years of sexual abuse before dismembering her body.

A pre-trial hearing is set for 19 October.

Lawyers Blair Berk, Marilyn Bednarski and Regina Peter said in a statement to the BBC that the court had granted their request to withdraw from the case and had appointed the Los Angeles County Public Defender's Office to represent the singer.

The statement said that D4vd "qualified for appointed counsel".

"We continue to support David and his defence against these serious charges," they said.

"We are grateful that the Los Angeles County Public Defender's Office has taken over the representation and that David has a highly capable and committed team of attorneys and investigators behind him."

Berk, who led the defence team, has previously represented US actor Mel Gibson and film mogul Harvey Weinstein, as well as singer Britney Spears and actress Lindsay Lohan.

Deputy public defender Walid Kandeel said in a statement that Burke was "entitled to a defence that takes his circumstances seriously and carefully examines the evidence".

"We are committed to providing him with that defence," he said.

Los Angeles County's top prosecutor, Nathan Hochman, said outside the courtroom on Monday that his office was "ready to proceed" with its case against Burke.

He also acknowledged that the singer's change in lawyers could delay proceedings, require additional time to review the evidence, or result in the filing of a motion to dismiss the case.

His team was ready for "zealous representation" by the defence, he said.

Burke had already entered a not guilty plea to charges of first-degree murder, mutilation of human remains and child sexual abuse.

He returned to court on Monday to have the charges against him formally read and re-entered the plea.

The murder charges include special circumstances linked to financial gain that could make Burke potentially liable for the death sentence.

Prosecutors allege Burke killed Hernandez because the teen had threatened to reveal his relationship with a minor and destroy his multi-million dollar music career.

Evidence read in Los Angeles court during the preliminary hearing showed threats she made against him on 22 April 2025, stemming from arguments about his friendship with another girl.

"I swear to GOD I will kill u," one expletive-laden text from Hernandez read, followed by a threat to strangle him and tell her dad lies about him. "i will end ur career and ur life I will damage anything," the text went on.

The following day, Hernandez went to Burke's Hollywood home in an Uber he had sent to pick her up.

Prosecutors alleged that Burke stabbed her once she arrived.

Nepal rescuers blast hillside in search of hydropower workers as families wait anxiously

BBC News Mon, 31 Aug 2026 17:30:47 GMT

The families of more than 600 workers believed to be trapped in a vast network of mud-filled tunnels along Nepal's Trishuli River are clinging to hope their loved ones can be found alive.

Rescuers continued battling to reach them on Monday, using explosives to blast into the hillside before pumping air into the Trishuli-3A site - fearing a critical window to reach survivors is closing.

"I wish we could find him. I wish he would come home," Anushila Bhandari, wife of Aurus Bhandari, a 33-year-old engineer missing on a project site, told BBC Nepali.

It comes as the death toll from the flood disaster on the Nepal-Tibet border reached 939, according to the country's disaster management authority.

The agency also revised its estimate of the number of missing to 3,925, of whom 592 are foreign nationals.

Roughly one in seven missing people are believed to be workers at the hydropower plants. Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah said on Monday that 279 people had been rescued from the sites.

The rescue operation is being spearheaded by an international team made up of Chinese and Nepalese military personnel, while experts from India, Korea and Australia are also involved.

"I still have a 50% hope that he is alive because there is an oxygen system inside," Sita Pandey, whose husband was working in the plant when the floods hit, told Nepalese daily Kantipur.

Nepal relies heavily on hydropower and has spent years developing the projects along its mountainous river systems. At least 11 projects either completed or under construction were damaged in the floods, authorities said.

Rescuers began pumping air into a tunnel over the weekend, but the families of those trapped say that should have been done earlier.

A team was able to get into a tunnel leading to one hydropower plant earlier on Monday, but withdrew after finding no one there.

"The longer it takes, the more our hope dies. This operation must move much faster because every second is meaningful to us," Jiban Khadka, whose relative is also trapped inside the plant, told Kantipur.

"It's a frustratingly slow operation," Khadka added.

Nepalese leader Shah said rescue operations had been "intensified", noting that 11,379 people had been rescued so far.

Another family member anxiously awaiting news is Priya Kharel, whose brother Milan was working as an engineer in the Upper Trishuli-1 plant when the floods hit.

"Those who returned from the hydropower site said there were people inside the tunnel," she told BBC News Nepali. "So there is hope that if the army reaches them quickly, they can be saved."

Australian engineer Arnold Dix, who has been helping Nepalese authorities with the underground search operations remotely, said rescuers had been struggling to find the tunnels.

"The actual signature of them has gone - everything is just missing. It looks like a lunar landscape," he told BBC Radio 4's World at One.

Once rescuers knew where the power stations were, Dix said they could then decide the best way to access them, which typically involves digging and "blasting boulders".

"There's boulders bigger than houses - I've never seen that before in my life. It's just an extraordinary operation," the former head of the International Tunnelling Association said.

He said he still has some hope for those trapped underground, given the protection the subterranean environment might have offered from the deluge above.

Meanwhile, in Chitwan, a district far downstream from where the floods first hit, makeshift burials were taking place after the Himalayan nation's river systems brought nearly 300 dead bodies to its banks.

The air was thick with the smell of decay, as men wearing white Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) including masks carried unidentified corpses into trucks.

Over the weekend, a large portion of the forest outside the city was dug up. Medical staff and volunteers worked to extract DNA from the unidentified remains.

Ganesh Aryaal, the chief district officer, told BBC Nepali that relatives will still be able to extricate the remains of their loved ones, once they are identified through DNA testing.

"We don't have enough freezers here... We had to choose this last alternative of temporary burial system. We are really overwhelmed," he said.

In Tibet, the official death toll is 16, with 546 reported missing, according to Chinese state media. Footage of the floods has been heavily censored in China.

Chinese authorities have imposed "administrative penalties" – which can range from warnings and fines to short detentions – on people speculating online that the casualty numbers are a lot higher than reported.

In Nepal, authorities have also ordered the removal of online content that they deem to be misinformation about the floods.

Additional reporting by Jugal Purohit in Chitwan and Binita Dahal, BBC Nepali

The transfers to watch before window closes

Julian Alvarez, Cody Gakpo and Enzo Fernandez are among players who could have new clubs by Tuesday

The summer transfer window may have been open since 15 June but several Premier League clubs are still scrambling to get key deals over the line before Tuesday's 23:00 BST deadline.

From Julian Alvarez and Enzo Fernandez to Cody Gakpo and Ismaila Sarr, some of football's biggest names could yet be on the move.

But they will have to battle the clock to earn their dream moves before the market closes.

With that in mind, BBC Sport's football reporters have picked out the high-profile moves which could go through during what promises to be a busy ending to the window.

Julian Alvarez reached the World Cup final with Argentina this summer

Julian Alvarez's potential move to Arsenal could be the biggest deal to watch, with the Atletico Madrid striker's future now hanging in the balance.

The 26-year-old is caught between his desire to leave Atletico and the club's refusal to sell him to Barcelona. But they would do a deal with Arsenal.

The Gunners have had a long-term interest in Alvarez and have been monitoring the dramatic situation, with Atleti looking for a fee of 150m euros (£128m).

Alvarez has missed multiple training sessions and did not travel to face Sevilla on Saturday, with Simeone saying he wasn't well enough.

Simeone, meanwhile, has attempted to keep the door open, saying he will "do everything" he can to make Alvarez feel important when he returns to training.

This video can not be played

Will Enzo Fernandez move to City?

Enzo Fernandez missed Sunday's Premier League win over Brighton and his future is under increasing uncertainty, having been linked with a big-money move to Manchester City.

Enzo Maresca worked with the Argentina midfielder at Chelsea and needs to bolster his ranks following the departures of Rodri, Bernardo Silva, Nico Gonzalez and Tijjani Reijnders this summer.

Any potential move would likely be a club record deal, surpassing the £116m paid for Elliot Anderson earlier this summer.

Lamine Camara has already made 49 appearances for the Senegal national team

Fernandez potentially leaving for Manchester City could open the door for fellow midfielder Lamine Camara to arrive at Stamford Bridge from Monaco as his replacement.

It could be Chelsea's 13th deal coming in, with exits exceeding 30 players as the Blues are expected to surpass the Premier League player sales record they set at £300m last season.

There is further intrigue around departures with Mykhailo Mudryk looking for a loan move and still a lack of clarity on the futures of Pedro Neto and Tosin Adarabioyo. The likes of Dario Essugo, Deivid Washington and Shim Mheuka could also leave.

This video can not be played

Why do Manchester City want Cody Gakpo?

Manchester City have opened talks with Liverpool about signing attacker Cody Gakpo and the Netherlands international is open to the move.

But Liverpool would only be willing to sanction the transfer if they can bring in one more attacking player, in addition to Bradley Barcola.

Spurs are also interested but City are willing to offer a deal worth around £80m, and sources indicate that City is Gakpo's preferred destination.

However, City's proposed move for Gakpo is now close to collapsing, with the Reds expected to keep the 27-year-old unless they are able to revive a deal for a new winger before Tuesday's deadline.

Ismaila Sarr has scored 23 goals in 81 appearances for Senegal

With Gakpo's future up in the air, Liverpool have turned their attentions to Crystal Palace's Ismaila Sarr after having two bids for Yankuba Minteh rejected by Brighton.

The Seagulls want more than the £60m offered by Liverpool and it remains to be seen whether Iraola's side go back in for him.

Like the Gambian, Sarr is a right-sided winger and the Reds initially enquired about the Senegal international last week, but that was rebuffed by Crystal Palace.

Brazil striker Richarlison has entered the final year of his Tottenham contract

Tottenham are in advanced talks to sign Iliman Ndiaye from Everton, with Richarlison set to move in the opposite direction.

Although a deal for Ndiaye is largely agreed between the two clubs, it remains unclear whether he will make the switch to north London, with Manchester City among the clubs to have expressed an interest.

Everton are open to selling Ndiaye, 26, after he rejected multiple contract offers and held talks with Saudi club Al-Hilal earlier this summer.

Meanwhile, Everton have agreed terms in principle to re-sign striker Richarlison after he told Spurs head coach Roberto de Zerbi "too many times that he wants to leave".

Jack Grealish scored twice and provided six assists in 20 appearances for Everton last season

Everton are growing increasingly confident of completing a loan deal to bring Jack Grealish back from Manchester City, although the precise terms of any agreement remain complicated as the England international enters the final year of his contract at Etihad Stadium.

Grealish has prioritised a return to Everton, where he spent last season on loan, over the option of rejoining his boyhood club Aston Villa, who have also expressed an interest.

Matias Fernandez-Pardo made his Belgium debut in June and was part of their World Cup squad

Just a few hours after the unveiling of Nico Gonzalez, Matthias Jaissle made it clear he would continue to push for further deals in the final throes of the window.

Another forward is on the German's wishlist and Newcastle have a longstanding interest in Lille's Matias Fernandez-Pardo, whose creativity and ability to play in a number of positions across the frontline is a huge draw. The 21-year-old also fits the age range Newcastle have targeted this summer.

This would be a complicated deal to do in the final days of the window, but it was a little telling that Lille manager Davide Ancelotti left Fernandez-Pardo out of his squad for the weekend's game against Paris St-Germain and has decided to exclude him from training until the window shuts.

Joshua Zirkzee has enjoyed two previous stints in Serie A, with Parma and Bologna

Unless there is a very late, and unexpected, development around Marcus Rashford, it feels as if Manchester United's deadline-day business will centre around Joshua Zirkzee and the smaller deals they can do.

Fiorentina wanted to take the Netherlands forward on loan, with an option to buy.

United, ideally, would prefer to sell, or at least get a loan with an obligation.

With no agreement possible, Fiorentina are now looking elsewhere.

However, Juventus are keen on Zirkzee, although a move for the 25-year-old hinges on Canada forward Jonathan David leaving for Atletico Madrid.

Zirkzee's exit might open the door for a left-back or a reinforcement in the forward department, although that too might initially be a loan.

Victoria Beckham's company makes its first profit after 18 years

BBC News Mon, 31 Aug 2026 17:28:19 GMT

Victoria Beckham's fashion and beauty business has made an operating profit for the first time since she founded it in 2008, the company has said.

Victoria Beckham Holdings Ltd, which is led by the former Spice Girl as creative director, made an operating profit of £7.3m in 2025, accounts show, after years of losses.

"We have all worked hard for a long time for this moment of profitability and growth," Lady Beckham told the Financial Times.

"We've been very transparent about the problems that we had in the business but have recovered and are now growing at a sensible pace. After 20 years, people don't look at my brand as a celebrity brand any more."

Last year, a Netflix documentary told the story of her attempting to establish a fashion brand and achieve profitability - and the series itself helped boost sales, "with particularly strong momentum in denim and jersey", according to the accounts.

The fashion side of the company delivered "strong double-digit growth" overall in 2025, they said, while the beauty side, which launched in 2019, "delivered one of its strongest performances to date".

That was led by the popularity of her Foundation Drops, which had a 25,000-strong waiting list and which doubled the size of the skincare part of the company.

The Netflix documentary showed the former pop star talking about her attempts to overcome doubters to be taken seriously as a designer and entrepreneur, then running into financial trouble when the company was "tens of millions in the red".

The business was bailed out by her husband Sir David, who told the programme: "For her to have to come to me and say, 'Can I have some... We need some more money, the business needs more money' - that was hard for both of us because I didn't have the money to keep doing this."

Lady Beckham said: "If he hadn't believed in me I wouldn't still have a business now."

She went on to get £30m investment by selling 30% of the company to NEO Investment Partners in 2017, who launched a restructure.

That included tackling what Beckham admitted was "mindblowing" waste, including "flying chairs from one side of the world to another" and spending what NEO's David Belhassen said was "70,000 a year" on office plants.

In a statement on Monday, Belhassen, who is chairman of Victoria Beckham Holdings, said: "With two complementary growth engines in fashion and beauty, an increasingly international customer base and a focused operating model, the business is powerfully positioned for its next phase of profitable growth."

CEO Sybille Darricarrère Lunel said: "Achieving our first operating profit is a landmark moment for Victoria Beckham and reflects several years of disciplined execution and strategic investment.

"Delivering this result against a more challenging luxury market and macro backdrop makes it an even more significant milestone for the business."

AI could cause global economic downturn, Andrew Bailey warns G20

BBC News Mon, 31 Aug 2026 16:49:11 GMT

The governor of the Bank of England has warned G20 finance ministers that artificial intelligence could cause a global economic downturn and pose a significant cyber security risk to financial systems.

Andrew Bailey said any collapse of growth in the AI sector could lead to a "future market correction" that spreads worldwide.

In an open letter to finance ministers in the US on Monday, he said companies around the world should prepare for security breaches "involving simultaneous disruption across multiple firms".

Earlier this month, a group of 100 firms, including Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI, urged countries and groups to beef up their cyber defences before AI grows powerful enough to override them.

Bailey told the G20 finance ministers that a combination of highly priced stock markets, increased borrowing by investors, and the growing concentration of money into a small number of major technology companies could amplify any future market correction.

"The issue is not simply that investors are borrowing more, but that leverage is interacting with high valuations and market concentration, in particular the increasing cross-investment between artificial intelligence (AI) companies and hyper scalers, in a way that could amplify a future market correction," he said.

Bailey has called on those in charge of financial security to develop "appropriate steps to support safe and responsible model release and deployment on a global basis".

Bailey, who was writing in his capacity as chairman of the Financial Stability Board international watchdog (FSB), expressed concern about the "volatility" prompted by the effect of energy supply shocks caused by the US-Iran war.

His warning comes several months after UK Chancellor John Healey announced a £100m fund aimed at backing British AI start-ups.

That is part of the government's efforts to grow the country's "sovereign AI" capacity, developing homegrown AI technology to ensure the UK is not dependent on services from abroad.

Ministers want to see companies compete for the funding to help tackle challenges like cutting waiting lists in the NHS and bolstering cybersecurity and defence.

A UK government spokesperson said its' new AI economics institute was working with international partners to build "a stronger shared understanding of how AI is transforming economies around the world."

"The institute is the first government-backed body of its kind focused on AI's economic impact, helping policymakers understand what AI means for growth, productivity, jobs and public services as the technology develops at pace," the spokesperson said.

But there is growing concern that AI companies are increasingly developing models that can easily override the safeguarding systems of banks and financial centres.

This summer has seen OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta all reveal their AI tools doing things they should not, with some AI agents going so far as to impersonate real people in order to get past security hurdles.

The FSB which Bailey leads is a global watchdog which monitors finance ministry officials, banks and securities regulators. It includes officials from the US, UK, France, Germany, Canada, Japan, Australia, China and Saudi Arabia.

Notting Hill Carnival revels in 60th anniversary celebrations

BBC News Mon, 31 Aug 2026 16:09:54 GMT

Notting Hill Carnival has celebrated its 60th anniversary with three days of revelry fuelled by drummers, dancers and colourful costumes.

Europe's biggest street party continued on Monday with the adults' parade, live bands, more than 30 static sound systems and the scent of jerk chicken floating through the air.

The carnival, which celebrates Caribbean culture and history, was first held in west London in 1966.

"We are the greatest when we come together as people," said Jackie, from Jay Dee's Catering, who has been trading at the event for 15 years with her family business.

The three-day event began with a steelband competition on Saturday, followed by the children's parade and carnival on Sunday.

Across the bank holiday weekend, more than two million people were expected to join in the celebrations, featuring thousands of parade performers in sequins, feathers and bejewelled headpieces.

At 15:00 BST, a 72-second silence was held to remember the 72 people who were killed in the Grenfell Tower fire in June 2017, close to where the carnival is held.

Soca band musician Evan said he would be spending Sunday performing "all of the traditional Calypso and Soca songs".

"Caribbean music is everything," he said.

"It's a culture, it's a lifestyle. How we walk, how we talk, how we smile, how we eat - it's a combination of a lot of things."

Soul-Rebel Marley said performing at this year's carnival was "a blessing", after he played on the Rampage Sound stage on Sunday.

The grandson of Bob Marley said he did not feel pressure from his family's musical history, and instead described it as "a guiding light".

Sophie, Rachel and Sara flew in from the Netherlands to perform in the long-running Mangrove Mas band.

"We took part in the parade in Rotterdam, but now we're ready for the real one," Sophie said.

For Rachel, the carnival is all about "the energy, the colours, the music".

"And, most importantly, the cohesion of all the vibes and cultures coming together," she said.

Patricia said for her, Carnival was about "carrying the ancestral presence".

"A lot of people tend to lose the whole purpose behind the carnival," she said. "A lot of them are more into revelry rather than portraying a theme and enacting something.

"I feel like carrying an ancestral presence, because if they didn't go before me, then I couldn't do this. It's almost like I'm paying tribute to my ancestors."

Tashma, owner of glitter and body art stand Litty Glitty, said that festival adornment was "not just putting on glitter".

"It's deeper than that, and it brings everything to life," she said.

"You find so much glitter in festivals but people forget that costumes like these originated from our culture.

"My mum is from Barbados, my dad is from Jamaica, but we are all one. When we celebrate today, whether it's glitter, your hair, what nails you decide to do - every little detail matters.

"It always goes back to our culture because we want to make sure that people understand and remember that this isn't just a big party; we have history and that's never going to be forgotten."

For many traders, Monday's preparations began early.

Lorraine, from Luv Jerk, said her team began setting up at 02:00 BST in order to prepare for the day ahead.

"It is really hard work but it is really fun," she said.

"This being its 60th year, we're really excited to bring all the energy and the great food and to serve all the lovely customers.

"Ackee and saltfish is my favourite dish but it's also the Jamaican national dish. I just love it, I could eat it for breakfast, lunch and dinner."

Jackie, from Jay Dee's Catering, said this 60th year was also an anniversary for her.

"I've done Carnival for 15 years," she said. "It's very hard. I got three hours' sleep last night and I'm back here again.

"Most of the customers, they come again every year, we see the same faces.

"It's such an exciting time, coming together, seeing all of these lovely costumes and lovely people – we are the greatest when we come together as people and come as one."

Down the street, Christine from Jam Vybz Kitchen was preparing for her first time working at Notting Hill Carnival.

"We have jerk pork, we have rice and peas, we have jerk chicken, curry goat, stewed chicken, fried dumpling and plantain," she said. "We're keeping it simple but authentic Jamaican style.

"As a Jamaican, jerk chicken is one of our main dishes and jerk chicken is what we are proud of. We are proud of knowing how it's done and need to make sure the authenticity of it."

For Lizzy, who has been attending the carnival for years, an early start was necessary in order to find a prime spot for the parade.

"We've been getting old with Notting Hill Carnival," she said.

Reflecting on what the day meant to her, she said: "Carnival is for everybody and it was made to get people to socialise, all different countries.

"All their problems have gone away because they've come to Carnival for a happy day."

Speaking ahead of the weekend, the event's chief executive, Matthew Phillip, said it was "unfair that Carnival is always targeted as a cause" of violence, adding: "It is a victim of crime rather than a perpetrator."

Across the weekend, more than 3,000 stewards were on duty, double the usual number, and more than 7,000 Metropolitan Police officers were deployed to west London.

Ahead of the event, the force said officers would "relentlessly" pursue the "small minority who come intending to do harm", and had banned more than 330 people from attending as part of bail conditions.

The Met Police said 243 people were arrested on Sunday during the first full day of Notting Hill Carnival, for offences including possession of drugs, assaults, sexual offences and possession of weapons.

Two people were treated for non-life-threatening slash wounds from knife assaults.

Last year, the Met made 528 arrests across the two main days of the carnival, including 167 for drug offences, 50 for possession of an offensive weapon, 21 for sexual offences, four for violence with injury and 49 for other violence.

There were two stabbings, neither of which resulted in life-threatening injuries.

In 2024, there were eight stabbings, one of them fatal. Another person was killed in a separate attack.

Three more held in post-crash crime crackdown

BBC News Mon, 31 Aug 2026 16:06:55 GMT

Three more arrests have been made as part of a wider police operation against organised crime, following a head-on car crash that left two police officers and five young people dead.

Two of the arrested men, aged 19 and 24, were held after one vehicle rammed another in Derwentwater Road, between Grangetown and Eston near Middlesbrough, at about 23:00 BST on Sunday, Cleveland Police said.

An 18-year-old man arrested in connection with another suspected motoring offence in the town has now been charged with dangerous driving.

Cleveland Police said a total of 27 people have been arrested since the crash on the A66 on 22 August which killed the two officers and five youths.

The pair arrested following the Derwentwater Road car ramming are being questioned on suspicion of possession of a firearm with intent to cause fear of violence.

The 18-year-old, charged with driving dangerously in Middlesbrough on Saturday, appeared at Teesside Magistrates' Court on Monday and was remanded in custody, police said.

Assistant Chief Constable Wayne Fox said the arrests "would not be the last" as Cleveland Police continued to target crime in the wake of the A66 crash.

PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died when a Volkswagen Passat, which other officers had been pursuing until seconds before, collided with their marked armed response car.

The five occupants of the Passat - all male and aged between 17 and 23 - also died at the scene.

John Galliano exhibition at New York Met cancelled after backlash

BBC News Mon, 31 Aug 2026 15:30:05 GMT

John Galliano has cancelled an upcoming major exhibition celebrating his work as a fashion designer after it prompted criticism due to his previous conviction for making antisemitic remarks.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York had announced an exhibition titled John Galliano: Horizons that was due to open in May 2027.

But Galliano said on Monday: "After much reflection and discussion with the Met and all those involved, I have decided, with great sadness, that it is best for the exhibition not to take place at this time."

The British designer was sacked as creative director of Dior in 2011 and found guilty of abusing a Jewish curator in a restaurant in Paris.

A court also heard that he hurled racist insults at her friend, who is of South Asian origin, and in a separate incident declared a love for Hitler.

At the time, he apologised for his behaviour and his lawyer blamed it on "work-related stress and multiple addictions".

Galliano said in his statement on Monday: "I remain fully accountable for the pain caused by my words in the past, particularly the hurt I caused to the Jewish and Asian communities, and I remain deeply sorry for it.

"I understand that meaningful atonement is not achieved through an exhibition, institutional recognition or a single public gesture.

"It is a continuing responsibility, demonstrated through listening, learning and one's conduct over time."

Galliano added that he did not want "to distract from the remarkable work" of the Met's Costume Institute and said he recognised and respected that "an exhibition honouring my work would be painful for some".

Galliano's new statement noted his "15 years of sobriety and recovery from alcoholism and addiction".

As well as being the focus of the exhibition, Galliano and his work in fashion would have provided the theme for the next Met Gala.

The star-studded event is due to take place on 3 May, coinciding with Yom HaShoah (Holocaust and Heroism Remembrance Day).

Vogue global editorial director Anna Wintour, a trustee of the Met and co-chair of the Met Gala, gave her support to Galliano on Monday.

"John's decision that the exhibition devoted to his work should not take place at this time is very courageous and a measure of the man he is," she said.

"I believe this is the right decision, and both he and the Museum have my full support."

Others had previously voiced their opposition to the Met's plan to commemorate Galliano.

Julie Menin, speaker of New York City Council, said: "After my numerous and lengthy meetings and conversations with the Met, I am pleased that they have agreed to not honour John Galliano.

"From the beginning, I have told them that I strongly disagreed with this decision, and at this rising time of antisemitism, it had served as a gut punch to the Jewish community.

"This is the correct decision, as the harm and pain this was causing was simply unacceptable."

Meanwhile, Jonathan Greenblatt, chief executive of the Anti-Defamation League, which aims to counter antisemitism, said that with antisemitism at "crisis levels", honouring Galliano would be "misguided".

"Even Galliano ultimately recognised what the Met should have done from the start," he added. "This was the wrong move at the wrong moment. Timing matters."

Galliano is regarded by some as one of the greatest fashion designers and returned to the fashion industry following his conviction, serving as creative director of Margiela for a decade until 2024.

Messi retires from Argentina duty with 'nothing left to give'

BBC News Mon, 31 Aug 2026 15:18:39 GMT

Messi says ending his Argentina career 'hurts me deeply'

Argentina great Lionel Messi has announced his retirement from international football, saying it was a decision that "hurt" but "the time has come".

The 39-year-old, who captained Argentina to World Cup glory in Qatar in 2022, has scored 125 goals in 207 appearances, making him the country's all-time leading scorer and most-capped player.

In a statement, Messi said he has given everything to the national side but now has "nothing left to give".

He added: "Time is running short, chapters come to a close, and this is one that hurts me deeply.

"I love, have loved, and will always love being part of the national team.

"I've given it my all, I have nothing left to give, and besides, there are some really great young players coming through behind me who deserve their chance."

This video can not be played

Messi rescues Argentina with equaliser against Egypt - his final goal for Argentina

Earlier in August, Messi said he was considering his future in football after the death of his father, Jorge, who died aged 68 following a a long illness.

The eight-time Ballon d'Or winner said he wrote his retirement message on 21 July, two days after Argentina lost to Spain in this summer's World Cup final.

He added on Instagram on Monday: "Today, after what happened with my dad, I'm even more convinced than before."

His career will continue at club level with Major League Soccer team Inter Miami, where he has a contract that runs to the end of the 2028 season.

Messi made his debut for Argentina in 2005 as a 63rd-minute substitute in a 2-1 friendly win over Hungary. However, he was shown a straight red card less than a minute later, after he swung his arm and his elbow connected with full-back Vilmos Vanczak.

Despite his tough start on the international stage, Messi went on to become one of the all-time greats, winning the World Cup and two Copa America titles with Argentina.

He is the second-highest goalscorer in World Cup history, with 21, behind France's Kylian Mbappe (22), and second for goals in all internationals (125) behind his great contemporary and rival, Portugal's Cristiano Ronaldo (146).

How Messi's decade of dominance almost never happened

Rivals: Messi v Ronaldo

5 June 2026

The rivalry between Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo, which transcended clubs, countries and competitions for over a decade, to become the defining story of modern football.

Messi first retired from international football in 2016 before reversing his decision.

That followed a defeat by Chile in the Copa America final, in which he missed a penalty in the shootout as Argentina lost a fourth major final in nine years.

Messi scored eight goals and registered four assists at this summer's World Cup.

He took his career assists tally to 12 in World Cups, of which 10 have come in the knockout rounds. No other player on record has more than eight in total.

"Thank you for all the love over the past 20 years," he added in his message, addressing supporters. "I'm going to miss hearing you from the pitch so much.

"Now I'll be just one of you, always cheering and supporting from the sidelines.

"I'm leaving with the peace of mind and pride of having given you, together with my team-mates, moments we'd only dreamed of.

"It was incredible to have experienced this with you all. I love you!"

This video can not be played

Messi in tears after 2026 World Cup final loss

The pinnacle of Messi's career came when Argentina won the 2022 World Cup

In the race between athlete and time, there is only ever one winner.

Messi has pushed that defeat date back for a long, long time now. But I think maybe two things hastened it a little bit.

One is the recent death of his father and the other is - although it was 1-0 on the scoresheet - the World Cup final defeat by Spain. The distance between the two sides was so, so large.

You could see Messi, as he looked around the stadium almost thinking, "I don't think I can go through this again".

What memories he has given us. This little man has been a part of my life for 21 and a half years - but it had to end some time and that day is today.

Could Messi move back to Newell's Old Boys to finish his career? I think there are two problems there.

One is moving his family back to the city of Rosario. It is a little bit provincial, and there are problems with violence there. True, his old mate Angel di Maria has done it with Rosario Central without too many problems. But I think Messi would worry about taking his family back into a goldfish bowl.

The other is that the level of football might not attract him quite so much. It could happen for just a few games, as a kind of romantic end to his career. He has talked about it plenty of times in the past. But I imagine Inter Miami might be the end.

Who knows? He will stop playing when he feels like it. If he doesn't feel like going on until the end of 2028, he could knock it on the head before then.

We will have to see. Inter Miami fans are the lucky ones. They will get the last drops of this little man's genius.

Who knows? He will stop playing when he feels like it. If he doesn't feel like going on until the end of 2028, he could knock it on the head before then.

We will have to see. Inter Miami fans are the lucky ones. They will get the last drops of this little man's genius.

Trump pushes Apple to change 'Lake Ontario' to 'Lake America' on its maps

BBC News Mon, 31 Aug 2026 15:00:11 GMT

US President Donald Trump has asked tech firm Apple to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America on its Maps platform to comply with his executive order changing the name of the Great Lake, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has said.

Burgum told Fox Business' Mornings with Maria programme on Monday that "the president has reached out to Apple directly", adding: "I'm sure we may be seeing that change coming up soon."

Google made the switch for its US-based users over the weekend, though users in Canada still see the lake, which borders the province of Ontario and the state of New York, as Lake Ontario.

The BBC has contacted Apple for comment.

The renaming has faced pushback in Canada, where one electrical utility company apologised on Sunday for its map displaying the Lake America name.

Hydro One, a utility company based in Toronto, said in a post on X that the name appeared due to their use of a third-party mapping service.

"We are working with our vendor to correct the issue as quickly as possible and restore the proper geographic reference," the company said in its statement. "We regret the error and apologise for any confusion it has caused."

Maps by other Ontario-based agencies also appeared to briefly display the name Lake America, including Hydro Ottawa and the Liquor Board of Ontario.

Trump signed the executive order on Thursday seeking to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, following the collapse of trade negotiations between Canada and the US.

The order directs Burgum to "take all appropriate actions" to rename the lake, including updating the Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), the official US government map database.

Google said in a statement on Saturday that its maps will display the Lake America name for US users to comply with the GNIS.

It added that those in Canada will continue to see Lake Ontario displayed. In the rest of the world, users will see the name displayed as: Lake Ontario (Lake America).

Not all map providers are changing the name. MapQuest, an American free web mapping service launched in 1996, said "we're not changing it" in a short Facebook post on Friday.

The platform also unveiled a tool that allows users to change the lake to any name they choose and share their creations.

After its announcement that it will not be changing the name of Lake Ontario, MapQuest rose to the top of the most-downloaded free applications as of Monday morning on the Apple App Store in Canada.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a large sign by the lakeshore on Saturday that read "Lake Ontario Now and Always" in both English and French, Canada's official languages.

"No one's going to call it Lake of America," Ford told American TV host George Stephanopoulos on Sunday. "It's been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It's going to continue being Lake Ontario."

The names of four of the Great Lakes - Ontario, Huron, Michigan and Erie - originate from indigenous words.

'She slipped out of my hand' - children missing after ferry sinks off northern Cyprus

BBC News Mon, 31 Aug 2026 14:50:36 GMT

Ayten Bicer felt her 12-year-old daughter slip from her grasp and disappear as the ferry they were travelling on capsized off the coast of northern Cyprus on Sunday, killing eight people.

Her daughter Miray and six-year-old son Memhet Asaf are among 20 people still missing after the vessel sunk while en route to Turkey from the coastal town of Kyrenia, in the self-proclaimed Turkish republic on Cyprus.

She and her husband Hayri survived, and like many other families are waiting for news of their loved ones back in port as rescuers continue to search.

"She was saying, 'Don't let go'. And I didn't let go of my daughter. I swear, I didn't let her go," Bicer told reporters through tears.

Bicer said a suitcase fell on top of her, which forced her daughter from her grip. She managed to grab hold of her daughter's foot, but her shoes were coated in engine oil from the overturned vessel and she slipped through her hands.

"It was slippery everywhere. It was like oil. She slipped out of my hand," she recalled.

The family was returning to Turkey after a holiday on the Mediterranean island.

"We couldn't intervene, we lost our children," Hayri Bicer said. "Two of my three children are gone. We left them. We are leaving them on this island as we go."

The vessel had been carrying 259 passengers and eight crew members. Nineteen passengers are currently being treated in hospitals in northern Cyprus, local authorities say.

The eight crew members, including the ship's captain, and one other man were formally arrested on Monday. They will be detained for three days, while warrants have been issued for several other people.

The privately owned ferry left the popular holiday resort of Kyrenia at about 12:30 (09:30 GMT), en route to the town of Tasucu in Turkey.

It had been scheduled to travel to Turkey on Saturday but its journey was delayed due to severe storms hitting the island. The seas were still rough on Sunday.

Some eyewitness accounts say the double-hulled ferry jolted violently before slamming onto the sea surface, with part of its bow bursting open on impact.

Ünal Üstel, prime minister of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC), which is only recognised by Turkey, told local media the boat was hit by two waves before it capsized.

While the captain of the vessel was trying to recover from the first wave, a second wave hit and it began taking on water, he said.

The boat has completely sunk and is lying at a depth of 514m (1,686ft), officials say.

Debris remains scattered across the water, including a black wheelie suitcase bobbing on the surface and a sheet of steel that appeared to have broken away from the ferry.

Authorities are attempting to recover the vessel's black box recorder to establish what happened.

A ship will be arriving from Turkey on Tuesday to help with search efforts, TRNC President Tufan Erhurman said.

Meanwhile, a three-day period of national mourning began on Monday.

The ferry - a high-speed 40m long, 10m wide Filo Jet vessel - sails under the flag of Turkey, according to Marine Traffic.

Filo Denizcilik, the company which operates the capsized passenger boat, said it was "deeply saddened by the tragic accident".

The TRNC controls the northern third of the island of Cyprus, which has been divided since 1974.

The jury's options in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial

BBC News Mon, 31 Aug 2026 11:53:21 GMT

Lindsay Clancy's murder trial has gripped the American public for the last five weeks.

The 36-year-old former nurse killed her three small children in the basement of their family home in Massachusetts.

Charged with three counts of first-degree murder, she does not dispute killing her two sons and daughter in 2023.

But her lawyer argues she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time, and therefore could not distinguish right from wrong.

The prosecution, on the other hand, argues Clancy made a calculated, intentional decision to kill them and knew right from wrong in that moment.

On Monday morning, a jury of nine women and three men will continue to deliberate, with several options before them:

This hinges on the postpartum psychosis defence - her legal team argued that Clancy hallucinated a voice after giving birth to her youngest child that told her to kill the children.

Expert witnesses told the court how severe this illness can be, and family members testified about Clancy's state of mind.

Under Massachusetts law, there is no burden on Clancy to prove her mental illness and that she lacked criminal responsibility.

Rather, it is on the prosecution to prove beyond reasonable doubt that she was criminally responsible when she killed her children, criminal defence lawyer Elyse Hershon told the BBC.

They can do this by either proving beyond reasonable doubt that she didn't suffer from a mental illness at the time or that, while she had a mental illness, she still controlled her actions and knew they were wrong.

A not guilty verdict would mean Clancy went free but that is considered highly unlikely. Much more likely is a not guilty by reason of insanity, which would result in Clancy being detained at a hospital.

"The case really comes down to where she is going to serve the rest of her life; the defence thinks it should be a psychiatric facility, the prosecution thinks it should be in a state prison," Hershon said.

Contains some upsetting scenes.

This is the most serious potential outcome for Clancy - being found guilty of first-degree murder, which is the intentional and premeditated killing of another person.

In the state of Massachusetts, this conviction carries a mandatory sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole.

As Heather Cucolo, a New York Law School professor and expert in mental health law, put it to the BBC, Clancy would effectively need to be seen as "a monster in the jury's eyes" if they pick this outcome.

Jurors would have to find there was extreme atrocity or cruelty or premeditation or both to convict Clancy of this, and it would mean the prosecution had proven there were no mitigating factors.

In this case, mental disease or defect - as the law describes it - could be a mitigating factor.

Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague said during closing arguments there was no dispute Clancy was suffering from mental illness but it was not so severe that she didn't know right from wrong.

Expert witnesses for the prosecution cast doubt on whether Clancy actually heard the voice that she said ordered her to kill her children.

This is a catch-all for any murder that is not first-degree, under Massachusetts law.

It applies to unlawful killings committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without prior planning.

"For this verdict, the jurors may not be convinced that the actions leading up to the murder rose to the level of pre-planned [or] premeditated but that instead, Clancy consciously saw an opportunity to commit the killings at the specified time," Cucolo said.

In the case of second-degree murder, Clancy would also face a life sentence - but with the possibility of parole.

The jury received yet another option when the judge allowed them to find Clancy guilty of manslaughter - previously a point of contention between the defence and the prosecution.

Manslaughter, which is defined as causing death by an unintentional, mistaken or neglectful act, carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison per count.

Intent is an important distinction between a verdict like manslaughter and the two murder verdicts, experts said.

"This option allows the jury to accept that the murders were not planned or calculated but that instead Clancy made a split-second decision to act," Cucolo said.

The prosecution is not obligated to demonstrate that she intended to cause the children's deaths for there to be a manslaughter conviction, she added.

South African airline defends low-altitude aerial stunt over packed stadium

BBC News Mon, 31 Aug 2026 10:18:07 GMT

A South African airline has defended itself against some criticism of a dramatic stunt that saw two of its aircraft in close formation fly reportedly within feet of the top of a stadium.

The jets roared over Cape Town's DHL Stadium, filled with more than 50,000 fans, as smoke flares shot up before the start of a rugby match featuring fierce rivals South Africa and New Zealand.

As videos of Saturday's aerial feat were shared, some labelled the startling manoeuvre reckless, while others have praised the precision and expertise required to pull it off.

In response, Airlink said it was carefully planned with the support of the aviation authorities.

"Planning. Precision. Performance," was the airline's message in social media posts accompanied by the footage.

In a statement reproduced on a government news site, Airlink went into more detail.

"The two aircraft were flown by highly experienced crew, with each comprised of three senior captains operating in the roles of commander, co-pilot and safety/technical officer," the airline said.

It added that the flights were performed with the "approved and rehearsed safety altitude and speed limits for the flypast".

The flight tracking website Flightradar24 said that according to its analysis "the lead aircraft passed less than 50 feet (15 metres) above the top of the stadium".

Questions have been raised over the risk and potential for disaster involving two planes and a packed stadium, but many South Africans have responded with expressions of national pride that its country's pilots could pull this off.

"It's a well known fact that we have the best pilots in the world, that was spectacular," Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie wrote on X.

The low-altitude flyby has become a feature of the build-up to some big matches in South Africa.

The most notable was when a South African Airways jet flew over Johannesburg's Ellis Park stadium before the start of the 1995 rugby World Cup final which saw South Africa beat New Zealand.

The match, immortalised in the Hollywood film Invictus, was highly symbolic as the country's first black president, Nelson Mandela, donned the jersey of the national side, which had been closely associated with the apartheid government and previously excluded players who were not white.

UK raises case of British activist detained by settlers in West Bank with Israel

BBC News Mon, 31 Aug 2026 10:00:23 GMT

The UK Foreign Office says it has raised the detention of a British national in the occupied West Bank with Israeli authorities.

Finn Joughin, a 22-year-old student activist, was arrested in Umm Al-Kheir on Saturday after he was forcibly detained by Israeli settlers who had advanced on the Palestinian village.

There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.

All settlements are illegal under international law. Outposts are also illegal under Israeli law, although they are often supported by state services and funding.

The confrontation on Saturday took place in a town near Hebron that has been recently surrounded by settlers.

According to other activists who witnessed what happened, Palestinian children were playing football when children from settler families started intervening. They then ran to a house and started to dismantle a fence.

Footage posted online by both settlers and activists and seen by the BBC appears to show Joughin standing by the fence and trying to protect it using his body as a child pushes against him.

Settlers removed Joughin forcefully and took the London-based student to an outpost.

Israeli police said a foreign national "who disrupted public order" was detained by security personnel of a settler community who suspected him of an indecent act against a minor and other offences.

In a statement on Sunday, police said the suspect was transferred to their custody for questioning before documents relating to the case were sent to the Population and Immigration Authority for review.

"This was carried out as part of ongoing cooperation and efforts to prevent provocative activity involving confrontations and disturbances," police said.

A lawyer for Joughin said: "We absolutely deny all the allegations."

Inbar Shaked Vardi told the BBC that the student was initially accused of assault.

But Shaked Vardi said police later added to the paperwork an allegation of an indecent act.

Joughin is being deported back to the UK on a flight scheduled for Monday afternoon, according to his lawyer.

"So far they have not decided officially on closing the case," Shaked Vardi said.

Joughin is the only one being investigated and as he is being deported, "it's safe to assume they won't continue to pursue charges against him", she said.

"Police use deportation in order to get what they want – which is to get activists outside of the West Bank while continuing to allow settlers to do what they do", she added.

Activists who were with Joughin at the time deny there was any inappropriate behaviour.

"In every single instance, it was the settler kids who approached Finn," fellow activist Matthew, who declined to give his surname, told the BBC.

The Foreign Office confirmed to the BBC that it was aware of the incident.

"Officials from the British embassy [in] Tel Aviv have raised the case with the Israeli authorities and are seeking further information," a spokesperson said.

Violence over the weekend across several areas of the occupied West Bank even prompted condemnation from Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu who accused settlers of harming Israel's standing in the world. President Isaac Herzog called it the "crossing of a red line".

In addition to the incident at Umm Al-Kheir, dozens of settlers attacked the West Bank village of Qusra on Saturday before the military was called to remove them. Foreign journalists were also injured by masked settlers in an attack in the West Bank town of Jalud.

"The half-million Israelis living peacefully … are most disgusted by a small group of thugs," said US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee who welcomed the Israeli leaders' condemnation.

She has been placed next to her late husband, Carl Dean, at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum in the Tennessee city.

Lainey Parton posted an emotional tribute a day after the burial, saying: "It still doesn't feel real that she's gone. I'm going to miss her voice, her laugh, her hugs, and just knowing she was there."

In the UK, 9 to 5 is on course to be number one in the singles chart this week, according to the Official Chart Company, after fans streamed it in big numbers following Parton's death.

The millennials swapping doom-scrolling for gardening

BBC News Mon, 31 Aug 2026 05:58:15 GMT

When Hannah Matthews lost her father and grandmother in the space of a year, she found comfort in her back garden.

"My mind would be really busy, and I'd suddenly be out here at 7am pulling up weeds," said the 31-year-old.

She is now an enthusiastic gardener, and one of thousands of young people sharing their green-fingered ways on social media.

Hannah, who has more than 70,000 followers on Instagram and TikTok, said the gardening community was "booming" and represented a way of "recapturing some space that feels less tense" on social media platforms.

"It brings me joy, and hopefully when someone else is just kind of doom-scrolling, they get a bit of serenity in their day as well," she said.

"I was born in '95, so my generation are the kind of ones who know what it's like to grow up with both analogue life and digital culture," said Hannah, from Newport.

She said hobbies such as cooking, sewing and gardening were her generation's "rejection of this hyper-digital world that feels really all-consuming".

She said it was a "tough time for young people" due to the cost of living, climate change, a "dire" jobs market and AI.

"I'm not saying we've had it harder than all other generations," she said.

"But it is challenging being young and maybe having different expectations to those that our parents and grandparents' generations had, and different opportunities."

Hannah said gardening offered a "safe space" to "take control of your little space of land or your balcony or your pots in the kitchen or whatever you're able to have".

It became that for her, she said, when she experienced the loss of her father and grandmother in 2023.

"I didn't use gardening as a conscious means of therapy but I kind of just found myself out here, pottering around," she said.

"It's cliché but kind of creating and nourishing new life and new growth is just really the circle of life."

Hannah considers gardening to be similar to preparing for a race.

"You'd normally train for a marathon 16 weeks out, which is roughly a season ahead, which is kind of how gardening works as well.

"You're planning joy into your life for the next season to be bountiful."

She acknowledged that owning a house and having access to outdoor space was "a real privilege".

"When I first starting posting I had some comments 'It must be nice, bank of mum and dad' sort of thing.

"I hope to inspire that gardening can kind of be done in whatever space you have - pots on the kitchen window sill, things like that - just the act of making something with your hands and planning it and seeing it flourish is amazing."

Naomi Saunders from Felinheli, Gwynedd, started gardening during lockdown and quickly found herself in possession of more than 300 houseplants.

"I started documenting my houseplants and my veg on Instagram quite early and gardening definitely was not a massive thing then," said Naomi, 32.

She has since gained thousands of followers, and was recently invited to the RHS Chelsea Flower Show to create content.

She thinks young people in particular are drawn to gardening content because they're "more conscious now of putting their phones down".

"It's an online community that really supports each other as well," she added.

"Gardening is something where people genuinely want each other to do well."

For Rachel Griffiths, 37, gardening became a "crutch" in 2020 when the "world was very crazy" due to the pandemic.

The mum-of-two from Church Village, Rhondda Cynon Taf, said she had navigated postnatal depression, anxiety and undiagnosed neurodivergence over the last few years, but gardening had offered her hope.

"I didn't need to make plans with friends, didn't need to try and see people, didn't have to get dressed, have a shower, and make a big deal about going out."

She said when the baby was asleep, she could "pop into the garden for 5 minutes" and have a "little moment" to herself.

She said the garden had also given her family hope during this summer's extreme heat.

"I'm not going to save the world with my garden but maybe if everybody had a little go, then it would help," she said.

"There are so many little things you can do at home which do make a difference."

When Georgia Featherstone, 26, moved to a new area for work, she was initially unsure of how to make new friends and decided to start a gardening club for women.

"The current gardening clubs that are out there are for people with a lot more horticultural experience, more experts, and a lot older," said Georgia.

In the last two months, more than 450 people have since joined her Girlie Gardening Club group chat in order to attend local events in Surrey.

"If you're a millennial, or you're the older part of Gen Z, you're kind of over going out to the pub every weekend," she said.

Georgia is hoping to plan more events in the future, including talks from horticulturalists and floristry lessons.

"With social media, everyone feels connected, but also so disconnected at the same time.

"You can swap knowledge, you can share seeds and cuttings, and that's when you really get the best of the hobby.

"People are looking for community and gardening brings that."

This actor was told he had Alzheimer's, now he's performing a one-man show

BBC News Mon, 31 Aug 2026 01:47:54 GMT

For four days running, Peter Marinker had arrived at rehearsals that were not even taking place. Dementia had muddled the dates in his mind.

Yet he is now preparing to do something most actors would find daunting even with perfect recall: performing a much-loved Samuel Beckett play alone on a London stage.

Marinker, 85, is best known for his voice work: from radio plays and video games to big-budget films like Labyrinth and Paddington in Peru.

On camera he was the adviser to the US president in Love Actually and one of the airline passengers in the drama United 93.

In 2023 he was playing Gandalf in a stage version of Lord of the Rings when he felt himself "switching off" and an understudy had to take over for the rest of the run.

MRI scans and other health checks followed. Then two years ago, he was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease.

"I just had to accept it," he says. "It explained why I kept losing things and I started laughing at myself, at all the other silly things I do again and again."

At that point, some actors may have stepped back from the pressure of performing in front of a live audience.

But "out of the blue" a call came in from someone Marinker had worked with closely in the past - Dave Wybrow, the director of the Cockpit Theatre in London.

The idea was to put on Krapp's Last Tape, an intense one-man play in which an ageing writer listens back to recordings of his younger self, remembering a lifetime of regrets and missed opportunities.

"It's a dynamite show and a dynamite piece of writing," says Wybrow, whose mother also lived with memory problems at the end of her life.

Rehearsals have been running since the end of June to give Marinker extra time to practise, and a whole team assembled to make the play happen.

A stage manager will stand next to the set throughout the performances, autocue screens will be dotted around the theatre, and Marinker will be wearing a tiny earpiece so he can be quickly prompted if he forgets his lines.

Wybrow is adamant this is not about "covering up" Marinker's illness, but showing that collaborative, creative work is still more than possible after a dementia diagnosis.

From day one, Marinker says he did not have any concerns.

"Dave asked would I like to do it, and I was just 'Yes. Oh yes, yes, yes, yes!'" he says.

"I'll still get nerves [on the first night] but I know how to deal with them – that's just the adrenalin."

This is not the first time Marinker has performed the play. He first took on the same role in 1983.

The production team unearthed reel-to-reel recordings of that performance more than 40 years ago, and they will be woven into the new production as his character listens back to echoes of his younger self.

One of the striking things about Alzheimer's is that memory loss can be selective rather than uniform.

Early in the disease, regions around the hippocampus, deep within the brain's temporal lobes, are among the first to be affected.

That area plays a key role in forming and retrieving what scientists call episodic memories: memories of specific events and experiences in a person's life.

That is why people with Alzheimer's may struggle to recall a family holiday, a conversation with a friend or somebody's name, for example.

But other memories linked to highly practised skills and routines can be more resilient.

"Something stored in long-term consolidated memory is often easier to access than new memories that have just been formed," says Tara Spires-Jones, professor of neurodegeneration at the University of Edinburgh and author of Fighting for Our Minds.

That helps explain why some people with Alzheimer's can still make a cup of tea, recall song lyrics, or even perform music or a well-rehearsed theatrical script after other memories may have begun to fade.

All the profits from the four-day theatre run are going to the Alzheimer's Society, an organisation which helped Peter after his diagnosis.

Research for the charity in 2025 suggested that 42% of people living with dementia felt ashamed about their symptoms.

One in five of those with memory problems said they had not seen a doctor about a diagnosis because they were worried about the reaction of friends and family.

Stigma is "still very much prevalent", says Taiyaba Zeria, who manages dementia support services for the Alzheimer's Society in London.

"What Peter is doing really highlights that a diagnosis is not the end, and a person living with dementia can still do so many things they enjoy and they are passionate about."

Marinker, meanwhile, describes the project as his "wonderful swan song".

"I'm in the early stage [of the disease], so I need to make the best of the early stage and prepare as best I can for the middle stage," he says with a wry laugh.

"I might just live through this [performance], or I might just drop!"

The mystery of why so many black Britons still can't swim

BBC News Mon, 31 Aug 2026 00:31:22 GMT

As I push through the doors, the smell of chlorine hits me. Instantly, I feel sick, and I remember why I don't go swimming. I'm getting ready for my first swimming lesson in over 10 years, trying to convince myself it won't be so bad.

Before I know it, I'm in the water.

I glance around the pool; I'm surrounded by other black women learning to swim, all at different levels. Some are confidently swimming lengths; others, like me, are learning how to feel at home in the water.

I'm learning to breathe properly, dunk my head under and let the water carry me, rather than fight against it. There are so many things to remember.

At the age of 27, I'm still unable to swim - and I'm far from alone.

Swimming ability is not spread evenly across the population; figures compiled by Swim England, swimming's governing body, based on a survey of 4,500 people suggest poorer people, for example, are much less likely to be able to swim, as well as Muslims, people of South Asian descent and children known to social care.

As a black woman, it's the figures for the black community that always jump out to me. Swim England's figures suggest that 67% of black women and 44% of black men in England cannot swim 25 metres unaided - far higher than the national average, and far higher than the numbers for white people (17% of white women and 12% of white men cannot swim 25 metres). Behind those figures, published in 2022, are very different stories.

Over Britain's record-breaking hot summer, we've seen a number of tragic deaths in lakes, rivers, and at sea, all of which will contribute to the UK's annual total of drownings. There's no official data yet for 2026, but in previous years we've seen black children and adults over-represented in the drowning figures (along with those other groups mentioned above).

I see this as a stark reminder: learn to swim. All children in the UK are supposed to leave primary school able to swim. But just why are there so many black people, like me, who can't? It's a trend that's existed for decades, but one that has never been fully explained.

Everyone can float.

That was the conclusion of the University of Portsmouth, the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI) and the Black Swimming Association (BSA) in 2023; together, they set out to test one of the most persistent myths surrounding black people and swimming: that black people have denser bones than white people, which makes it harder to float.

It's an idea with a long history. European accounts dating back to the 15th Century recorded that many west Africans were highly skilled swimmers and divers. But racial exclusion from pools in some countries, like the United States, helped to create the idea that black people were poor swimmers. In 1974, only a few years after the end of segregation in the US, an article by two white doctors in a respected US medical journal asked: "Can Blacks Float?". They concluded that black people were simply less buoyant than white people.

In fact, the Portsmouth study found that bone density could not predict whether someone could float. Of the 101 participants in the study, 89 floated unassisted for two minutes.

The UK did not have the same system of formal segregation as the US in the 20th Century. But Alice Dearing, a former Olympic swimmer and co-founder of the BSA, thinks that the US's history might have reverberated in parts of British culture too. Some black people have "ingrained within themselves to think that they can't swim", she says.

For Dearing, this is not just history. At 17, she says a coach used a racial slur about her to another swimmer. She later complained to her swimming club and school but ultimately decided not to take the matter further. "Why am I being victimised for swimming and for being black? It just didn't make sense," she says.

Experiences like these can shape how black people see themselves in the water. Heather Massey, a physiology professor at the University of Portsmouth who was involved in the floating study, says it's important to challenge those myths.

"If people believe they can't float, then they may be dismissing something that could eventually save their life," she says. "We need to make sure that we get the right information out there."

For most British children, swimming starts with their family. If parents swim, children grow up seeing the water as something familiar.

But if parents have not learned to swim - as is the case in some black families - then children are less likely to start swimming lessons at a young age.

I come from a family of non-swimmers: I'm one of five siblings and none of us can swim, neither can my parents. We still enjoyed days at the beach, but that usually meant walking along the coast or paddling in the shallows. Rarely did we go much deeper than knee height.

It's a pattern seen by Nathaniel Cole, co-founder of Swim Dem Crew, a swimming group encouraging more people of colour to get into the water. He remembers coaching children whose parents could not swim, and encouraging them to get into the pool with their children after lessons.

"But then the parents would be like, 'Well, I can't swim'," he says.

Cole says having parents who cannot swim can make the water seem dangerous. "Swimming underwater is something to be avoided. You don't go in there, there's danger. And unfortunately that's driven from parents that can't swim."

Dearing's experience was different. Her mother grew up swimming in the ocean in Accra, Ghana. "When she came over to the UK, she was going to make sure all of her children knew how to swim," she says.

Swimming was passed down in Dearing's family. In mine, it wasn't.

For those who never learnt as children, Cole says starting later can feel particularly exposing. "To be a beginner swimmer, you are humbled by the water," he says. "You have to be very vulnerable."

The barriers to swimming start long before you reach the water.

For Kevin Hylton, emeritus professor of equality and diversity in sport at Leeds Beckett University, that started with his childhood. "I grew up in a working-class Caribbean family where swimming wasn't a thing that was done," he says. "We had almost zero leisure as a family together. It was done through school."

His three children had a very different experience. By then, he and his partner had more disposable income and lived closer to swimming facilities. He says the difference, in his case, was not ethnicity. "It's because of class. And also because of location and the proximity to swimming facilities," he says.

That gap is reflected in the figures. Sport England figures said that 47% of children and young people in the most deprived areas could swim 25 metres, compared with 69% in the least deprived areas.

Access to pools can make that gap harder to close. More than 500 public swimming pools have closed across the UK since 2010, with almost half closing since 2020, according to Swim England and ukactive, the trade body for gyms and leisure centres. The charity classes one-fifth of local authorities as "water deprived", meaning they don't have enough swimming pool space to match their population.

But even when you take class into account, there's still a particular problem among black people. In 2022 Swim England also looked specifically at those in the most deprived neighbourhoods. On average, 73% of adults living in those poorer neighbourhoods could swim 25 metres; but for black adults in those neighbourhoods, it was just 38%.

And there are other thorny cultural factors too. In a 2023 survey by the BSA of more than 1,400 people, 33% of black British respondents named issues around their hair as a barrier to getting in the pool. The BSA wrote that "traditional aquatic headwear", like swimming caps, "doesn't cater to children with longer, thicker afro hair, nor does it cater to traditionally Black hairstyles including braids, dreadlocks and twists with extensions".

Back at my swimming class, I'm still struggling to hold down my fear.

Then something changes.

I'm floating, first on my front and then on my back. I'm doing things I never thought I'd be able to do. And somehow, I'm enjoying myself.

My fear started in primary school when I had compulsory swimming lessons. I would arrive armed with what I liked to call my anti-drowning armour: armbands, floats, goggles, and a swimming hat.

But it still wasn't enough to make me feel safe. There were dozens of children in the pool, all at various levels, and I remember feeling overwhelmed rather than taught. Swimming became something I associated with fear.

"See, you can do it, you're floating," my instructor, Omie Dale, tells me proudly.

Swimming is different from other sports; not learning the skill can have consequences far beyond missing out on exercise.

England's National Child Mortality Database found that black children were over three times more at risk of drowning as white children between 2019 and 2025. Putting ethnicity aside, risk was also more than twice as high for children living in the most deprived areas compared with the least deprived.

And Hylton points out another startling figure: 71% of children who drown (of any race) had been known to social care at some point in their lives, according to the Royal Life Saving Society UK (RLSS UK).

Hylton calls for more research into why these children are so much more likely to drown.

Standing at the edge of the pool, I wondered how different things might have been if I'd kept learning after school.

Dale says many of her students have also not had a lesson since primary school, leaving years to pass before they get another chance to build confidence.

Despite the fact that swimming is part of the national curriculum in England and Northern Ireland, financial pressures are making it tough; even just the cost of paying for a coach to a swimming pool is too much for some schools.

Dale believes getting black children into the water early, and giving them the chance to keep returning, can help. "We run free lessons and we get so many young people who are natural swimmers and just love the water. If we hadn't been there at that stage, they could have grown up thinking they can't swim."

Seeing people like yourself in the water can make a difference. But at the highest levels of swimming, black representation remains low.

In 2019, the BBC found that of the 73,000 competitive swimmers registered with Swim England, just 668 - less than 1% - identified as black or mixed race. (About 4% of England's population is black).

In 2020, Dearing became the first black British woman to represent Team GB in swimming at an Olympic Games, competing in Tokyo. Her achievement matters beyond the pool. Sport England research found that a lack of visible role models can reinforce negative stereotypes about the abilities of people from ethnically diverse backgrounds.

"No one wants to be the… only black person in the pool," says Cole.

When I got out of the pool after my lesson, I felt something I hadn't expected: I wanted to get back in. For years, I had accepted being unable to swim. It was easier to avoid the water than to confront something that had frightened me since childhood.

I'm still a long way from being a confident swimmer, but already the world feels a little more open to me: the sea, rivers and lakes; kayaking and paddleboarding.

Dale describes swimming as a "gateway", saying that once you learn, "it opens a whole new world".

At 27, I am not a swimmer. But I am ready to learn.
