The Kiwi politician who went viral after her drying underwear made an unplanned cameo in a Zoom meeting is embracing her online fame, saying she’s waiting by the phone for a call “from Victoria’s Secret or Bendon”.

Councillor Jo Galer logged into a Dunedin City Council meeting about local government reform from her bathroom while overseas on August 3, forgetting her handwashed underwear was hanging in the background.

Galer’s nonchalant reaction to Mayor Sophie Barker telling her she “might want to move your camera” as her smalls were visible has been watched four million times on the BBC News TikTok account alone, and stacked up views on other news outlets.

“Oh, okay … you can see my washing, you can see me,” Galer replied matter-of-factly.

She was surprised by the global interest in her smalls, but was ready for any opportunities that followed, Galer told Ryan Bridge TODAY, with a new lot of washing hanging in the background.

“I’m open to offers maybe from Victoria’s Secret or Bendon. I could do some advertising for them. So, yeah, I’m sitting by the phone.”

She’d dashed into the bathroom during the August 3 meeting to escape noise next door, “forgetting how incredibly clever” she’d earlier been by doing her washing in the bathroom and hanging it to dry.

“And it was almost dry, by the way – and it was clean, despite the cartoon in the ODT (Otago Daily Times) that said it was dirty washing.

“[We’re] busy people, juggling a lot of roles. And to me, that was a really important speech I needed to make, and I was on a timer, so I just felt I had to crack on.”

Some viewers alleged Barker was trying to embarrass her councillor, but she accepted the mayor’s word that she was “simply trying to warn me”, Galer told Bridge.

Asked if she liked Barker – an old classmate – the first-term councillor demurred.

“Look, we work together and we’re trying to be constructive is all I can say. Actually we did go to school together. I mean, you can kind of tell, can’t you?

“That little schoolgirl giggle that starts at the beginning, and then she says, ‘You might want to fix your background’. So … there is history there, but I take her word for it that she was simply trying to warn me.”

Galer’s not the first Dunedin councillor to make headlines for an online meeting flub.

Former councillor David Benson-Pope was caught with his pants down in a 2020 Zoom call, after he was spotted dusting his office in a suit jacket and bare legs.

Farmers to fund OSPRI’s new NAIT software and $1.38m under collection with levy hike

New Zealand Herald August 31, 2026

Levies would help fund a new replacement software for the NAIT service.

By RNZ

Farmers are facing higher levies for a mandatory livestock tracing programme from today, despite most opposing cost increases.

OSPRI — funded by the industry and Government — runs the National Animal Identification and Tracing (NAIT) programme, tracking livestock movements for biosecurity and animal disease management.

Its board decided to raise prices for NAIT ear tags by 39% to $1.35 for deer and cattle, and slaughter fees up 28% to $1.91 per cattle beast, from September 1.

During consultation in June and July, levy increase proposals were supported by industry groups such as DairyNZ and Beef+Lamb New Zealand.

But 63% of 69 submitters — including farmers and meat processors — opposed them, because of concerns about affordability, governance and confidence in delivery.

Deputy chief executive Simon Andrew said it made the decision around levies carefully.

“There were mixed views on the levy increases itself, and that’s understandable in terms of an added cost of their business,” he said.

“So we had to balance those concerns around the affordability themselves with our responsibility to modernise the NAIT system and maintain a fit-for-purpose and reliable traceability system.”

Levies would help fund a new replacement software for the NAIT service.

Earlier reports cited concerns about the current platform’s unsatisfactory farmer user experience, frustrating technological barriers to compliance and limited data access.

Andrew said it was working with an experienced New Zealand third-party provider — which he did not name — to build and develop the new software.

“First and foremost, it’s going to be modernised to the point that it’s enhanced for modern-day applications, whether that’s on your phone, a tablet or your desktop computer.

“The current system is not effective in terms of that particular situation. It’s very clunky to use on your phone, for example.”

Andrew said it would have guided workflows for required actions for its users, and links with other third-party integrators, such as the Livestock Improvement Corporation’s MINDA herd management system, among others.

West Otago sheep farmer Mike McElrea of Tapanui agreed that the NAIT software was hard to use for particular functions such as downloading information, that he hoped would improve.

Farming in an area once considered a bovine tuberculosis (TB) buffer zone in the 1990s, he said disease testing was most important.

However, he said testing was not as frequent as it should be, which representatives told him was because of funding issues.

OSPRI faced a $1.38 million funding shortfall due to historic under collections of beef and dairy levies, that new levy revenue would address.

Andrew said levies were based on forecast slaughter numbers, which did not always line up.

“The levy increases are also on the basis of under collection and recovering under collection in terms of the levy previously,” he said.

“It’s important that we go through a reconciliation process and set the levies based on that moving forward as well.”

The consultation document said it would contribute levies to the under collections to “restore the intended funding contribution split between industry and government”.

OSPRI also worked to tackle bovine tuberculosis in livestock herds by controlling possums, a common vector of the disease, in addition to Mycoplasma Bovis testing and surveillance.

Recently, OSPRI announced changes to its TB-Free programme, including carrying out less blanket testing across all farms in surveillance areas and doing more testing in higher risk areas it said would reinvest savings back into possum controls.

There were 17 herds infected with TB nationwide, including five in Hawke’s Bay, four in Waikato, three in Otago, and one herd each in Bay of Plenty, Canterbury, Manawatū-Whanganui, Marlborough and the West Coast.

TB-wildlife risk remained across 4.8 million hectares.

A wintry start to spring is set to give way to warmer weather as temperatures climb into the low 20s later this week.

MetService meteorologist Devlin Lynden told the Herald that while South Islanders might wake to snow this morning, the week’s weather is set to become gradually more seasonable.

“We have a southwesterly flow, southwesterly winds, kind of gripping the country at the moment, which is bringing some quite interesting weather to some parts of the country, particularly down south.”

Snowfall is expected to slow down today after accumulating at low levels across the South Island overnight, with the southwesterly winds easing as the day goes on.

The winds will then shift to a westerly flow, bringing showers and heavy rain to the west coast of both islands, before turning northwesterly and ushering in warmer air tomorrow.

Temperatures are then set to rise heading into Thursday as the warmer air mass moves across the country.

“It’s been pretty variable lately, and, as we get to sort of spring-type weather, we do see these quite wild swings.

“These temperatures and weather patterns kind of reflect that changeable nature, with warmer temperatures then colder temperatures, showers, rain, snow and kind of everything that you can imagine.”

Daytime temperatures will climb into the early 20s in some places.

Christchurch can expect highs of 22C on Thursday, while in the North Island, Napier and Hastings will both be “circling” 23C.

“It’s not just the daytime highs that are quite warm, the overnight lows are also quite warm, sitting in the teens - sort of 12 to 13 degrees overnight for many places,” Lynden said.

“So, it will be a noticeably warmer period come the second half of this week.”

The brighter conditions will become less settled heading into the weekend, with a temporary return to milder temperatures on Saturday before temperatures rise again on Sunday.

“We sort of flip flop between this northwesterly and then southwesterly-type air direction through the next wee while.”

Young Grower: Pukekohe champ James Blair claims 2026 title

New Zealand Herald August 31, 2026

James Blair has won the 2026 Young Grower national title.

James Blair has won the coveted 2026 Young Grower national title.

Blair, an agronomist for AS Wilcox, is also the Pukekohe regional champion.

The 29-year-old competed against six other regional winners in a series of challenges on Thursday and Friday, with the practical day events hosted at 45 South Cherries in Cromwell.

The runner-up was Amber Davy, the Canterbury regional champion.

Davy, a quality and field manager for seed potato supplier Eurogrow, also won the Innovation Award.

Third place went to Nelson regional champion Amelia Marsden, a nursery manager at Thomas Brothers Orchard in Riwaka, who also won the Leadership Award.

The seven finalists competed in a series of practical and theoretical horticulture modules, testing their vegetable and fruit-growing knowledge and skills needed to be successful growers.

The finalists also took part in a leadership panel and presented speeches at the sold-out gala dinner in Cromwell on Friday.

Blair grew up on a dairy farm in the United Kingdom before gaining a degree in agricultural crop science.

After working for two years as an agronomist in the UK, he worked in Australia before heading for New Zealand where he joined AS Wilcox, as a technical crop supervisor for potatoes, and discovered a passion for horticulture.

He is now technical support for four regions, from Pukenui in the Far North to Ohakune, as well as overseeing the seed programme for the South Island.

“The Young Grower final was incredible,” he says. “It was very tough competition, the calibre of the other contestants was unbelievable, but it was a lot of fun.

“Thank you to all the organisers and sponsors, you can see the huge amount that goes into organising the regional and national events.

“Initially, I wasn’t sure when it was suggested I enter the regional competition because it’s putting yourself out there and it seemed a bit daunting but I’m very glad I did. I’d say to other young growers, ‘just back yourself and have a crack at it’.

“It’s been great to meet many like-minded young people from across the industry, talk to people working with different crops and make some good friends.”

The Young Grower competition celebrates the success of young people in the industry as well as encouraging others to consider a career in horticulture.

Winners were announced at the annual awards gala dinner held at the Te Puna Mahara – Cromwell Memorial Events Centre on Friday.

Regional organisers host and run the regional competitions independently, with Horticulture New Zealand (HortNZ) hosting the final in a different part of the country each year.

Entry is open to both commercial fruit and vegetable growers from across the regions, up to the age of 30.

HortNZ chair Bernadine Guilleux said the regional and national competitions played an important role in raising awareness about the many career and personal development opportunities across the horticulture sector.

“Once again, across all growing regions, we have seen dedicated organisers working so hard and highly skilled young growers undertaking a lot of preparation and giving their all to make the competitions such fantastic events and highlight the opportunities offered by careers in the sector.”

HortNZ chief executive Kate Scott said all the Young Grower events had provided excellent examples of the range of different roles in the sector, the opportunities for career progression and the support provided to enable young people to gain skills and qualifications and step up into leadership roles.

“It was a fantastic final. Thank you to all the sponsors, organisers and competitors. The event really summed up for me that we have exceptional talent among our young industry members.

“We are focused as a sector on implementing the Aotearoa Horticulture Action Plan and doubling the farmgate value of horticulture in New Zealand.

“This is a sector offering many opportunities and both on and off the job training to gain skills and qualifications that will be highly valued by employers countrywide.

“We are always very happy to hear from young people who would like to know more about the range of options the industry offers.”

Fellow 2026 finalists were:

Bay of Plenty

William Kenna, orchard and innovation lead at KWKIWI.

Central Otago

Luke St John, a trainee orchard manager for Fortune Fruit in Cromwell.

Gisborne

James Torrie, a crop manager with Wi Pere Trust.

Hawke’s Bay

Maddi Sheridan a quality and compliance manager — growing at T&G Global.

Ten fatal crashes in Central Hawke’s Bay in 18 months have prompted a police crackdown on the main highway through the district.

Central Hawke’s Bay officer in charge Sergeant Neil Baker said the six-month “Get Thru on 2″ campaign would focus on the straight, flat and disarming stretch of State Highway 2 between Waipukurau and Takapau.

Of the 10 fatal crashes in the past 18 months, eight of those killed were locals, four on the stretch between Waipukurau and Takapau.

“That’s pretty horrendous for a straight piece of road in such a short space of time,” Baker said.

Jane Dasent knows the impact of that more than anyone.

Her father, Takapau dairy farmer Matthew John Dasent, 58, died in a two-vehicle head-on crash on State Highway 2 at Takapau on April 29.

She said her life had not been the same since.

“My dad’s car crash has altered our lives entirely.

“It’s now made me scared of everything on the road... as crazy as it sounds, I’ve been in other people’s cars while they are driving and I’ve asked them specifically to slow down, because I’m not ready to see my dad yet.

“Stuff like this, when it happens, it’s not just ‘oh no somebody else has died on the roads’; it creates such a huge ripple effect for so many people.

“We are now stuck dealing with learning how to be without him.”

She said the campaign was important to remind drivers to slow down and make smart decisions behind the wheel.

“There is no need to rush; if you are tired, pull over and sleep, and it’s so much better making it to your destination five minutes late than not making it at all.

“That split-second decision is what caused us to lose our dad, and has caused so many people to lose their loved ones.”

Baker said that from Tuesday, police would have an increased visible presence and focus on driver restraints, impairments, distractions and speed.

He said this included checkpoints, breath testing, drug testing, and “spotters” looking for phone and seatbelt use.

He said officers would also monitor Te Hauke through to Waipawa and Waipukurau townships, rural communities, and State Highway 50, which connected with SH2 near Takapau.

“Even though our main focus is SH2, people are dying on our rural roads as well.”

Police would also undertake prevention and community engagement activities across Central Hawke’s Bay.

The activities will be targeted at behaviours contributing to fatal crashes.

These include excessive or inappropriate speed, alcohol or drug impairment, failure to wear restraints, driver fatigue, and poor decision-making and risk-taking behaviour.

He said he and his officers wanted to prevent further road trauma.

“We are noticing that our roads are getting busier; there are more and more people commuting between Palmerston North and Hawke’s Bay ... driving to the conditions could not be more important.”

Eastern District road policing manager Angela Hallett said education was an important part of the locally driven campaign for safer roads.

“What we are dealing with here is driver behaviour, and wanting to influence good decisions from drivers.

“The idea is to be seen, be visible and through that there is prevention; people see us on the road, they do slow down.

“We can’t be there all the time; we can’t be in the car with people while they are driving; they have got to learn to make good decisions when there aren’t police around.”

Mayor Will Foley said the community needed to take the road safety message seriously.

“Ten fatal crashes ... in just 18 months is a devastating number, and the fact that eight of those who lost their lives were local Central Hawke’s Bay drivers makes this especially close to home.

“Every one of these deaths has a profound impact on families, friends and our wider community.”

Foley said the council was proud to support police and local road safety partners in raising awareness.

“Whether you’re a local heading to work or school, or simply travelling through our district, please slow down, stay focused and make safe decisions.”

Michaela Gower joined Hawke’s Bay Today in 2023 and is based out of the Hastings newsroom. She covers Dannevirke and Hawke’s Bay news and loves sharing stories about farming and rural communities.

Should the Govt go back to picking economic winners? Let’s revive ‘industrial policy’ – Toby Moore

New Zealand Herald August 31, 2026

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon has met with US President Donald Trump on the sidelines of Apec. Photo / Pool

New Zealand’s long-term productivity problem has been a preoccupation throughout our recent history, but what if part of the problem is that we have taken the lessons learned from history too far?

This debate can be understood as being shaped by two paradoxical mindsets. The first is New Zealand’s persistent disillusionment with our relative economic performance and the failure of various attempts to close the gaps to our OECD peers. The second is an often close-minded adherence to a view of which policies work and which do not.

As I argued in a chapter in the recent Helen Clark Foundation book, Facing Up to Our Future, there is a need for New Zealand to think differently about what role the state plays in shaping economic development. In part, this is because the challenge goes well beyond just dealing with our underperformance on productivity.

When right-wing populism has taken root overseas, it has done so in areas where people have not been provided economic opportunities, and the sense of dignity and security that good jobs provide. An environment where citizens feel a loss of control amid economic and technological shifts is one in which the foundations of liberal democracy themselves are at risk.

Deep global integration means that New Zealand shares in the benefits of the global trading system, but it also means that bad things arrive on our shores much more readily. In the years since 2020, this has included a global pandemic, Covid-related supply chain disruptions and energy market shocks associated with conflicts in both Ukraine and Iran. Disengagement from the global economy is not an option for New Zealand, but our policies do need to take account of how to build more resilience amid a global system that looks increasingly volatile.

One area that New Zealand firmly consigned to the discard pile of economic approaches is industrial policy, or what is commonly referred to as ‘picking winners’.

Industrial Policy is an approach focused on the transformation of the economy toward particular objectives – often a more innovative or productive economy, though industrial policy has increasingly been directed toward other goals such as decarbonisation or national resilience.

For some commentators, the failure of 1980s-style liberalisation is always a matter of not going far enough with this project. When the promised growth fails to eventuate, the answer always seems to be that there is some further area that needs cutting or deregulating.

We can understand a free-market approach as being about getting Government out of the way, removing barriers and minimising taxation in the hope that the resultant economy delivers what is important to people. In contrast, industrial policy starts with an idea of what we want the economy to deliver. It then prescribes a more active role for the state in pursuing those outcomes, through working in partnership with businesses, unions and others, and consciously supporting some activities ahead of others.

The post-WWII rules-based international order seems to be fraying by the day. Yet one constant that we have observed throughout the fluctuations in US international policy has been a renewed focus on industrial policy – while displaying both its promising and its troubling aspects.

The Trump administration’s approach to industrial policy has been explicitly nationalistic and protectionist, making or extracting deals with specific companies for US-focused investment and treating international trade as a zero-sum game where foreign imports are counted as a loss. If critics were ever short of examples of what can go wrong when the state is actively involved in directing economic development, the Trump administration has ticked practically all of the relevant boxes.

The end of Trump’s first term saw a Biden administration that instead wanted to use the power of the state to drive a green transformation. Bidenomics was also focused on more inclusive economic growth, motivated by the perceived loss of economic opportunities among the working class. The signature achievement of this agenda was the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act, a somewhat misnamed package of measures that was largely focused on investment in green technology and decarbonisation through carrot-rather-than-stick incentives for businesses and households.

But what did not change with Trump’s loss in the 2020 election was that the US remained noticeably sceptical of its previous embrace of globalisation and free trade. Biden administration officials talked openly about viewing trade liberalisation not as an end in itself, but as something to pursue to the extent that it was consistent with a domestic agenda of green transition, job creation and national resilience. The Biden administration was also explicit about the industries that it wanted to maintain control over ahead of China, such as semiconductors.

We can see some stirrings toward renewed thinking on industrial policy in the Ardern Government’s work on Industry Transformation Plans, in Labour’s more recent announcement of New Zealand Future Fund, and in the Green Party’s focus on a Green Industrial Strategy.

Shifting away from a mindset that government should leave things to the market does not mean jumping to a position that government has all the answers. A strategic approach to industrial policy should be one in which we are clear about the ends that we are trying to achieve but flexible and adaptive as to the means of doing so. Government should be engaged and aware of relevant barriers that businesses face, without falling into the trap of being subservient to business.

Thinking around the world has shifted toward much greater interest in industrial policy. At the same time, the world has become a more challenging and hostile place for positive-sum international co-operation and working together to solve major challenges. If New Zealand is to build the sort of economy that truly works for all New Zealanders, this should start with a conversation about whether this aspiration can credibly be left to markets to deliver.

Toby Moore is a member of the Labour Party’s policy council. He previously was a senior adviser to former Finance Minister Grant Robertson. These views are his own.

Saka settles gruelling battle with Aston Villa to extend Arsenal’s winning start

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 21:08:55 GMT

The smile on Declan Rice’s face a few minutes from time said it all. The Arsenal midfielder had just shut down Ian Maatsen as the Aston Villa full-back zoomed into the box. Arsenal were hardly imperious, Bukayo Saka scoring the only goal, but Unai Emery’s side struggled to hurt the champions, David Raya untroubled. The records will show Villa have lost their first two league matches of a season without scoring for the first time since 2002 but, despite successive defeats, this time there was no capitulation.

For Villa, this was a marked improvement on defeat at Brighton in their opener. After 31 minutes in their last game, they trailed 4-0 and after 40 were down to 10 men. Here they could take plenty of encouragement from a promising first-half performance, the debutants Zion Suzuki and Nicolas Jackson impressing, having taken the Nos 1 and 11 vacated by Emiliano Martínez and Ollie Watkins respectively. Suzuki’s eye for a pass was particularly noticeable, pinging 50-yard balls to the 19-year-old George Hemmings and John McGinn, the pair operating on opposite flanks.

Suzuki and Jackson were the only changes to Villa’s starting XI but they appeared far more cohesive, Ross Barkley partnering Boubacar Kamara at the base of midfield. Emi Buendía smacked the crossbar after Kamara overawed Christos Tzolis – Martin Ødegaard subsequently asked questions of the referee, Jarred Gillett – but Jackson otherwise created Villa’s best opening. The Senegal forward, who worked under Emery at Villarreal, pinched possession from Gabriel Magalhães a few yards into the Villa half and galloped into the other before sending in a near-perfect cross from the right. Hemmings burst into the six-yard box but was unable to convert. How Villa welcomed having an orthodox striker on the pitch after Watkins’s omission at Brighton.

This was an advert for a new-look Villa, on and off the pitch. A handful of staff in hard hats were positioned in the closed North Stand moonlighting as ball boys; the corner of rubble between the remaining skeleton and the Trinity Road Stand is akin to an excavation site. Ibrahim Mbaye, whose £47m move from Paris Saint-Germain is to be announced on Tuesday, was in the directors’ box. Six of Villa’s starting XI from their Europa League triumph may have departed but Emery has made no complaints and has relayed his no-excuses mantra to his squad. “We do not look backwards,” Villa’s manager said in the buildup.

“Champions of Europe, you’ll never sing that,” crowed Villa’s supporters as Arsenal players huddled before kick-off close to the visiting support. Ezri Konsa was on the bench on his return to Villa Park and received a warm welcome as he headed for the away dugout. Suzuki grew into the game, his first action of note failing to claim the ball at a corner, allowing Gabriel to send a header off target. Up the other end Kai Havertz sent a shot wide after a neat pass from Ødegaard at the end of an intricate move, though the Arsenal forward was offside. Matty Cash largely muted Tzolis, such an influence in Arsenal’s previous matches.

Tzolis got little change out of Cash and was booked for bringing him down after the Villa full-back snatched the ball. Cash celebrated winning the free-kick by revving up the home crowd, the stadium’s capacity down to 37,000. Cash had to focus on marking a different opponent in the second half and Tzolis’s replacement, Eberechi Eze, was involved in Arsenal seizing the lead approaching the hour. Arsenal slowed things down and then came alive, punishing Villa for switching off. Cristhian Mosquera pushed a pass to Eze, who Cash afforded space, Villa’s defender concerned about an unmarked Riccardo Calafiori. Eze promptly spied Calafiori’s underlapping run and the Italian steered the ball across the six-yard box, where Saka beat Maatsen to the punch and scrambled the cross into the net.

Five minutes earlier Villa survived a scare. Maatsen clipped Saka’s heels as the winger raced on to Declan Rice’s through ball and Gillett initially awarded a penalty. But a VAR review showed the foul was outside the area and soon the Arsenal players in lemon yellow gathered by the spot moseyed towards the edge of Villa’s 18-yard box. Ødegaard sent the free-kick into the side netting. Mikel Merino and Bruno Guimarães arrived from the bench as Villa pushed for an equaliser. Up the other end Suzuki made a mess of a routine save from Havertz but almost instantly made amends, diverting Havertz’s shot wide after the forward, subsequently flagged offside, was released on goal.

Tea With Judi Dench Featuring Sir Ian McKellen review – TV that will make you cry thunderous tears

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 21:00:35 GMT

Two icons share cake and take us on a touching trip down memory lane. Dench is mesmerising, and McKellen is such a devilish guest that he’ll make you weep and giggle too

I am writing this in the wake of Dolly Parton’s death, so I am very much in the mood for the gentle celebration of ageing icons while we still have them. An hour of 91-year-old Judi Dench having tea with 87-year-old Ian McKellen? Sign me right up and I will not so much as breathe heavily in their direction lest anything go wrong.

McKellen – Sir Ian, “Serena” to his friends – navigates the “treacherous” pavement leading to Dame Judi’s fairytale 15th-century home in Surrey, which is as cosy and sparkling as its owner (if anyone is listening, I will take an hour of just Dench, taking us around the house and garden, like the world’s most mesmerising estate agent), and unwraps two lumps of parkin cake to go with their tea. One from Yorkshire, where Dench is from, and one from Lancashire because McKellen was – is – a Burnley (then Wigan, then Bolton) boy.

They go through his childhood as they wire into the cake. Seeing Peter Pan at three, falling in love with panto, being aware of the local professional actors as he reached school age and hoping to become one of them one day. Then a scholarship to Cambridge University in 1958, “where I met all these boys and girls who were as crazy about the theatre as I was”, and he started to dream bigger. I suppose you do when the boys and girls include Trevor Nunn, Corin Redgrave, Derek Jacobi, Miriam Margolyes and Clive Swift. “Well,” says McKellen, “I thought – if Derek Jacobi can do it …” The devilish twist of his lips and Dench’s throaty giggle should be put on Unesco’s intangible cultural heritage list instantly.

Some of his pals went on to drama school but the Burnley boy felt he had better start earning a living as soon as possible and was soon treading the boards in regional theatre. He and Dench began their friendship at Oxford Playhouse, appearing with Ian McShane in a 1967 production of The Promise. They remember actorly moments – the time she saved him from stage fright in a George Bernard Shaw play (“It’s nice that you don’t remember it,” he says. “Just an actor helping another actor out, which is what we do, isn’t it, at best?”), whether it’s nice to know that friends are in the audience or not, entire performances that become slightly reorientated towards a Peter Brook or an Olivier in the stalls – and they sigh a bit over the youth of today who can’t manage on stage without microphones.

Intimations of mortality are briefly dealt with, because while McKellen thinks about death “every day” Dench banishes it firmly from her thoughts. She does look back, though, “with a little bit of everything – but mainly thinking about how lucky I’ve been”.

There are, of course, lots of clips of them acting – McKellen especially, as he’s the guest – and they are something to behold. You hope that those who only know him as Gandalf or Magneto (“Lovely jobs”) will one day see footage of him as Edward II or Coriolanus or as Max in Bent, or of the two of them as the Macbeths in Nunn’s minimalist 1976 RSC production (filmed by Philip Casson for Thames Television in 1978). There are only fleeting glimpses here and you long to see more. The set and costumes cost £250, McKellen notes. And a man of the cloth came to multiple performances to sit in the front row holding up a crucifix. McKellen always thought it was to protect them. Dench thinks it was to protect himself. “Ooh,” says McKellen, who you suddenly see is a sweet optimist at heart, deflating.

His work as a gay rights activist is limned. The grace and eloquence of his turn on Wogan in 1988, explaining the ramifications of section 28, evoke a vanished past. So too, in sadder ways still, does his memory of the letter his loving and beloved father wrote to him on his 21st birthday, possibly asking between the lines if there was anything Ian wanted to tell him and assuring him that he could. Both of McKellen’s parents died long before he felt able to come out. So he wonders. He wonders and he reads Armistead Maupin’s Letter to Mama and makes us all cry thunderous tears.

There are moments in Tea With … that you find yourself wishing that it was A Drink With … (though McKellen himself doesn’t drink any more – Dench looks suitably aghast). Because put any two actors together, let alone this pair, and the anecdotes are always much, much better than the ones that pass muster here. But perhaps it’s enough to hear about lives well lived, and contentment gained, and pay homage to a few of the tears shed along the way.

US supreme court allows Trump to keep building $400m White House ballroom

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 20:40:08 GMT

Justices’ 5-4 ruling permits Trump administration appeal to block lower court order halting above-ground work

A divided US supreme court has permitted Donald Trump to continue building his controversial $400m White House ballroom despite legal challenges, raising the likelihood it will be completed.

In a 5-4 ruling, the justices permitted the Trump administration’s request to ⁠block a lower court order which had halted above-ground construction of the project while a lawsuit by a historic preservation group seeks to block it.

The US president, who demolished the historic East Wing of the White House last year to make way for planned ballroom, has repeatedly touted it as “a gift” to the US people.

Monday’s decision from the supreme court comes after the court’s conservative chief justice, John Roberts, issued a temporary order that had enabled work to continue.

However, Roberts joined the court’s three liberal justices in dissenting from the majority’s decision and wrote that the construction was “likely unlawful”.

The court’s decision may allow Trump to bring to fruition a project that is at the center of his ambition to remake the US capital in his image. Since taking office, he hass ordered the National Mall’s reflecting pool covered in blue liner, proposed a $250m renovation to the Kennedy Center performing arts center that would see his name emblazoned on its side, and is pursuing plans to renovate a golf course and build a massive arch.

While some projects have hit legal roadblocks, such as when a judge ordered Trump’s name removed from the Kennedy Center, or descended into farce, like when the reflecting pool line began falling off, the supreme court’s decision today is a victory for the president.

Trump celebrated Monday’s ruling in a social media post, boasting that the White House would be “one of the Greatest ever constructed in Washington DC” and predicted that construction would be completed in the summer of 2028.

“The Ballroom is totally funded by Great Patriots and Corporations and, therefore, is a Gift — At no cost to the American Taxpayer,” he wrote on Truth Social.

In an unsigned opinion, the five conservative justices said the National Trust for Historic Preservation in the United States lacked standing to bring a lawsuit against the project. The trust had centered its argument on the declaration of a board member, the architectural historian Alison Hoagland, who said the ballroom was an “aesthetic, cultural and historical” affront because of its design, and that she would suffer “injuries” when viewing it in Washington DC.

“The government is likely to prevail in showing that the Trust lacks standing to challenge the East Wing project,” the majority opinion read.

“This court has not found standing in circumstances like these before. To the contrary, we have repeatedly held that mere offense, disagreement, or distaste does not qualify as a concrete and particularized injury.”

The justices also agreed that the government would suffer “irreparable harm” if construction is stopped, or only allowed to continue on a military installation set to be built underneath the ballroom while the above-ground portion remains unfinished.

The majority ultimately side stepped the question of whether the president’s decision to tear down a chunk of a building that rotates between presidential officeholders was actually legal.

“Today, we do not pass upon the legality of the government’s East Wing project,” they wrote.

The dissenting justices – Roberts, together with Democratic-appointed justices Elena Kagan, Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson – argued that the project is unlawful because Congress has not approved it.

In his opinion, Roberts wrote that the construction is a “likely infringement of the legislature’s power of the purse and authority to regulate federal property in the District of Columbia to continue,” and says the majority’s ruling “is no victory for the separation of powers”.

“The ballroom is a building or structure being erected on federal park grounds – President’s Park – in the District of Columbia. Yet Congress has not passed any law resembling ‘express authority’ for the executive’s construction of it,” the chief writes.

He also disagreed that the potential injuries to Hoagland are insufficient for the historic trust to sue, saying she was “deeply committed to the preservation of such historic American buildings” through her work with the association.

“Hoagland’s injury suffices for standing,” Roberts wrote, likening the impact of the White House’s transformation on her to how “an environmentalist can sustain a concrete, particularized aesthetic injury from the extinction of a particular animal or the transformation of a particular forest or river that he regularly enjoys”.

Tennessee to wear Dolly Parton tribute on helmets during 2026 college football season

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 20:19:33 GMT

Beloved singer died last week at the age of 80

Parton was born 30 miles from college campus

The Tennessee Volunteers will be honoring Dolly Parton with a helmet sticker this season, the college football team’s head coach, Josh Heupel, announced on Monday.

Parton, a Tennessee native, died last week at the age of 80 from cancer.

“I’d be remiss if I didn’t also talk about the passing of Dolly Parton,” Heupel said Monday. “All that she’s meant across the world, this country, and certainly, the queen of East Tennessee – a lady that was extremely proud of her roots.”

The singer grew up in Sevierville, roughly 30 miles east of Knoxville, where the University of Tennessee is located.

“You look at [Parton’s] impact, you know, just her ability to give back, make an impact to people, certainly here in East Tennessee. She means a lot to people across this country,” Heupel said. “We’ll be wearing a sticker patch on the back of our helmet to recognize her accomplishments and everything that she’s meant.”

Parton often spoke about her upbringing as one of 12 children in what she described as a “dirt poor” family. Inspired by her youth, Parton led several initiatives to give back to her home town, including her nonprofit Imagination Library, which provides children with access to free books.

The sticker, in the Volunteers’ signature orange, features a butterfly similar to the one in the logo of Dollywood, Parton’s theme park. The logo also has “Dolly” written at its center.

Parton had a close relationship with the university. She twice played on Tennessee’s campus during world tours. In 2023, before a football game, she was walked to the stage at Neyland Stadium by former NFL and Tennessee star Peyton Manning. She then led the crowd in a rendition of Rocky Top, a staple at Volunteers games.

Tennessee host Furman in their season-opener on Saturday.

Lionel Messi’s international retirement serves as a reminder: Watch him while you still can

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 18:51:49 GMT

The Argentine’s career with Argentina was singular, and his exit is a reminder that all good things come to an end

It was among the defining moments of the 2026 World Cup: Lionel Messi standing arms akimbo, looking up towards Argentina’s fervent supporters after losing the final. Tears streamed down his face after his team’s embarrassing loss to Spain in what we now know was Messi’s final match wearing that famous Argentina kit.

It was not the first time he’d cried at the tournament. There had been tears of joy in Argentina’s opening match, when Messi rolled back the clock to his glory days with a trio of spectacular goals against Algeria. There had been more when his brace against Austria pushed Argentina through to the knockout round as group winners, and even more when his equalizer against Egypt threw la Albiceleste a much-needed lifeline. Later, the world found out that Messi had been struggling all the while with the health struggles of his father, Jorge, a fact that clearly weighed heavily on him as Argentina made a dramatic return to the final in a bid to defend their 2022 title.

There were tears in the weeks that followed the tournament as well, when Jorge passed away. It led Messi – among the most private, reserved megastars in the world, football or otherwise – to provide a rare moment of public vulnerability as he mourned the loss of his father on social media. But buried in that remembrance was something that caught many football fans off guard.

“All I did was play football,” Messi wrote, “and now I have serious doubts that I’ll do it for much longer.”

Messi announced his retirement from international football this week at age 39, a move that was somewhat expected given his age and the sheer emotional exhaustion that had clearly accompanied his final tournament. He finishes his Argentina career with the most men’s World Cup appearances of all time – 34 spread across six tournaments, the joint-most tournaments played alongside Cristiano Ronaldo and Guillermo Ocha. He scored or assisted 185 times in his 207 caps, a record 35 of which came at a major tournament. And of course, he was the leading figure in that legendary run that saw Argentina win the 2021 Copa América, the 2022 World Cup, and then defend their Copa América title in 2024. Internationally, there was little left for him to accomplish.

Yet Monday’s announcement still came as a bit of a surprise to many, largely because Messi’s brilliance is still so readily apparent. Few, if any players, have assembled the run of major tournament performances that Messi just put together, regardless of age.

He remains the best player in Major League Soccer as well. Just this past weekend, the Argentinian scored four goals and provided an assist against Montreal, pushing him into the lead for the league’s golden boot.

He remains under a guaranteed contract at Miami through 2028, but Messi’s international exit has now cast understandable doubt on whether he will play that deal out. Messi essentially runs the show at Miami, a club that signs and discards players and coaches at his whim. Guaranteed contracts mean little to the club’s megastars. Just last year, Jordi Alba walked away from a three-year contract after just a few months, choosing retirement and making the MLS Cup final his last professional game. Messi is an idol at the club and would seemingly face little resistance if he chose to bring his career to a close at the end of this season.

Sign up to Soccer Desk

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

after newsletter promotion

All of which is to say: If you’re in North America, or if you can make it there, go see Lionel Messi now, while you still have a chance.

Three years after his arrival, those of us who live and breathe soccer in Canada and the US have grown almost accustomed to Messi’s presence and all of the magic that accompanies it because it has become so routine. Miami’s traveling bazaar of Messi and aging European megastars was a genuine sensation at first but has since retreated into the shadows at times along with the rest of MLS. His four-goal effort against Montreal would have made international headlines in 2023 but now does little to move the needle. If anything, it’s to be expected. Even in Miami, where Messi was embraced readily, Messi’s presence no longer guarantees the hysteria it once did.

Yet Messi’s level, in MLS at least, has not declined. He remains a must-see player and Miami remain a must-watch team. MLS has a sometimes deserved reputation for being a “retirement league,” yet that same reputation provides fans in North America with an opportunity few of them would have otherwise: to witness global greatness in person, and for a relative bargain.

For other players – Thierry Henry, David Beckham and the like – those moments of greatness were sometimes sporadic in MLS. Messi, though, seems to provide those moments at each and every turn.

His star no longer shines as brightly as it did years ago at Barcelona or even months ago, in an Argentina shirt. Yet even the slightly dimmed, more fleeting light Messi produces in Miami is worth watching. His first, presumably permanent, exit from the global stage is a good reminder that soon enough it will be gone for ever.

A remainer, he has also said he does not support leaving the European convention on human rights, which puts him at loggerheads with Badenoch.

Tugendhat stood as the moderate option in the Tory party leadership contest in 2022, but was beaten by a long way by Truss. He tried and lost again against Badenoch when Sunak stood down in 2024.

Turkish deep-sea search vessel joins efforts to retrieve 20 still missing after Cyprus ferry disaster

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 18:37:06 GMT

TCG Isin expected to play vital role in locating Filo Jet’s voyage data recorder 514 metres below surface

A deep-sea search and rescue vessel is on its way to Cyprus as Turkey joins efforts to retrieve the 20 people still missing after a passenger ferry capsized off the island’s northern coast.

The TCG Isin will join the vast operation to find survivors after the high-speed ferry sank on Sunday barely four nautical miles outside the port town of Kyrenia.

Authorities confirmed late on Monday – the first of three days of national mourning in Turkish-held northern Cyprus – that the tragedy had claimed eight lives, increasing the number of passengers still unaccounted for from 17 to 20.

A total of 241 of the 267 people aboard the Filo Jet, bound for Taşucu on the Turkish mainland when it began to take on water, had been rescued, they said. Almost all were either Turkish or Turkish Cypriot.

International sympathy for the victims was highlighted as the Anglo-Cypriot founder of easyJet, Stelios Haji-Ioannou, offered €260,000 (£223,000) in support for the families of the deceased and missing, in a move hailed by Turkish Cypriot officials.

Visiting Kyrenia’s new port, where relatives gathered for news of loved ones on Monday, Tufan Erhürman, the self-styled state’s president, vowed search efforts would “continue with the same intensity, with no interruption, through the day and night”.

The Isin, capable of searching up to 3,000 metres below the sea surface, was due to arrive on Tuesday, he said, as he comforted the families of those still missing.

The ship is expected to play a vital role in recovering the ferry’s voyage data recorder, or black box, now viewed as key in deciphering the cause of a maritime disaster not seen since the breakaway territory declared independence in 1983.

Turkish Cypriot officials told the Guardian it was likely “all those responsible” would be charged with gross negligence as the seaworthiness of the 26-year-old ferry was also questioned.

The owners and shareholders of the privately owned company operating the passenger vessel have also been ordered to appear in court.

It remained unclear whether those still missing had been trapped on board.

“Nobody is saying it publicly, but the hope of any survivors being found at this point is very slim,” one official confided. “Those who weren’t rescued very likely didn’t find a lifejacket. We believe many were elderly people and mothers with babies and young kids.”

In testimony – and video footage – that emerged on Monday, panic-stricken passengers could be seen desperately looking for lifejackets and screaming before the double-hulled ferry flipped over. One mother, Ayten Biçer, described feeling her 12-year-old daughter slip from her hands and disappear as the ferry capsized and sank in a matter of minutes. “She was saying, ‘Don’t let go.’ And I didn’t let go of my daughter. I swear, I didn’t let her go,” she sobbed. Two of Biçer’s other children are among the 20 still missing.

The captain of the ferry and seven crew members were detained on Monday as judicial authorities launched an inquiry into the tragedy amid claims they had been among the first to abandon ship.

Appearing before a local magistrate, the crew attributed the disaster to the bow of the catamaran-style ferry breaking apart in turbulent seas. But eyewitness accounts contradicted that version of events, with passengers telling officials that appeals to turn back to port had fallen on deaf ears as the ferry began to take on water.

Ünal Üstel, the northern Cyprus prime minister, told reporters the Filo Jet was lying on the seabed at a depth of 514 metres and that he foresaw the Turkish salvage ship “reaching [it] tomorrow afternoon”. Boats, helicopters, aircraft and other search and rescue teams had joined the operation, he said, adding that search efforts were continuing “on a 24-hour basis”.

Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when a coup aimed at union with Greece – engineered by the military junta then in power in Athens – prompted Turkey to invade and seize the island’s northern third. Ever since, as many as 45,000 mainland Turkish troops have been stationed in the north.

In 1983, the territory unilaterally declared independence, but in the absence of a settlement, decades of international isolation have ensued.

Andy Burnham will drive home his pledge to bring more essential services back into public control, telling MPs in the Commons on Tuesday that it will be the only way to improve growth across the country.

Burnham will address the house for the first time in 16 years from the frontbench, and six weeks since he became prime minister, after spending the summer recess announcing a slew of policies that will now be put before MPs.

He will use the statement to put public control of services at the heart of his priorities for the coming months, sources told the Guardian, saying he would make the case that it would unlock investment, jobs and growth.

Burnham will say that the cost of everyday services to family budgets is holding back the economy and promise a plan to regain control of the costs.

The prime minister will face an early test of his commitment to public control as he mulls legislation to make it easier to bring struggling utilities such as Thames Water under government ownership. The Guardian reported last week Burnham was considering laws to make it easier to put companies into insolvency proceedings and then take control of them afterwards.

He will also face crunch decisions on possible changes to the immigration bill to exempt carers, as well as pressure from MPs to back moves towards electoral reform. A quasi-judicial decision on whether to allow more North Sea drilling is also expected soon: a highly divisive issue within the party.

Burnham will tell MPs that he wants to “bring back hope” in politics and pledge to work constructively with opposition parties.

He will point to action already being taken to bring more bus routes under public control, including through a partnership between No 10 North and the West Midlands Combined Authority. The Liverpool City Region will start taking control of bus services from next weekend.

Burnham has promised a 10-year project to take public control of utilities which is expected to be a major focus of his next few months in power. Allies have said the prime minister is “completely committed” to putting utilities such as energy and water companies into public control, and is looking at every option.

As well as setting out key priorities for his first months in office, Burnham will face a two-hour grilling from MPs about policies announced over the summer – including a cut to VAT on energy bills, £2 bus fares, the scrapping of digital ID, a major expansion of devolution and a plan for a national care service.

Opposition MPs are expected to ask tough questions on how the pledges will be funded as well as how Burnham expects to fill a £4.7bn gap in the defence investment plan left by his predecessor, Keir Starmer.

On Tuesday, the justice secretary, Alex Norris, will also present the government’s plans to cut the number of prisoners eligible for early release, including the killers of PC Andrew Harper.

Body of victim thought to be in her 70s found in bin bag in walled garden area of Stanley Park on Friday

Police in Liverpool have urged members of the public to come forward with information after the body of an unknown woman believed to be in her 70s was found in a black bin bag in a popular park.

Merseyside police were contacted by a passerby who had found the woman’s body in Stanley Park, in the Anfield area of Liverpool, at about 5.25pm on Friday 28 August.

The body was found in a black bin bag in the walled garden area of the park. It is believed that it may have lain there undiscovered for a number of weeks.

“A postmortem took place on Saturday 29 August, the result of which has been withheld for investigation reasons,” Det Supt Rachel Wilson said at a press conference on Monday. “Our team have since been carrying out extensive enquiries to identify the woman, but we have so far been unable to do so.”

Wilson said forensic work continued, adding: “We’re carrying out house-to-house, CCTV and other enquiries as a matter of urgency, but of course the methodical nature of such work can mean it takes time.”

Officers believe the woman was in her 70s. She was described as white, about 1.57 metres (5ft 2in) tall, of small build, and with strawberry-blond hair. She was found wearing a pink Nike T-shirt.

“Missing people reports in Merseyside and elsewhere have been checked but, so far, these have not resulted in an identification,” Wilson said. “Sometimes people go missing without those close to them realising, through holidays being planned or simple misunderstandings, and so we may not have received a report of any concerns.

“While we do not want to worry people unnecessarily, it is vital that we follow every possible lead, both to rule people out and ultimately to identify the woman, notify her next of kin and apprehend the offender.”

Describing the murder as a “shocking crime”, Wilson said police were “doing all we can to identify the person or persons responsible and bring them to justice”.

Stanley Park separates the Anfield and Goodison Park football stadiums, which are respectively home to Liverpool FC and Everton Women.

Assistant chief constable Andy Ryan said he understood “how unnerving” the discovery and the heightened police presence would be for local people, adding: “This is the exact reason that we are so determined to get answers as soon as we possibly can.”

He described the park as “a very busy and popular green space, especially in the recent warm summer weeks”.

“It is visited by dog walkers and families, as well as people walking and exercising,” he said. “It is quite possible that one or more of these visitors may have seen something suspicious recently and not reported it at the time.”

“I want to reiterate Rachel’s appeal,” Ryan added. “If anyone recognises the description of this woman or you have any concerns whatsoever about someone you may know and haven’t seen or heard from recently, please tell us as a matter of urgency.”

Potential witnesses are urged to contact Merseyside police via social media or to call 101, quoting reference number 26000706383.

Reports can also be made anonymously by calling Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

Trump threatens further action as US and Iran exchange fire in new flare-up

The US president, Donald Trump, on Monday threatened further action. The US is to trying to prise open Tehran’s grip on shipping going through the strait, which before the war accounted for a fifth of the world’s seaborne energy supply. US Central Command said it acted late on Sunday, launching the first strikes on Iran since July, after it detected the Iranians were planning to deploy fresh mines in the strait. The UAE defence ministry said it intercepted a drone over its territorial waters.

Trump responded to the Iranian reprisals by telling Fox News: “We’re going to hit them hard. There will be a response.” The US president called Iran “officially a failed nation without an airforce, a navy or a currency”, adding that inflation was at 300% and its leaders were incapable of representing their country.

The White House last week signalled that Trump was shelving military measures in favour of a campaign to destroy the Iranian economy by enforcing sanctions.

Officials later said Iran had targeted three ships trying to navigate the southern route that Tehran says is unauthorised.

The IRGC warned that other ships violating ⁠its rules would face ​the ​same fate and ​said compliance with ​its regulations ‌for ​passage ​through the strait was mandatory.

However, the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, told Pakistan’s prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, in a bilateral meeting on the margins of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan on Monday that continuing the war was not in Iran’s interest, adding he was still ready to implement the memorandum of understanding with the US that Pakistan had mediated in June.

The Iranian currency was under renewed pressure on Monday and the inflationary impact of its rapid depreciation is causing growing concern to MPs.

Iran and Oman last week reached a verbal agreement on a new single temporary route for shipping through the strait in which Oman retains controls on shipping in Omani waters.

One western diplomat familiar with the talks said the message had got through to Washington that this bilateral agreement would not be enough for Iran to open the strait and that to do so would at least require the US to end its blockade of Iranian oil exports, something Trump is not currently prepared to do. “There are many in Iran determined to torment Trump right up to the end of his presidency,” the western diplomat said. “We are stuck.” He said some oil was getting through but not very much.

The latest fighting broke out late on Sunday with the US claiming it attacked Larak Island in the strait. A US official said: “I can confirm that earlier today US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island. Islamic ⁠Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait of Hormuz.”

The IRGC said the US attack had killed three soldiers and wounded two citizens. Iran’s Mehr news agency quoted the IRGC as saying its air defences shot down a US MQ-9 drone over the strait, causing it to crash ‌into Gulf waters.

The US said all missiles fired towards US forces in Jordan had been intercepted with no significant impact.

The White House claim that the US now controls the strait and ships are free to navigate its waters is heavily contested. Tanker Trackers, an independent tracking agency, said on Sunday: “Past seven days daily average of crude oil exports via the strait of Hormuz was 3.8m barrels per day. The German finance minister, Lars Klingbeil, who is facing difficult regional elections, is to urge the US to bring the conflict to a diplomatic end, pointing to the war’s inflationary impact.

The US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, echoing Trump, claimed on Monday the resumed exchanges of fire showed Iran was “lashing out” because the fresh sanctions were taking ​a heavy toll on its already battered economy.

“They’re taking it very seriously ... they’re in shock at the state of their ‌economy,” Bessent told reporters at the G20 finance ministers ‌meeting in North Carolina. “I would think that they are lashing out kinetically because they are losing economically.”

China, a key Iranian customer for its oil, has said it opposes the new US sanctions campaign. In Kyrgyzstan, Pezeshkian will be looking for concrete assurances from the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, that he will not allow the US to spread economic chaos through Iran.

The Guardian view on Trump’s immigration crackdown: who will have fewer rights next?

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 17:04:53 GMT

The president’s deportation machine is creating a class of people inside the US who have fewer protections against the power of the state

Is the Trump administration creating a group in the US with fewer protections against executive power owing to their immigration status? Its often openly racist actions suggest so. US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) claims to target “the worst of the worst” – undocumented migrants who commit violent crimes. Yet the Guardian reported that over half of those arrested in July had no criminal convictions or pending charges. That month, ICE made record arrests and deportations, apprehending 1,500 people and removing 1,100 daily.

When campaigning, Donald Trump falsely claimed that Haitians were “eating the pets”. In office, his administration moved to end temporary protected status (TPS) for Haitians. In June, the supreme court let the protection expire, leaving about 350,000 people at risk of deportation to a country gripped by violence and instability. The court’s decision means more than 1 million TPS holders from 13 nations previously considered too unsafe to return to are now at risk of deportation. Many have lived and worked legally in the US for years.

Although Barack Obama deported a record 430,000 people in 2013, his administration focused largely on border-crossers. Mr Trump’s crackdown reaches deep into America, targeting those who call the country home. The Economist reports that Trumpian legal tactics have left 1.7 million more immigrants open to deportation.

Mr Trump’s dehumanising rhetoric does political work: it turns groups into threats, making harsh treatment easier to justify. By calling migration an “invasion”, he sought to suspend habeas corpus – the ancient safeguard against arbitrary detention. When that proved too much even for Mr Trump, his administration attacked due process instead. In July 2025, an ICE directive quietly rewrote detention policy, treating many migrants arrested inside the US as if they had just arrived at the border, denying them bond hearings. For many, the only recourse was to go to the federal courts. Judges repeatedly ruled the policy illegal yet thousands languish in detention for months awaiting relief.

The White House has sought to deport immigrants for protected political speech. Last week, a federal judge ruled visa cancellations for noncitizen students’ pro-Palestinian advocacy unconstitutional. Mahmoud Khalil, a Columbia graduate and permanent resident whose arrest by ICE in 2025 after Gaza protests made global news, is still fighting a final deportation order – a stark threat to liberty.

Mr Trump’s immigration crackdown still fires up his Maga base, but is unpopular with many Americans. In one week in July, three ICE encounters ended in death. ICE’s masked thuggishness is a disgrace. So is the president’s cruelty. The Brookings Institution thinktank estimates that more than 100,000 children, three-quarters of whom are probably US citizens, have been separated from their parents during Mr Trump’s second term.

The argument within the US right is moving beyond undocumented migrants and noncitizens. Some Republicans are pushing to restrict the rights of naturalised and dual citizens – including their right to run for office. They may be spooked by the success of the Ugandan-born New York mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose family has Indian roots. Mr Trump has long spoken about – and treated – people differently according to their race. He is still doing so. The US has been down this road before. Abraham Lincoln understood the danger: once equality admits exceptions, where do they stop?

The Guardian view on regulating big tech: Meta has got off too lightly

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 17:04:05 GMT

New child safety measures are welcome, but the wider risks posed by these platforms remain unaddressed

“Hook, hold, harvest and hide” was how Megan O’Neill, a lawyer for the US state of California, characterised Meta’s business model in the trial that ended last week with an $18bn settlement, to be shared between the states and territories that brought the case. It was a clever way to describe the company’s approach to users’ attention and data. But the sharpness of her words was not matched by the deal. While the strengthening of child safety features is welcome, the tech giant once again batted off efforts to alter its products.

Meta’s decision to settle enabled it to avoid any admission of liability. It put a stop to the awkward questions being asked of witnesses including Adam Mosseri, Instagram’s CEO, and the damaging claims made by whistleblowers such as Arturo Béjar. This former Meta safety engineer told the court that his own daughter had been sent unsolicited photos of male genitals on Instagram.

The $18bn that Meta agreed to pay over 10 years, some of which is conditional on other platforms making similar changes, will hardly dent its profits (Meta plans to invest up to $145bn this year). More significant by far are its concessions in relation to child users. Safety features will become “opt-out” instead of “opt-in”, increasing the likelihood of their being switched on. Parents will be able to change the settings on young people’s accounts so that their feeds no longer show personalised, algorithmically driven content.

A new two-hour daily limit, blocks on use during the night and on notifications during school hours, backed up by compulsory age verification, improve on the current free-for-all. So does the commitment to disable obviously harmful “social comparison” features such as cosmetic surgery image filters.

But the package falls short of the restrictions on social media companies’ access to children that Australia, the UK, Malaysia, Indonesia and the EU have either imposed or are in the process of imposing (UK ministers have indicated that in areas where US rules may be stricter, they plan to follow suit). By accepting the terms that they did, while declining to raise the “digital age of consent” (at which accounts can be marketed to children) from 13, this deal’s negotiators left crucial aspects of Meta’s business, including its algorithms and addictive design features, largely untouched.

There are good reasons why children’s mental health is a central focus of online safety campaigning. But the harm caused by big tech’s monetisation of attention goes wider. The addictive, tribalist and narcissistic behaviours that platforms are widely recognised to promote have implications for societies as well as individuals.

One of many outstanding cases against Meta is being brought by Abrham Mearag, whose father was murdered in Ethiopia in 2021, after Facebook’s algorithm allegedly promoted posts calling for his killing. A US court blocked another case against the company regarding its role in the Rohingya genocide.

Measures designed to protect American children from anxiety, depression, unlawful data gathering and addiction are important. But they will not reduce the risk of social media being linked to murderous violence, or undermining democracy, elsewhere in the world. It is now for other courts, or foreign governments, to take the next steps in holding Meta and its peer companies to account for their role as overseers of the global digital commons.

Dolly Parton laid to rest in private Nashville funeral

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 16:17:24 GMT

The queen of country was interred next to her late husband in an intimate ceremony attended by close family

Dolly Parton was laid to rest in a private ceremony in Nashville on Friday, her family has confirmed.

The queen of country music, who died aged 80 on 25 August “after bravely facing a brief battle with cancer”, was interred at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum alongside her husband of 60 years, Carl Thomas.

Parton’s great-niece Lainey Parton wrote on Instagram on Saturday: “I wanted to wait until after my granny was laid to rest yesterday before I tried to put any of this into words.

“From the time I was little, my granny always had a way of making me feel like I was enough. She never made my dreams feel too big or made me feel like I couldn’t do something. She believed in me before I even knew how to believe in myself.

“Because she couldn’t have kids of her own, she always made us feel like we were hers,” Lainey continued. “She loved us that way, and I’ll forever be grateful for that.”

Only immediate family attended the small ceremony, People reported. Parton had her name engraved on the large mausoleum plaque at the cemetery before she died, as well as an engraving of the cabin in Sevier county, Tennessee, where she grew up.

On Saturday, Parton’s niece Jada Star took to the stage at Nashville’s Grand Ole Opry as part of a tribute concert to the country legend. Star performed a song titled The Orchard that she had recorded with Parton for her 2024 album Smoky Mountain DNA: Family, Faith and Fables.

In an Instagram post ahead of the performance, Star said, “I am walking around in a fog of sadness, like all of you have.

“I do not take this honor lightly. I will stand on that stage tonight, the stage she loved so much, and share my song I wrote for her and for my whole family.”

On Monday, the estate of Parton announced DollyFest, a two-weekend event which will take place in Nashville and London next year. Before her death, Parton had been planning the festival for January 2026 but had to take a step back due to health issues.

“As far as a traditional memorial goes, that is not something Dolly wanted,” said Parton’s manager, Danny Nozell, in a press release. “So, instead, it feels more appropriate for us to take a beat, let all the tributes that immediately make sense occur naturally, and then, see through this festival-style concept that was truly dreamed up by Dolly.”

Last week, Parton’s team confirmed that the projects she was working on before her death would continue to be brought to life, including a line of coffee grounds, a home decor collection and a Broadway musical to launch in New York later this year.

“Dolly worked up until the day she died,” Nozell said. “As the leader of the team responsible for overseeing her legacy, we will ensure the many dreams she had yet to fulfill are brought to life.”

Active projects that Parton was working on at the time of her death also include Dolly Parton’s SongTeller Hotel and Dolly’s Life of Many Colors Museum, which are both scheduled to open next month in Nashville. Meanwhile, Dolly Dolls and a range of Dolly’s Dog Treats are scheduled to be released in the coming months.

The family has asked for donations in Parton’s memory to be dedicated to Imagination Library, the organization she founded to encourage literacy and the love of reading in children.

Marseille’s squad is being gutted but their manager is staying – for now

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 16:11:23 GMT

It has been a tough transfer window for Marseille and a 2-0 defeat at Monaco suggests it could be a long season

By Get French Football News

A humid night in Monaco provided an opportunity to gauge the temperature of the Marseille supporters. Despite the ban on away fans at the Stade Louis II, plenty were in attendance for their 2-0 defeat in the Principality. There were cheers for their new manager, Bruno Génésio, and boos for Geoffrey Kondogbia, but it was the silence for much of the second half that spoke volumes.

Génésio, who replaced Habib Beye in the summer, has been appointed to keep a lid on things. The former Lille manager has been part of a larger reshuffle at Marseille, with the president and the sporting director also replaced. The new arrivals have inherited a mess. After making promises to Uefa and the DNCG – French football’s financial watchdog – Marseille were allowed to compete in Europe this season. However, if they fail to reduce their wage bill drastically, they will not be allowed to do so next season.

Every single player was put up for sale in the transfer window. This was always going to be a difficult summer and their new sporting director, Grégory Lorenzi, has been open about that, but Génésio has been taken aback. “Did I expect such a complicated situation? Not exactly,” said the Marseille manager last week. “I knew there were difficulties, but I didn’t imagine it to this extent. I never imagined that we’d be in this position.”

Marseille have sold Mason Greenwood, Facundo Medina, Gerónimo Rulli and Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang, with the former captain Leonardo Balerdi leaving on loan to Roma. But those sales have not been sufficient for the club to dip into the market themselves; not one player has come through the door. “There won’t be any recruits,” said Génésio on Sunday night. “Three of four more players have to leave us for us to be able to register one or two arrivals”

Could the manager walk? “There is no news on an eventual resignation … for now,” he said before the trip to Monaco. Two games in, the threat is there, though. Despite his links to Lyon, Génésio has quickly endeared himself to the Marseille fans. He is the vanilla manager that their fans have previously turned on. How could we forget the ill-fated stint of Marcelino, judged to have lacked that Marseillais fire and hounded out by fans after just seven games.

When Génésio stepped on to the pitch for the warm-up on Sunday night, the Marseille fans behind the tunnel chanted his name. In contrast, when Kondogbia limped back to the tunnel after having been run ragged by Paris Brunner – who scored both of Monaco’s goals – he was booed. One of the club’s top earners, his exit would have given Marseille more room to manoeuvre in the market.

Instead, it could be Igor Paixão, the most talented but also the most bankable asset in the squad, who is sacrificed. The absence of the injured Brazilian was particularly felt on Sunday Quinten Timber, who could yet also depart, filled in. He is not a winger by trade and it showed. “For sure, when we have an absent player, we are significantly weakened,” said Génésio.

Keyliane Abdallah replaced the Dutchman at the break. The academy product, in just his fourth game for the first team, did not prove an upgrade. Marseille are many things but a consistent developer of young talents they are not. That may have to change. That is one of only two solutions. It is preferable to the alternative. The situation has given players such as Himad Abdelli, Angel Gomes, Amine Harit, Derek Cornelius, Neal Maupay and Faris Moumbagna second chances; they have not shown themselves deserving of a reprieve.

Génésio, however, has no choice. Everything at the club is out of obligation, not choice, and always counter to the club’s competitiveness. The value of this side has plummeted over the summer and so have their prospects. Beyond the lack of strength is a glaring lack of depth. Kondogbia is already on the treatment table and the half-time substitute Tochukwu Nnadi did not complete the match either. Playing in the Europa League will stretch their already thin resources even further.

Through all of this, Génésio’s air of calm could be vital. Just as he didn’t get “overexcited” after their 4-0 win over Strasbourg last weekend, he said that there was “no reason to be worried” after the defeat to Monaco.

Silence fell over the Marseille fans inside the Louis II as the game slipped away from them in the second half. Génésio is trying to turn down the volume. Such tactics have previously proven unpopular among the fervent Marseillais. Not this time. Instead, there is tacit acceptance, a resignation, you could say, although that is a word the fans won’t want to hear coming out of Génésio’s mouth again. At a penniless club, he could be their greatest asset.

After years of following his dad around the world, Davide Ancelotti was probably happy the roles were reversed on Friday night. Ancelotti Jr – who has previously served as an assistant to his father – was appointed Lille manager over the summer, his first such role in Europe. Carlo was present at the Stade Pierre Mauroy on the pretext of observing Brazil players Marquinhos, Alexsandro and Lucas Beraldo. The match also happened to be his son’s biggest challenge yet – and against one of Carlo’s former clubs no less – so he could hardly be anywhere else. It proved to be a dramatic night.

As they showed last week, Paris Saint-Germain are not yet up to speed. Having come from 2-0 down to draw with Rennes last weekend, they did the same against Lille. Another sluggish start required another fightback and this one was even more dramatic. Lille took a 2-0 lead when Dilane Bakwa curled a peach of a goal into the top corner, having come off the bench for his debut. It was cruel for Davide Ancelotti, but he is showing promise as he looks to step out of his father’s shadow.

Lyon dropped into the Europa League after losing to Fenerbahce in midweek and, for the first time, Paulo Fonseca is fielding some uncomfortable questions. “I am the best manager in Lyon’s recent history,” said Fonseca. “I won’t say anything else. The numbers are hard to contest.” Their failure to qualify for the Champions League could mean that important players, notably Malick Fofana, leave before the transfer window closes.
