We need to get better at talking about death and grief

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 16:10:54 GMT

Readers respond to Polly Hudson’s article about the things people said to her (or didn’t) after her mother died

I do so agree with Polly Hudson’s piece about how the bereaved are addressed (My mum has died – and there is one kind of response I can’t stand, 26 August). After my teenage daughter was killed in a road traffic accident and I returned to work people would keep asking: “How are you?”. To which the only response could have been: “If you really want to know have you an hour or two to spare?”

The idea that walking down a corridor en route to the office kettle was the venue for any rational response was plainly idiotic. A more thoughtful colleague suggested that I wore a notice around my neck that read: “Terrible, actually, but thanks for asking.”

One colleague got it right when he said: “Good to see you back.” And that’s a line I’ve since used myself. It required no answer from me unless I’d wanted to say something, but acknowledged that there had been an event. The worst I had said to me was: “You’re never asked to bear more than you can carry.” Well, thanks for that. Francis Masserick Ballaugh, Isle of Man

Perhaps Polly Hudson is being a little harsh. Three months after my young son died I returned to work, still crippled by grief, but needing to ease back into “normal” life. A characteristically kind member of staff made the effort to come to my room, welcome me back and offer sympathy. She looked at my dead son’s photo on the desk and suggested I remove it to help me “get over it”. Rather than ridicule her crassness, I explained why that wouldn’t work. Nor were they bad people who avoided me, or didn’t know what to say; they were simply bewildered, not having been in the same dreadful situation. They could not – or dared not – imagine my suffering. They remain friends; losing a friend over this just adds to the sadness, and one day they might be in your shoes.

Surely the better response is to explain. That will help both of you (although to be told “it’s part of God’s plan” can be challenging). Name and address supplied

I’m afraid I have been guilty with a couple of friends of not saying anything because of not knowing what to say. Even to this day I try to avoid them because I feel so awful that I didn’t get in touch to sympathise. I feel awful as I had no idea what to say at the time, and the usual platitudes about deepest sympathies and condolences feel as meaningless to me as it sounds like Polly Hudson finds them to receive.

It’s made more complicated by the fact that I only know about these things because of social media, otherwise I probably wouldn’t know about their loss. Responding on social media to somebody’s loss feels performative. And I’m not sure if that is worse than being nonperformative. Sending a card avoids the subject, but does the job.

It’s hard to know how to talk about death unless you’ve experienced it, but avoiding bringing it up is mortifying and embarrassing. We need to talk about grief more to make it easier all around. Glyn JonesCardiff

I was reminded of my mum’s death and something a good friend said to me outside the church after the funeral mass. His mother had died a year earlier and he approached me with the full knowledge of what I needed to hear. He looked me in the eyes kindly, and gave me a firm hug as he said: “All that can be said is: it’s shit, shit, shit.”Michael O’Rahilly Dublin, Ireland

Polly Hudson’s article made me think about how extraordinarily difficult we find death – not only experiencing the death of someone we love, but knowing how to respond to another person’s grief.

Losing a parent is profoundly painful, whatever our age. But I wonder whether we sometimes expect too much of people trying to comfort us. There are enormous cultural, religious and personal differences in how we speak about death. What sounds like an empty platitude to one person may be a sincere expression of sympathy to another. “Passed away”, “resting”, “my condolences”, “be strong” – these words may feel inadequate, but perhaps that is because words themselves are inadequate.

Even silence or avoidance, painful as it can be, does not necessarily mean indifference. Some people simply don’t know what to say. Others may be frightened of saying the wrong thing, of making the grieving person cry, or perhaps of confronting their own fear of death and loss. Crossing the road to avoid someone who is grieving may seem terribly insensitive, but sometimes human awkwardness and fear can look remarkably like cruelty from the other side.

I have come to believe that when someone reaches out after a death, however clumsily, it is worth looking beyond the words to the intention behind them. Most people are simply trying their best to say: “I see your pain. I care.”

And perhaps there really is no perfect thing to say. When someone we love dies, no combination of words can make the loss smaller. Sometimes all we can offer one another is our presence, our imperfect words and our humanity. Fatima AliRoselands, New South Wales, Australia

Polly Hudson writes about the difficulty people face when trying to find something to say to the bereaved. It is precisely because nothing anyone can say will meet the terrible circumstance that shiva traditions in Judaism – which has a far more extensive system of formulaic language than any Christian faith – prefer you say nothing at all. One enters the home of those sitting shiva to sit with them and to speak only if spoken to. Even though I am not religious, I find the tradition shows a deep understanding of our human inability to speak about death. Tadzio KoelbForest, Belgium

The case of future datacentres demanding more electricity than the entire United Kingdom (Two planned datacentres will have higher UK carbon emissions than ExxonMobil, analysis finds, 25 August) is an example of corporates transferring their problems to society and the electorate. This must not be allowed to happen.

One solution would be to make each datacentre responsible for generating all its own electricity and for reducing its CO2 emissions to zero. These installations will have vast areas of roofing and car parks that could be covered in solar panels, space for wind generation and battery storage, and for emissions scrubbers.

If the corporate response is that this is not possible, that is their problem, not ours. Perhaps some innovation is called for. Richard LammingShaldon, Devon

You report on the cost of a proposed new “hyperscale” datacentre in Havering, east London, in terms of its likely carbon footprint (Proposed London datacentre ‘incompatible’ with net zero with 1m-tonne carbon footprint, 21 August) – though the article doesn’t mention the huge use of water, which seems ironic in a period of drought. Locals and others are quite rightly up in arms about this and indeed many other datacentres that have been built or are under development.

Nevertheless, we should all consider our own culpability here. Datacentres exist because we want to send, receive and store digital communications. Understandable enough, but a huge quantity of digital data is either junk or unnecessary. Research suggests that if each person in this country sent one less “thank-you” email a day, there would be an annual saving of more than 16,000 tonnes of CO2. We can all contribute to reducing and managing the problem. A structure of small charges by the government for digital communications would deter us all from generating junk. We pay to post letters, why not for digital communication?Michael McClellandDevizes, Wiltshire

If AI is so clever, it should be required to design itself datacentres that do not command all our water and energy before we let its oligarchs build. Malcolm FraserEdinburgh

Thriving lichen-loving moth is an exception to the rule

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 16:10:26 GMT

Mark R Shaw says airborne pollutants have caused a massive decline in insect numbers, in response to a Country Diary

Nigel Brown’s understandable joy in finding a rosy footman in his moth trap (Country diary, 25 August) ends with “an important ecological message” that the substantial elimination of airborne sulphur dioxide pollution, which was devastating to the lichens and algae on which caterpillars of footman moths largely feed, has allowed recovery and even geographical spread.

However, what might be a more realistic message is that the balance has changed in our major airborne pollutants since the 1990s, from sulphur dioxide to nitrogen oxides (a byproduct of internal combustion engines, among others), and this has benefited lichens and algae, which thrive under the current regime – and hence also footman moths as a special case.

But environmental pollution from a host of sources is undoubtedly contributing in an ever more disastrous way to the widespread and massive declines in the numbers of most groups of moths and indeed other insects in today’s Britain. It’s OK for footman moths, but they are not a good model. Mark R ShawEdinburgh

Move follows pressure from players’ unions

Fifa has extended worldwide the ban on a former match official and SCR Altach employee found guilty of taking secret videos and photographs of members of the club’s women’s team.

In February, a regional court in Feldkirch, Austria, handed the man a seven-month suspended prison sentence, a €1,200 (£1,046) fine and ordered him to pay the victims €625 (£545) each in compensation after he was found guilty of filming and taking photographs of players, including minors, in the changing room, gym and showers of Altach’s women’s team between 2018 and 2025.

The sentence provoked outrage from former Altach players and more widely in Austria. After a request from the Austrian players’ union (VdF) and the global players’ union Fifpro, the Fifa disciplinary committee extended on 4 August the man’s ban from football-related activities to a global one.

For a toy? Oh yes. That’s what Louis Vuitton’s Doudou Vivienne XL retails for, anyway.

Do say: “Please look after this bear.”

‘Superhuman’ AI tool spots heart disease in less than 2 seconds

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 16:00:29 GMT

Technology trained on millions of routine ECGs could fast-track high-risk patients for treatment

Doctors have developed a “superhuman” AI tool that can spot heart disease in less than two seconds.

The groundbreaking technology has been trained on millions of patients and works by extracting more information from a routine electrocardiogram (ECG) than the human eye can typically see.

The traditional ECG, which records electrical activity in the heart, including the rate and rhythm, has been a vital medical tool in diagnosing heart attacks and abnormal heart rhythms for a century.

But it cannot detect heart disease. That requires an echocardiogram, a type of ultrasound scan, which patients often have to wait months for.

Now a team have developed an AI tool that can spot signs of heart failure and heart valve disease – two of the most common forms of heart disease – from ECG results in “the blink of an eye”.

Details of the breakthrough, which could boost early diagnosis of heart disease, were presented to thousands of delegates at the European Society of Cardiology annual congress in Munich, the world’s largest heart conference.

Early diagnosis is vital for heart failure and heart valve disease, enabling those who need lifesaving medicines to be spotted sooner, before they become dangerously unwell.

The development is being seen as potentially significant, because ECGs are one of the most common tests in medicine, with about a billion performed worldwide each year.

In a trial involving 67,000 patients in the US, the AI tool was able to identify up to 81% of those who had heart failure, and up to 90% of those with heart valve disease.

Dr Sonya Babu-Narayan, a consultant cardiologist and clinical director of the British Heart Foundation (BHF), which funded the trial, said: “It is exciting to see that AI can now deliver a read-out from an ECG in what feels like the blink of an eye.

“Technology like the AI ECG in this research, which has the potential to identify high-risk patients early, will not detect everyone with a heart condition. But it could be a solution to help fast-track the patients who are most likely to have a heart abnormality. When it comes to the heart, earlier diagnosis and treatment saves and improves lives.”

after newsletter promotion

The tech cannot be used on its own to definitively diagnose or rule out heart failure or heart valve disease, but it gives a very strong indication someone may have them.

Someone judged as highly likely to have either could be sent rapidly for an echocardiogram, rather than wait months on the standard waiting lists. That could mean a quicker diagnosis which would enable them to start treatment earlier.

Prof Fu Siong Ng, a professor of cardiology at Imperial College London, said: “Patients can often wait several months for a heart ultrasound scan after being referred for one by their doctor.

“This makes it exciting that our technology could identify patients most at risk of heart failure and heart valve disease, so they could be prioritised for scans faster and more urgently.”

The aim of the tool is to speed up diagnosis of those suspected to have heart failure or heart valve disease. But Ng said it could also prove lifesaving by spotting signs of the conditions in people who may have undergone an ECG for different reasons.

“Another potential application of this AI model is to opportunistically diagnose heart failure and heart valve disease in whom these conditions are not suspected,” he said. “The AI model could be run on all ECGs done in a hospital to flag those at highest risk of these diseases, so that they can be diagnosed earlier.”

Dr Ahmed El-Medany, a BHF clinical research fellow, who led the Imperial College London analysis, described the tool as a “superhuman AI” and said the next challenge would be to design handheld AI-led ECG readers for healthcare professionals to use.

Delegates in Munich also heard how AI-based analysis of facial videos could rapidly and accurately detect undiagnosed high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes.

Researchers at the University of Tokyo and the Institute of Science Tokyo said AI analysis of five-second facial videos could hep improve diagnosis. Millions of people who have high blood pressure or type 2 diabetes do not know they have the conditions.

Why are prisons overcrowded? Because no government will stand up to the tabloids

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 15:58:41 GMT

Whatever happens to the early release scheme, Andy Burnham needs to consider the possibility that sentences are just too high

Prisons in England and Wales are full because sentences have increased, and everybody knows this. Lord chief justices know this – four of them said it outright in a report for the Howard League two years ago – ministers know it, and anyone who can count knows it. The prison population in England and Wales was 40,000 in 1991, 88,000 in 2024 and is estimated to hit 105,000 by 2028. Every government promises to increase capacity; no government this century has been able to do that fast enough to cope with the numbers.

One prisons inspector, lamenting conditions that were creating unacceptably high levels of violence, said: “The bath was in danger of overflowing, and they either had to turn the taps off or they had to let some water out.” But the taps have not been turned off, the bigger baths (new, often private jails) have been offset by existing baths (old Victorian prisons) disintegrating, and as soon as a government found the energy and maturity to let some water out – in the form of the early release scheme – it immediately hit the wall of tabloid outrage that created this problem in the first place.

The fact is that Andy Burnham can press ahead with the early release scheme; he can create problematic caveats; he can overturn indeterminate sentencing, the measure created in 2003 whereby prisoners could spend years over their tariff in prison because the onus was now on them to prove they weren’t dangerous (which is quite difficult to do from prison, and more difficult still from a failing one). Or he can not do any of these things. But he won’t get a grip on the problem until he allows the possibility that sentences are too high for stupid reasons. The act of murder hasn’t changed in 100 years (or 1,000). There is nothing to stop a prime minister bringing sentences back down to where they were in the 90s.

“Tough on crime” is a very easy win, politically speaking: it makes you sound like a firm leader, without having an impact on any ordinary person’s life, except in a good way, and you can modify to it to the right (by being tougher still on crime) and to the left (by also being tough on the causes of crime). This puts you at the mercy, however, of people for whom there is no tough enough. There will always be a murder so heinous that the maximum existing imprisonment doesn’t feel like enough; there will always be a comparison ready that if x violent act warranted four years behind bars, how can y merit only three and a half? There will always be people who blankly do not see the point of parole, believing it to be somehow an insult to the expectations of victims, because they have never engaged with its purpose. When you can’t decide when or what to eat and how often to shower, the principle that you will be released sooner if you cooperate is an important buffer between you and the abyss, without which prison populations are hard to manage. You really have to be yelling “Life should mean life” at the top of your voice not to understand this but, regrettably, some people always will be.

The purpose of prison itself has always been threefold – punishment, public protection and rehabilitation – which is completely understood except by those who choose not to understand it. Those aims can all be met only if they are complementary. If prisons can’t rehabilitate because they are overcrowded and violent, the public will not be protected when prisoners are released. If the deprivation of freedom is not seen as punishment enough, if only cruel conditions count, then the chances of returning prisoners to society as better-adjusted, more stable people are reduced to nil. Those who argue for a more humane approach in prisons are always painted as living in a fantasy land, while the direct opposite is the case: people who want ever-lengthening sentences in the harshest possible conditions are the fantasists, since they leave us all with only two options, both of them absurd – return prisoners to society as dangerous as before, or keep them inside for ever.

Burnham knows all this; Keir Starmer knew it; even Liz Truss, as justice minister in 2017, sabre-rattling that early release wasn’t the answer, knew it. Tony Blair and David Blunkett knew it in 2003, when they introduced statutory starting points for murder – never again would a lenient judge give them a comms headache on a slow news day. Successive governments have tried to make law to satisfy the tabloids, but they are never satiated, only emboldened.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

Nepal rescuers race to reach hundreds feared trapped in hydropower tunnels

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 15:56:31 GMT

Workers thought to be stuck in underground areas at 11 sites after last week’s devastating flash floods

Rescue teams are working to reach more than 900 missing hydropower workers, hundreds of whom are feared trapped in the tunnels and underground areas of 12 hydropower projects in Nepal after the devastating flash floods, ​the ⁠country’s disaster ​management authority has said.

The death toll from the ⁠unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud ​and debris on Wednesday last week has risen to 939 people, with 16 more dead reported in Tibet. More than 4,400 are missing on the two sides of the border.

About 500 of the missing hydropower workers at projects damaged by the flooding in Nepal’s Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts are thought to be trapped in tunnels built to control the flow of water.

As rescue efforts drag on, experts fear the chances of finding survivors in tunnels are diminishing as oxygen levels fall.

Some workers called for help when flooding started on Wednesday and those who had managed to escape tunnels said many of their colleagues were still trapped, said Mohan Kumar Dangi, the president of the Nepal Independent Power Producers’ Association.

Rescue efforts have been complicated by difficult terrain, persistently high flood waters and difficult weather. With more than 40 bridges destroyed, rescuers are relying on helicopters, while India and China are sending prefabricated truss bridges to help restore access.

The swollen Trishuli River has also continued to change course unpredictably, making planning a challenge. Areas that were dry one day are flooded the next, and further floods are a constant concern.

Hundreds of bodies, many unidentified, that were swept down the mountains by the torrent, have been buried in shallow graves after DNA testing on the plains ⁠of the Himalayan region.

Nepali officials said on Monday that the focus was on reaching the 933 people missing from ‌hydropower plants. “A large amount of debris has been deposited and that is posing us a big challenge to open the tunnels,” the Nepal army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told Reuters.

About 250 people were rescued from the Upper Trishuli hydroelectric project over the weekend, and army engineers began blasting operations at the site to rescue another 42 workers thought be missing.

The damage to hydropower infrastructure is estimated to have taken 700 megawatts out of service, about 10% of the country’s power capacity. Pictures and videos shared by rescue teams ⁠showed earth-moving equipment shovelling mud to try to reach the tunnels.

Ashish Gurung, who normally works as a guide, was among the rescuers. “There is just mud everywhere,” he said. “Inside the tunnel it was worse. It’s so difficult to move, the mud is so deep.”

His team was trying to access the Chilime hydropower plant in Rasuwa, one of the worst-hit areas. At least eight people are believed missing there, and an Indian team is working alongside the Nepali army using pumps and excavators to locate them.

The Nepali prime minister, Balendra Shah, said rescue efforts were “challenging due to adverse weather, difficult terrain and ongoing risks.”

Gurung said mountaineers were improvising by using planks of wood to check the depth of the mud, before using them as makeshift bridges along with a system of ropes to keep themselves safe.

“Walking in it is very difficult, at one point it was up to our chests,” he said. “We got close to the first station, about 130 metres in. Inside that far … it looked like it was just bodies.”

The hydropower company had given his team a map and it looked as if there was a chance people in the tunnels could have survived. “They have a safe area inside,” he said. “Some of them could potentially be alive. I am hoping they are alive.”

The Red Cross estimates that more than 93,000 people have been affected by the disaster, heightening fears that the climate crisis is destabilising the geology of mountain and polar regions.

Shah said the flood was an “unprecedented and devastating natural disaster” and that it was difficult to compile a complete assessment of the damage.

“Despite the adverse weather, difficult terrain and continuing risks, we are moving forward with determination to save the lives of our citizens,” he said in a Facebook post late on Sunday. Almost 21,000 security personnel were involved in the rescue operations alongside civilian workers and volunteers, he said.

Whole communities had been destroyed by the flooding, leaving families homeless in heavy rain.

“There are no roads, they have all been washed away, and many areas are just not accessible,” said a police officer coordinating rescue efforts in Nuwakot district. “It is very difficult for my men. The area is still flooded, and elsewhere it is all marshland.”

Nepal’s disaster agency said on Monday it had counted 903 deaths, with 4,793 people, including 592 foreigners, missing. Chinese authorities had reported 16 deaths and 546 people missing as of Sunday. State media said 261 of the missing were foreigners, including more than 100 Nepalis.

Among those missing are more than 30 British nationals. On Saturday, a rapid deployment team from the UK arrived in Nepal to support Britons and their families. The UK government has given a £5m support package to assist Nepal in its disaster response.

Amid the soaring toll of death and missing was some hope. On Monday, rescuers pulled a six-year-old girl out of mud after hearing crying. “Her body was trapped in mud, but her head was outside,” the Nepali armed police spokesperson Netra Bahadur Karki told Agence France-Presse.

China’s state-run CCTV said Beijing had mobilised more than 2,100 rescue workers and allocated at least ​220m yuan (£24m) to support relief efforts and had been airdropping equipment and supplies to frontline rescuers, while its soldiers used life-detection equipment to look for the missing.

Nepal has said it does not need foreign help in general search and rescue operations, but it has leaned on its neighbours, India and China, for their expertise in tunnel rescues.

Rescue operations have been suspended several times since Friday because of bad weather and concerns that a lake formed across the Nepal-China border by the disaster could trigger fresh flooding after it began overflowing into Nepal’s rivers.

The weather was good on Monday, however, and rescue ⁠work picked up pace, said Narendra Pariyar, the district administrator of Rasuwa, one of the two hardest-hit districts.

In the holy ​town of Devighat on the banks of the Trishuli, residents walked around the shells of what had once been ​homes, trying to salvage their belongings from the debris.

The flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming”, CCTV reported, saying ​it was a “new and prominent feature of cryosphere ‌disasters” on the Tibetan plateau.

Two ​Nepali officials said China had ​not shared much information on glacier risks and water levels after a meeting to strengthen cooperation earlier this year, and they feared that could hamper future disaster preparedness.

China’s foreign ministry said Beijing had continuously provided Nepal with meteorological and hydrological data and will continue to “strongly support” Nepal’s disaster relief efforts and safeguard the two countries’ common interests.

Kyiv suffers hours of daytime air raids as Russia deploys new jet-powered drones

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 15:48:20 GMT

Volodymyr Zelenskyy says about 800 Shahed drones fired into Ukraine in four days in effort to ‘wear down’ country

Kyiv is enduring hours of daytime air raids and air raid warnings as Russia has fired 800 jet-powered drones into Ukraine in four days, using the faster weapons to sustain prolonged waves of attacks

The new-model Shahed drones have a cruising speed of 200mph to 250mph , about double the 115mph achieved by the piston-engine version and beyond the speed of Ukraine’s cheap interceptors, making them harder to stop.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s president, said on Sunday that the jet-powered models now accounted for more than half the drones used by Russia to attack and “wear down” the country.

“There were almost 1,500 drones of all types in these four days alone – about 800 of them jet-powered,” the president said. Ukraine was currently relying on combat aircraft to shoot them down, he added.

A Geran-4, the latest jet-powered model, struck an ammunition dump at Myla, a village 15 miles west of Kyiv on Thursday. Thirty-eight people were killed as the strike unleashed hours of secondary explosions in one of the deadliest single attacks of the war, destroying warehouses and damaging nearby homes.

Russia has also made heavy use of the drones in waves of daytime attacks in the past five days, leading to hours of air alerts, particularly in Kyiv. Eight air raid alerts sounded in Kyiv by lunchtime on Monday.

Daytime attacks, although far from unknown, were uncommon previously, prompting some businesses to halt operations until the alert had passed, and leaving residents with the decision of whether to remain indoors, seek shelter, or ignore the warnings entirely.

Close drone threats also force emergency services to leave an attack site, potentially worsening the impact of any fire caused by a hit, as happened when a food storage facility was struck in Boryspil, to the east of Kyiv, earlier this month.

Kremlin forces have attacked warehouses around Kyiv in the past month, in retaliation to a Ukrainian campaign targeting the Wildberries and Ozon distribution chains inside Russia. The attacks have led to food shortages in the shops, but a Ukrainian official urged people not to panic.

Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy on defence technology, urged people “do not give in to rumours, misinformation, and panic” and said that companies were rebuilding supply chains in response to the attacks. “We will not die of hunger,” he wrote in a social media posting.

Shahed drones, with a distinctive delta wing, were originally designed in Iran, and the technology transferred to Russia. The jet Shahed, the 238, was first unveiled by Iran in autumn 2023, and appeared in Ukraine shortly after.

It was not until spring that Russia began to manufacture and deploy its latest jet-powered variant – the Geran-4 – in numbers. Russia now makes more jet-powered drones than the original piston-engined variants, in two models, the delta winged Geran-4 and the Geran-5, which looks like a missile with wings.

Beskrestnov said that at least 2,500 of the jet drones had been launched into Ukraine during August, up from 1,500 the month before. Production date stamps found on the bodywork suggest they are being fired within days after being made at a factory in Yelabuga, he added.

Ukraine had successfully devised a range of low-cost ground-launched interceptors fast enough to eliminate a piston-engined Shahed, raising interception rates to above 90%. Over the weekend, the president said that level had to be maintained into the autumn.

Engineers are now racing to make faster interceptor drones able to knock out jet-powered Shaheds, though details are scant. “Four companies have developed the relevant interceptor drones, and one company has the most successful technology,” Zelenskky said.

Reading and Leeds festival review – post-GCSE blowout shows how dominant dance music now is

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 15:45:20 GMT

Bramham Park, LeedsCharli xcx and Fontaines DC are spellbinding and there’s an awesome array of genres, but the biggest turnouts are for tech house names like Kettama and Josh Baker

Charli xcx, Reading festival review – Pretentious? Just a bit. But Nietzsche would have loved it

Reading and Leeds festival will probably always be a post-GCSE rite of passage: a gleefully riotous taste of freedom before having to make actual life decisions. But the sibling events have been struggling for a sense of identity beyond this, particularly post-Covid. In 2025, the festival decided to theme days based on genre, which felt out of touch – but, this year, organisers have decided to tackle gen Z’s borderless approach head on. There are new stages, such as the chandelier-adorned Ballroom, and overall the lineup is wonderfully mazy.

On the festival’s second stage, you can catch everything from UK underground rap selector DJ EJ, warbly US rockers Geese, and raw, live-drummed jungle from 4am Kru. “I dedicate this one to all the bad bitches from small places. Let’s make a song about the bad bitches from Leeds,” Slovakian pop star Adéla gleefully giggles during her own set here, before launching into neon-streaked megahit Ain’t in LA. In a ping-ponging journey across styles, other highlights include London singer Dexter in the Newsagent’s blue-skied bedroom pop, Australian artist Mall Grab’s Game Boy grime beats and Bar Italia’s insouciant rock, which is significantly more fun and dance-y than their recent lukewarm album reviews might suggest.

Thursday is headlined by a tired-sounding Kasabian, who don’t move a crowd of kids that, for good reason, would much rather be at LS23, the trippy dance stage in the woods. Chase and Status’ festival-sized drum’n’bass scratches that dance itch as Friday’s main stage headliner, while Charli xcx (reviewed in full here) and Fontaines DC are a spellbinding double bill on Saturday. The latter play new material from their forthcoming album Dopamine Chamber, including beguiling single Marianne, and an unreleased new track called Happy for You – it’s driven by a Sundays-sounding guitar line and a peppy rimshot, but moves with melancholy, the band members’ features obscured against a humming green light onstage. Their set is the best from a guitar band all weekend.

Another new stage, the Canopy, replaces the BBC Introducing stage at both festivals and is a showcase of new artists curated by Festival Republic, who are majority owned by Live Nation – it has been dubbed the “nepo baby” stage for platforming the offspring of Dave Grohl, Liam Gallagher and the Beckhams. For the most part, the programming is disastrously bad, and the stage is underattended until festivalgoers can catch a perfunctory glimpse of someone semi-famous. Then it swarms, making sets look like a moment that doesn’t actually exist from the outside, and to the detriment of other artists who would benefit from not being juxtaposed with celebrities’ kids. The two best acts are young alt-rock four-piece Tooth and brilliantly talented singer Sade Olutola, and yet they only get 20-minute opening slots on the Saturday and Sunday.

If Reading and Leeds can be defined by anything this past year, it is young people’s ongoing affinity for tech house DJs like Josh Baker, Omar+, Max Dean and Luke Dean; Irish producer Kettama’s set is one of the most packed-out of the weekend. These artists play perfectly engineered going-out music, with chantable vocal samples and mixes that build and change a little too fast, like doomscrolling in audio form.

The dance music is mainly on the Warehouse stage, which is not unlike a mockup of Manchester’s Warehouse Project, and is where the most crowd energy is directed across the weekend. Issues with overcrowding mean that Silva Bumpa and a Skepta b2b with East End Dubs are cancelled, with calls online for Reading and Leeds to recognise the popularity of dance and move it to bigger stages. Baker clashes with Dave on Sunday, and despite cameos from Kano, Tems and Central Cee, the Dave crowd is by far the most sparse out of all the headliners.

You can really see Reading and Leeds’ transformation at Hedex’s set, when the drum’n’bass DJ drops a mix that begins with a sped-up version of Nirvana’s Smells Like Teen Spirit. There’s a slight bit of confusion at a tune that once embodied this festival. Still, the crowd join in singing the verse, before Hedex pulverises the track to the same effect as the distorted drop in the original and everyone’s back to dancing with that same immediacy, that same teenage freedom.

Argentina’s Lionel Messi retires from international football: ‘This hurts me a lot’

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 15:19:13 GMT

Argentina great’s last game was in World Cup final

Player’s father Jorge died earlier in August

Lionel Messi has announced his retirement from international football seven weeks after Argentina were beaten by Spain in the World Cup final in the US. The 39-year-old captained Argentina to World Cup glory in 2022 and two Copa América titles after winning his first cap in 2005.

On Monday, Messi posted a picture on Instagram of notes that he wrote on 21 July, two days after the World Cup final, confirming he was ending his Argentina career and said the death of his father, Jorge, in early August made him feel “more convinced than before”. Messi was often visibly emotional during the tournament and revealed in the knockout stages that Jorge was undergoing medical treatment.

Messi’s statement, addressed to Argentina fans, read: “After the time that has passed since the final, thinking a lot, I want to let everyone know that I am retiring from the national team. It is a decision that hurts my soul but I know it is time. I can say for sure that I always gave everything, not only in the last few years when we won everything [but] before as well, and I always fought and gave everything for the shirt, to give you joy and make you proud of being Argentinian through football.

“There’s not long left and chapters are coming to an end – and this is one that hurts me a lot. I love, have loved and I will always love being part of the national team. I have emptied myself: now I have nothing more to give and, besides, there are great young players coming through who deserve to be [selected].”

Messi thanked his family for accompanying him on a “beautiful but difficult journey”. He previously announced his retirement from international football in 2016 after Argentina lost on penalties to Chile in the 2016 Copa América final – at the time his fourth defeat in a major final out of four. The then Barcelona forward was often criticised for not producing his club form at international level and comparisons were constantly made with the World Cup-winning Diego Maradona. However, Messi was persuaded to continue and finally lifted silverware with his country at the 2021 Copa América in Brazil.

“I take with me unforgettable memories and moments,” his statement said. After victory against Brazil at the Maracanã in the 2021 Copa América final, Messi was central to Argentina’s first World Cup triumph since 1986 and scored in every knockout round in Qatar, including twice in the final against France – two years after the death of Maradona.

Argentina defended their Copa América title in 2024 amid speculation that Messi, by then playing for Inter Miami, would call it a day. He turned 39 during the World Cup this summer, briefly becoming the tournament’s all-time record scorer before being overtaken by Kylian Mbappé.

His statement finished by returning to address Argentina fans: “I go with the satisfaction and the pride of having, along with my teammates, giving you moments we dreamed about. I love you! I thank God for making me Argentinian.”

Messi retires as Argentina’s record appearance maker – he won the first of his 207 caps in a friendly against Hungary in August 2005 and was sent off almost immediately for catching Vilmos Vanczak with an elbow. He is also Argentina’s record scorer with 125 goals. Before playing for the senior team, he won the Under-20 World Cup and also won Olympic gold in 2008.

Since the end of his sixth World Cup, Messi has featured seven times for Inter Miami and scored four goals in the 7-1 rout of Montreal in Major League Soccer on Saturday. Messi signed a contract extension last year to 2028, when he will be 41.

A job that changed me: Being a theatre usher cracked open my heart to beauty

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 15:00:29 GMT

The performances often gave me goose bumps, but I also got to observe the highs and lows of audience behaviour

Read more in this series here

I was 24, had just moved into a share house I couldn’t afford, and my job as a nanny was proving less than ideal. I’d graduated from my music degree a few years prior and was floating along, feeling a little lost.

A friend had told me to apply to become a front-of-house staff member at Australia’s busiest performing arts centre, Arts Centre Melbourne. It was a rare opportunity, as people rarely quit. To be surrounded by art again sounded like a dream.

I progressed to the final interview round. Anxious about nailing it and unable to study for it – for some unknown reason, a maths quiz was involved – I focused purely on appearance. I blew my budget on a blow wave, planning to charm the interviewers with my perfect hair and Target office-casual best.

Whether it was my hair or the secret texts to my friend asking for help answering the maths quiz, I got the job.

My first shift was inside door 1 of the centre’s State Theatre. It was the easiest place to avoid royally stuffing things up, and I could be kept under close supervision. I watched Madama Butterfly from my little fold-down seat, goose bumps exploding all over my body. I had never had any interest in opera and, apart from being an unwilling audience to my grandfather’s car DJ set – which consisted entirely of opera – I had rarely listened to it. But watching these incredible performers in a historic theatre, I felt like a wide-eyed kid discovering music for the first time.

From there I ricocheted around theatres, learning the labyrinth under the complex’s famous spire. I saw Summer of the Seventeenth Doll no fewer than 17 times; I savoured spine-tingling performances by the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra. When my box seat patrons didn’t show up, I cried alone in my section during the Australian Ballet’s production of Arvo Pärt’s Spiegel im Spiegel. Boyband Human Nature got audience members, of all ages, dancing out of their seats – to this day, their show is one of the best performances I’ve seen.

I also saw the highs and lows of patron behaviour. I thought of the audience as my precious babies, albeit ones I could watch from a distance with love and fascination. I saw a little girl’s first ballet concert; a grown man who, when I said he couldn’t take his ice-cream in, angrily threw his unwrapped Magnum in the bin; a woman, breathless after a coughing fit, graciously accepting that she couldn’t return to the show she’d been so looking forward to because of the door policy. People came as they were – joyful, messy, broken, hopeful, and I relished the hours of people-watching.

A few years into the job, I was stationed outside the door of an over-the-top musical when I met a fellow usher who would become my best friend. Within minutes of meeting Stef, we were dancing all over the empty foyer, recreating our version of Chess. We bonded over our feminism and anxiety, and she later became one of my bridesmaids. My kids now call her Aunty Steffy.

I’ve never felt safer in a workplace, despite the dark corridors and hidden spaces.

Many colleagues were also queer artists who took their ushering jobs seriously, while also having fun on the job. Looking back, having lived and experienced life and now nearing 40, that place felt like a cradle. Being an usher cracked open my heart to the beauty of humans experiencing art and I had the privilege of watching along with them.

The law won’t save us from Meta’s ‘pervert glasses’. The only solution is mockery

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 14:56:47 GMT

These things are undermining not just our public spaces but the very nature of being human. Let’s shame them off the streets

So far I am yet to be tempted into purchasing a pair of Ray-Ban Meta glasses. To a certain extent this is a function of possessing a large, misshapen and comically convex head upon which no pair of sunglasses has ever looked remotely appropriate. Nor am I one of those consumers who professes to be “really into gadgets”, a preference I’ve always found weirdly unspecific. It’s subtly telling when people claim to be into “gadgets”, because they’re never talking about, say, a tin opener. What they really mean is something gimmicky and expensive that almost certainly requires the services of a datacentre and enough water to irrigate Kent.

And even if I were to surmount these two obstacles, you then get into the ethics of the thing. I’m nobody’s idea of a PR expert, but if your shiny new product keeps requiring patches and updates to prevent people from using it to do degenerate things to women, perhaps it might be worth walking it back to the research and development stage.

Of course, Meta has no intention of doing anything quite so dignified or responsible as that. The prospect that users of its new glasses might wish to film people covertly and without consent appears not to have occurred to one of the world’s leading tech companies. Nor the possibility that owners might try to disable or cover up the little LED that displays when the camera is recording. Instead, the company has embarked on a publicity blitz, reassuring us all that our privacy is, if not quite their number one priority, then certainly there or thereabouts.

But unlike most items of consumer tech, smart glasses are not the sort of thing to which one can simply opt in or out. These things are already out there – around nine million from Meta alone – scanning our streets, capturing and processing content, blurring the boundaries between the real and the virtual.

Unlike security cameras, they are not fixed but mobile, arbitrary and largely unregulated. They raise issues that go far deeper than a piece of overpriced eyewear, deeper even than the dense thicket of technology and regulation, into the most basic questions of how we treat each other, how societies function. Specifically: what happens to our shared public spaces when we are forced to confront the presumption that we are all being filmed, broadcast, processed? What happens to our cities? What happens to our trust, our bonds, our relationships with our fellow humans?

Much of the current concern over smart glasses has understandably focused on the lurid and the macabre: the creeps and the perverts, the changing room voyeurs, the internet pranksters and school bullies. But while any new technology will attract its share of malign actors, nefarious intent is not in fact a prerequisite to harm.

Simply put, the very act of filming somebody without their permission – for whatever purpose – is in itself a form of violation, perhaps even of theft. On a philosophical level, it is the blithe assertion of one person’s liberty and rights over those of another. On a political level, it expresses an asymmetry of power, a very capitalistic form of resource extraction. It strips the unsuspecting individual of agency and mines them for content.

And yes, we have long been bleakly aware of the surveillance apparatus around us: traffic cameras, security cameras, personalised ads, some bored lad at GCHQ with a list of keywords and access to the emails of everybody you know. But Kylie Jenner isn’t posing suggestively on the A46 trying to sell you a speed camera. Wearables, by their very nature, straddle the realms of fashion and culture, and are thus the perfect vehicle for reimagining the public panopticon, the AI training zoo, as a kind of chic lifestyle choice.

For the same reason, legislative fixes – inevitably reactive rather than proactive – only get us so far. Denmark recently introduced an innovative copyright law granting citizens ownership of their own likeness, which mostly covers deepfakes and AI-generated imitations. But who realistically has the time and will to trawl the entire internet for illicitly procured content? In any case, by the time it’s up, it’s up, and by a similar logic the tech giants have long operated under a praxis of launching first and dealing with the fallout later.

Which is why social stigma remains one of the most powerful weapons. The increasingly pervasive deployment of the term “pervert glasses” is a decent start, but other perfectly good slurs remain unclaimed: Stalker Specs, Nonce Goggles, Depraviators. Above all the ridicule must be merciless and unstinting, a ritual shaming entirely in proportion to the magnitude of deviance.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

But of course, even if society succeeds in killing the Meta glasses, others will surely learn and follow. Samsung and Google are launching their own glasses later this year. Apple’s effort will probably emerge sometime in 2027. And perhaps the thing few have considered is who – with the exception of the partially sighted, hard of hearing and those otherwise in need of assistive technology – asked for any of this? If smart glasses are the answer, what was the question? Perhaps, as with AI chatbots and fridges with web browsers, there was none: just the lavishly funded persistence of a tech sector intent on manufacturing consent for the things it has decided we must have.

In so doing, it may succeed in turning the high street into an unwitting hub of surveillance. A society fearful of itself, paranoid and mistrustful. A public sphere exposed and disassembled and reduced to its constituent pixels. Where there is no longer a right to be anonymous, to be inattentive, to be forgotten or left alone by our fellow citizens. Where something as simple and innocent as a human gaze has been reimagined as an item of transaction.

Jonathan Liew is a Guardian columnist

Sign up for our free newsletter here

Two Premier League games played for Chelsea under Xabi Alonso: two wins and seven goals scored. It’s the sort of start that would delight many new managers – only two other clubs can boast about a six-point start this Premier League season (albeit with Arsenal to play later on Monday). Points gained in this odd transitional phase, when almost nobody seems quite ready, could prove extremely valuable come the end of the season. And yet, for all the attacking potency, there must also be concerns about Chelsea’s openness and the five goals conceded.

Context must also be considered, and it projects both ways. It’s early in the season. There has been, as ever, a lot of change at Chelsea. They will get better; they will achieve greater coherence. But equally there has to be a sense of realism about the nature of the teams they’ve played. Brighton may have thrashed a shambolic Aston Villa 4-0 last weekend, but they were missing seven frontline players at Stamford Bridge and still put three past Chelsea on Sunday. And while Fulham looked very lively as Chelsea won 3-2 on the opening weekend, they couldn’t muster a shot on target against Sunderland on Sunday.

How good are Brighton? Were Villa just terrible on that first weekend? Was it really just Granit Xhaka’s appeal for Sunderland to be themselves again that made a side that had lost at Ipswich capable of dominating Fulham through midfield? It’s very hard at this stage to trace any patterns, other than perhaps to say that Xhaka’s performance against Fulham showed why Chelsea wanted to sign him in the summer.

The systems are different, so the comparison perhaps isn’t entirely fair, but Xhaka, and his midfield partner Noah Sadiki, offered a level of control that Chelsea under Alonso have so far been entirely lacking – striking, given the degree of control Enzo Maresca insisted upon as manager last season. Both Chelsea games so far have felt almost like a pastiche of the modern Bundesliga: all high tempo and turnovers, chaotic and fun and slightly unserious.

This is not how it’s meant to be. Alonso’s Bayer Leverkusen side, in which Xhaka was partnered in central midfield by one of Robert Andrich, Aleix García, or Exequiel Palacios, won the Bundesliga in 2024 conceding only 24 goals in 34 league games. They averaged 59.5% possession, whereas Chelsea so far this season have had just 32%. Perhaps when Moisés Caicedo returns to fitness – he managed 14 minutes from the bench on Sunday before being forced off again – his energy and mobility will bring an immediate improvement, but the way both Fulham and Brighton have at times sliced through Chelsea suggests there are structural issues.

The usual criticism of the 3-4-2-1 formation used by Chelsea is that it is too blockish, that creativity comes almost entirely from the two inside-forwards, making the side playing it predictable if they dominate possession. Its usage, at least in the Premier League, tends to have been as a counterattacking system – this is how, for instance, Oliver Glasner deployed it at Crystal Palace over the last two seasons. Two holding players operating in front of a back three should provide the trapezoid shape that has become the default for sides hoping to guard against the counter. Yet with Roméo Lavia alongside either Reece James or Malo Gusto, that solidity has been lacking.

Why, then, is Alonso’s system suffering the opposite problem? The issue really stems from a positive: Alonso’s 3-4-2-1 is not the blockish formation often seen. Rather it is a basis from which multiple variations stem. It has a variety that helps overcome a potential over-reliance on the two inside-forwards. That’s how, for instance, center back Maxence Lacroix ended up bursting through to set up a goal against Fulham. Breaking the lines and varying the pattern is part of the pattern.

The defensive concerns predate Alonso. It’s been 18 games since Chelsea last kept a clean sheet, their longest run in the top flight since 1961. While the signing of Emí Martínez should give them a more assertive, less error-prone figure in goal than Robert Sánchez in goal, there will be issues, at least in the short term, in getting the balance right at full-back. Plus, defences are best when they are stable, when interactions become automatic; while Lacroix is the sort of central defender Chelsea have been short of and will almost certainly make them better in the long term, and while Josh Acheampong, who played well against Fulham and came off the bench against Brighton, looks a hugely promising presence (he started only eight league games last season); incorporating both of them while adapting to a new goalkeeper will take time. There is a cost to the constant churn at Chelsea.

after newsletter promotion

Arsenal, next Sunday, will provide a far stiffer test. Chelsea’s front three of João Pedro, Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer give them a puncher’s chance, but there is a chance Arsenal render them irrelevant by dominating the game through the midfield. They are two teams at very different stages of their development.

100 ultramarathons in 100 days: former rugby pro hit by brain injury nears end of feat

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 14:00:26 GMT

David ‘Jacko’ Jackson has aimed to raise awareness of brain injuries, with fellow runners sharing their stories

The key for David “Jacko” Jackson is to take each stage nice and gently. “It’s not about running fast,” he said. “It’s more like the hare and tortoise story. Slow and steady – and do it again tomorrow.”

So far, so good. Jackson, a former professional rugby player who retired after a traumatic brain injury, is nearing the end of an extraordinary bid to run 100 ultramarathons (50km, or about 30 miles) in 100 consecutive days.

He began from his home in north Wales in May and, if all goes well, will finish back there, at Caernarfon Castle, on Saturday (5 September).

Jackson’s run has taken in Scotland and England, and he has been joined by more than 700 people, aged eight to in their 80s, who have run alongside him. He has used seven pairs of shoes.

“I should be feeling tired now,” said Jackson, 44, when the Guardian caught up with him in south Wales. “But I’m getting excited about getting to the end and, hopefully, making a bit of a difference.”

Jackson is raising money for the brain injury charities Headway and Head for Change, but the idea is also about drawing attention to the issue and hearing people’s experiences.

“All the way through, the highlights have been the people,” he said. “We’ve been to some really cool conversations.

“When you’re running side by side, people tend to share a lot. So many people have things they wanted to talk about. Some were excited because they’ve overcome something, others were in the midst of something really horrible but find running a great way to … keep them sane. People tell you some really, like, deep stuff.”

Jackson’s rugby career ended abruptly in 2013 due to a traumatic brain injury and seizure on the pitch during a training session. For months, he experienced symptoms including fatigue, sensitivity to light and cognitive issues.

When he recovered, he became a strength and conditioning coach and became interested in breathing techniques and then running. “Running is quite rhythmical and your breathing when it’s good is rhythmical. Running is a great way to train better breathing patterns and habits,” he said.

Jackson also became fascinated in the “marathon monks” of Japan, who train for years and run huge distances in search of enlightenment.

He set off on this challenge intending to do two marathons a day, but suffered a leg injury on day 14 in the Lake District. “I’d done 26 marathons in 13 days and the wheels fell off. I was hobbling, crying my eyes out. I was in pain and felt like a letdown.”

His wife, Catherine, who acts as his physio, nutritionist and logistics supremo, encouraged him to keep going. “The mindset was, if I can move, we’ll keep going until I can’t. If we manage to complete that leg, then we’ll try and do the same thing tomorrow. It sounds really cheesy, but it was one step at a time.”

The injury eased and Jackson was able to keep going, though he tweaked the challenge from two marathons a day to one ultramarathon.

The support vehicle is the couple’s camper van, where they prepare many of Jackson’s meals and drinks. Making sure he has enough fluids on board has been vital as he ran through the summer’s heatwaves.

Post-it notes are dotted around the van with inspiration and questioning messages including: “We choose our attitude”, “Is this a reaction or a choice?” and “Greatest ever comeback”.

Catherine Jackson said it had been an adventure. She thought people opened up to Jackson because he was prepared to make himself vulnerable by sharing his story. “Other people seem to follow suit. When he’s low, someone comes along with fresh energy or shares a heartfelt story that he gets locked into and it makes him keep moving.”

The couple have mainly slept in the camper van, but along the way well-wishers have offered them more roomy accommodation, cooked them meals and helped them with washing. “People have been very kind,” Catherine said.

Being away from home for so long has been a challenge. David said: “We’ve unplugged from society. We have no idea what’s going on. Which has been quite nice.”

He has not shaved during the run and has an impressive beard that brings to mind a famous movie runner – Forrest Gump.

“A few people have shouted ‘Run Forrest, run’ at me. It wasn’t intentional. You don’t look at yourself much in the mirror when you’re doing something like this and in any spare moment you’re eating or doing recovery. But the beard has become almost a symbol of how far I’ve run, so it’s staying for now.”

South African airline defends dramatic low-level flyby before rugby union clash

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 13:44:39 GMT

Cape Town stunt sparks major debate over safety risks

Airlink insists flyby conducted according to regulations

A pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets flying dramatically low over a stadium in South Africa drew huge cheers from the estimated crowd of 56,000 people, but also sparked a major debate over safety risks. The flyby by two Embraer jets, operated by the local airline Airlink, happened on Saturday before the second rugby union Test between South Africa and New Zealand in Cape Town.

The flight tracking service Flightradar24 estimated that the lead jet passed just 41-46 feet (12-14 metres) above the roof of Cape Town Stadium, with the crowd and the world’s top-ranked rugby teams below. The second jet, which was very close behind, flew through a cloud of pink dust that shot up from the stadium roof as part of the show.

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Airlink, a sponsor of the South Africa rugby union team, said the flyby was conducted according to safety regulations. The airline said that it was carefully planned and rehearsed, with the aircraft flying at 150 knots (172 mph), when they went over the stadium. Each jet had three senior captains on board, Airlink said, operating in the roles of a commander, a co-pilot and a safety officer. The jets were not carrying any passengers.

“Airlink notes the concerns expressed in various social media and online forums regarding yesterday’s formation flyby over Cape Town’s DHL Stadium,” Airlink said on Sunday. “The flight demanded careful planning and rehearsal, as it required navigating at low altitude, at around 150 knots. The South African Civil Aviation Authority and Air Traffic Navigation Services provided valuable guidance, approval and support to ensure a safe flyby.”

South African rugby union has a tradition of stadium flybys at big games, starting when a Boeing 747 flew over a stadium in Johannesburg before the 1995 World Cup final between the same teams, who are fierce rivals. But the flyby last weekend was especially low and dramatic, generating global interest after it was shown as part of the pre-game broadcast, and sparking a flurry of videos shot by witnesses.

Some aviation experts questioned whether the margin for error was too small. “Basically, that lead aircraft … was kind of like dodging over the roof and climbing over the one side and dipping below and then climbing over the other side. That was a little bit uncomfortable,” Chris Martinus, president of Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association South Africa, said. “[If] something adverse happens, you just don’t have options at that kind of altitude.”

Sign up to The Breakdown

The latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewed

after newsletter promotion

Keith Tonkin, an Australian aviation consultant and former military and commercial pilot, said yesteron Monday that the Embraer passenger jets – which are small-to-medium jets designed for regional flights – were not designed or intended for that kind of low-level operation and warned against the precedent.

“The bigger picture is that a benchmark has been established and others may expect to do something similar, and that’s not going to end well,” Tonkin said. He added that turbulence or a bird strike at such a low altitude could leave the pilots with too little room to manoeuvre without hitting the stadium. Airlink said flight data recorded by both aircraft confirmed their flights were performed within civil aviation safety limits for speed and altitude.

Fiorentina’s Serie A renaissance feels a way off after chastening centenary

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 13:27:14 GMT

The home game against Frosinone seemed a perfect way to celebrate their landmark. It did not work out that way

Fiorentina’s 100th birthday party had been going for four days, starting with a fan procession through the historic centre of Florence on Wednesday night and extending to their home game against Frosinone on Saturday afternoon. The club was founded on 29 August 1926, but a decades-old discrepancy in the reporting of that date has led supporters to celebrate traditionally on the 26th.

This time they started a few hours earlier, gathering in their thousands beneath the marble façade of the Basilica of Santa Maria Novella on the evening of 25 August and building to a firework show beside the river Arno at midnight. The club’s president, Giuseppe Commisso, stopped by to give a speech. At least one former player, Borja Valero, was among the crowd.

In the days that followed, historic monuments across the city were lit up in purple to match Fiorentina’s home strip. They have worn that colour since 1929, having played their first three years in shirts half red and half white. A limited-edition replica of those original tops, priced at €180, sold out in less than two hours.

Fiorentina’s players would wear them against Frosinone. Before kick-off, the club hosted some of their greatest former players and coaches for a lunch at their headquarters in Viola Park. The likes of Gabriel Batistuta, Rui Costa, Adrien Mutu and Cesare Prandelli gathered to eat and then head to the stadium, where they were greeted with a party atmosphere.

Not every preparation had gone to plan. Fiorentina had intended for renovations to their Stadio Artemio Franchi to be completed in time for this occasion, but delays meant the Curva Fiesole – the stand traditionally occupied by ultras – remains closed. Still, those same groups arranged a striking choreography at the opposite end instead, recreating the original club badge against a sea of purple flags.

Spirits were high. Despite an opening 4-0 drubbing by Roma, Fiorentina’s supporters had reasons to believe their team was on a good track. They had spent more than €120m on refreshing their squad with exciting young talent, including the Ivory Coast midfielder Christ Inao Oulaï and highly-rated teenage defender Víctor Valdepeñas from Real Madrid Castilla, as well as Arthur Atta and Mateo Pellegrino, coming off breakout seasons with Udinese and Parma.

And that’s not to mention the players they landed on loan. Real Madrid paid €45m to sign the Argentinian winger Franco Mastantuono from River Plate last August and now the 19-year-old would be lining up in Fiorentina’s attack. Radu Dragusin and Álex Jiménez brought Premier League experience from Tottenham and Bournemouth.

The new manager, Fabio Grosso, would need time to blend this group together. But a home game against newly-promoted Frosinone seemed a perfect opportunity for new faces to establish themselves while marking the club’s centenary in style.

It did not work out that way.

Fiorentina started well enough. After a clumsy first few minutes they began to dictate, Mastantuono on the right taking turns with Albert Gudmundsson on the left at getting behind the defence. Jiménez supported ably with overlapping runs from full-back. It felt like a matter of time before they scored.

But a warning arrived in the 25th minute, when Frosinone launched a counter from a Fiorentina free-kick. They reached the penalty area with a numbers advantage, three on two, but Seydou Fini dallied and got dispossessed as he checked back.

Frosinone’s centre-forward, Antonio Raimondo, roared in frustration. A minute later, he opened the scoring. This time Giorgi Kvernadze drove to the goal-line down the left, barely keeping the ball in, before cutting it back for Raimondo to force home at the near post.

Fiorentina responded well. Atta forced a save from Lorenzo Palmisani, before Mastantuono and Valdepeñas smacked shots against the left post. There were moments of quality. Mastantuono did outrageously well to salvage a ball played behind him, controlling with one heel, then knocking the ball across his defender with the second. The stadium appealed for a penalty as he went to ground under contact from Gabriele Bracaglia, but Mastantuono bounced back to his feet and nutmegged another opponent as he shot against the far upright.

Narrow margins. Instead of pulling level, Fiorentina fell further behind in the 38th minute when Bracaglia headed home from a corner. Now the wind truly came out of their sails. Despite a series of substitutions, Grosso’s team offered no hint of a comeback. Raimondo made it 3-0 to Frosinone in the 68th minute with a glorious chest-down and outside-of-the-boot finish.

An astonishing scoreline. Frosinone only narrowly avoided relegation to Italy’s third tier in 2025, when they were set to contest a play-out with Salernitana before a points deduction for Brescia bumped them up the Serie B standings. La Gazzetta dello Sport predicted them to struggle again last season, but their manager, Massimiliano Alvini used the pink paper as motivation, showing it off to players at the start of what became an unexpected run to promotion.

There is much more to say about Frosinone, and Alvini, whose only previous experience in Serie A was a winless 18-game stretch with Cremonese four years ago. An unassuming character, who even now maintains an active LinkedIn page but who has earned his place after finding continuous work as a manager – albeit mostly in the lower divisions – for a quarter of a century.

It is hard to move past Fiorentina as the story, however, on the weekend that they marked their centenary by making their worst-ever start to a Serie A season. They have lost their first two games now by a combined seven goals. It is the first time they have begun a top-flight campaign being shut out in back-to-back defeats.

Milan 2-0 Venezia, Sassuolo 2-1 Torino, Monza 2-3 Udinese, Fiorentina 0-3 Frosinone, Juventus 2-0 Parma, Napoli 1-2 Como, Lazio 1-0 Genoa, Cagliari 0-1 Inter

Perhaps this will all prove an aberration. We are still a way off yet from the horrors of last season, when Fiorentina took six points from their opening 15 matches, winning none. But this was certainly not the night Giuseppe Commisso wanted. His father, Rocco, had sought to transform Fiorentina after taking the club over in 2019, investing heavily to create what has been billed as Italy’s biggest sports centre at Viola Park, with upgraded training facilities for Fiorentina’s men’s and women’s teams, as well as their academy.

Since Rocco passed away in January, Giuseppe has spoken of wanting to carry forward his father’s legacy. “Our family’s total financial commitment to Fiorentina is €1.1bn,” he said on Saturday. “This summer Fiorentina made the largest single transfer window investment in new players in the history of the club.”

He was speaking from the pitch, part of a post-game show to mark the centenary. An event that could not escape the shadow of the 90 minutes that preceded it. Many fans did stay to applaud Batistuta, Rui Costa and other club legends who came out for reintroductions and reminiscences. But the current team were drowned in whistles.

“Today, on Fiorentina’s 100th anniversary, I am not declaring that we have arrived, I am declaring that we have begun again,” said Commisso, swapping between English and Italian. “From this fresh start, Fiorentina’s Renaissance will commence.”

All words that fans love to hear. And all a little harder to buy into, in the aftermath of yet another chastening setback.

Readers reply: If all car tyres were filled with CO2, would this cut atmospheric carbon significantly?

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 13:00:25 GMT

The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions considers a change that might help the environment

This week’s question: Would equal pay create a better society?

If all the vehicles on the planet had their tyres pumped up with CO2, would this lock up enough carbon to lower the amount in the air significantly? Would there be other issues, such as the carbon cost of trapping it all into the tyres? Chris Coldwell, Lancaster

Send new questions to nq@theguardian. com.

Are we expecting the car tyres to stay pumped up for geological time, say the next 50,000 years? If they leak and go flat before then, they haven’t helped restore the natural carbon balance. It’s quite sobering how long the damage done by one generation of humans will persist in the environment. Randomusername222

An inflated car tyre will contain about 14g of air. CO2 weighs about 50% more than air, giving 21g of CO2 per tyre, or 105g per car. There are just short of 1.5bn cars on the planet. Multiplying this by 105g gives 157,700 tonnes of CO2 in all of the world’s car tyres. CO2 emissions in 2025 were 38.1bn tonnes, or about 100,000 tonnes per minute. DrLBlack

It would be interesting to compare the 157,700 tonnes stored here to the area needed to get the same carbon store in a rewilding project. I imagine that it would be a relatively small area of woodland on a map? KP8900

Four hundred tonnes per hectare per year. So, in very round terms, either thousands of hectares or thousands of years, to achieve capture of hundreds of thousands of tonnes. Which is well, well short of current emissions. mill1806

You have to pull the stuff out of the sky first and stop putting more there afterward. Locking it into tyres is a very short-term, fanciful solution. Bubble it through algae, trap it in basalt, turn it into bicarbonate and chuck it in the ocean. Plant one thing each day – preferably a tree. Turn it into kelp forests and sink it. Educate more girls. Make voting compulsory. king_tubby

First off, it is not easy or cheap to get carbon dioxide out of the air – certainly not easier or cheaper than just pumping air into the tyres. Plus, it does nothing about the other gases, such as methane, that are far more powerful drivers of climate change on a by-volume basis. If we could, we’d be better off extracting the CO2 and turning it into C and O2. Carbon is far easier to store and the O2 could be released to help dilute the CO2 remaining in the atmosphere. TotallyTukTuk

Actually while we are still using natural gas for heating, it would be useful to react captured CO2 with H2 to form methane, which then goes in the gas grid, reducing the amount of fossil gas needed. The energy to capture CO2, make hydrogen by electrolysis of water and run the combining reactions can be wholly renewable. canyoudoso

Err, but thermodynamics 101 says that the electricity you use to recreate the methane is equal or greater than the heat you gained by burning the natural gas. Electrolysis in particular is very wasteful of energy. Thermodynamics 102 says that a heat pump gives you four units of heat for every one of electricity you put in. So you’d be many times better off leaving the natural gas in the ground and heating your home with a heat pump instead. So the gas created in that way will be prohibitively expensive. Even an electric fan heater would be many times cheaper than synthetic methane. Randomusername222

The cost of collecting, transporting and storing CO2 for the specific purpose of filling car tyres would probably be astronomical compared to the current simple and cheap compressed air method. When punctured or removed, tyres release the same air back into the atmosphere. Billions of CO2-filled tyres would simply add to pollution levels upon deflation. There would be little or no point in using an esoteric gas in pressurised cylinders, particularly in the hands of unskilled operators on petrol station forecourts, etc. FrankieandDexy

No. The total volume of every car tyre on the planet is so much smaller than the size of the atmosphere that filling them all with 100% carbon dioxide would make no noticeable difference. Even if it did, the carbon would be held only until the tyre punctured or wore out, much quicker than the 100-year time carbon dioxide persists in the atmosphere. Mark, Cambridgeshire

Probably not. When you change a tyre, or get a puncture or at the end of the vehicle’s life, the CO2 has to go somewhere. Maybe it could be reclaimed/recycled, but I suspect the cost would be prohibitive. Pointy_Haired_Boss

On the face of it that’s a great idea, but the logistics of doing it would be huge so for that reason and the maths involved I can’t say if it would work. Meanwhile, planting trees and all the other stuff we’ve started doing helps a lot, with the possible exception of electric cars, whose advocates so miss the point that we need much better public transport, not more expensive little boxes that degrade the environment. Alan Webb

This would make the problem a lot worse. Several others in the comments already addressed with simple calculations that it would not make a significant dent in carbon storage. Next to that, it would cause many more problems. First: CO2 leaks out of rubber much faster then nitrogen (air). This means much more of it would need to be compressed and people would need to check their tyre pressure daily or have underinflated tyres, which is bad for fuel efficiency. Compressing air is relatively straightforward but compressing CO2 and keeping it in containers is harder, for several reasons: one is that if it is not completely dry, it will form carbonic acid that will corrode many materials at high concentrations. Another is the safety aspect of having an infrastructure with so much high-concentration CO2 everywhere. Carbon dioxide is not very toxic at low levels but at above 2% in air, it can become quite an issue, as our blood literally turns acidic. PolyphonicPoly

Given the environmental pollution hazard created by billions of tyres anyway, inflating them with CO2 seems like the old “lipstick on a pig” situation. Drspeedy

Planting more trees instead – a natural store of CO2 – would be a better option. jupiterblue

There are two things you can decide to do today that will reduce your carbon impact – and they don’t involve lashing out money to, for example, eg upgrade your home. 1) Don’t buy anything from the livestock industry; 2) Don’t buy air tickets. There really is no sustainable future which includes the mass-production livestock industry, and the mass aviation industry is very unlikely to be able to produce enough non-fossil aviation fuel within the timeframe required. So it is up to us to stop giving money to those two industries. rockyrex

It wouldn’t help the environment if you filled your tyres with nitrous oxide, but it would be funny if they burst. EddieChorepost
