Can Reform UK recover from its summer horribilis?

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 12:22:53 GMT

Clacton, funding, internal divisions – party prepares for annual conference next week after a season of missteps

Senior Reform UK figures like to boast that the summer time – and parliament’s longest recess – is when the party makes hay.

Supposedly, it is when Nigel Farage and co can muscle in on the news cycle with provocative statements and new policies, painting “establishment” opponents as workshy layabouts.

Last year’s summer break came with an added opportunity, which the rightwing populist party eagerly grasped, in the form of protests against hotels housing asylum seekers. As Labour and the Tories tempered their language, Farage eagerly weighed in, warning of the prospect of “civil disobedience on a vast scale”.

Yet as August comes to an end, and with Reform preparing for its annual conference in Birmingham later this week, the party might look back on summer 2026 as a damp squib, or worse.

While almost weekly Reform press conferences have taken place and new policies have been rolled out – Robert Jenrick has been particularly busy with promises to slash the benefits bill and scrap supposed “red tape” for businesses – there has been no repeat of last summer’s unrest in England, aside from disturbances in the Norfolk market town of Thetford.

There have also been missteps of Reform’s own making, not least the hint of internal divisions related to the noisy pronouncements of its home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf. Farage was eventually forced to reprimand him for calling Ben Wallace, a former Conservative defence secretary and veteran, a “traitor”.

Divisions also surfaced around the suspension of Tim Montgomerie, a high-profile activist who defected from the Conservatives.

However, perhaps the biggest error was Farage’s decision to spark a byelection in Clacton in an attempt to neutralise the pressure he was under over questions about an undeclared £5m payment by the Reform megadonor Christopher Harborne. Farage himself scaled back press events amid scrutiny after the payment was first revealed by the Guardian.

Though he cruised to victory over his closest challenger – Count Binface – the need to get the vote out meant Farage was pinned down in a corner of Essex for six weeks, rather than being free to roam the UK at will and entice media coverage in a way his lieutenants fail to.

The prospect of a “people versus the establishment” battle which Farage so clearly craved did not materialise when other main parties ignored the contest, while a parliamentary standards investigation into the payment has once again started after it was only paused during the byelection.

Opponents have taken note.

“You could say that Reform are quite good at tactics but bad at strategy, and with Clacton he made a strategic mistake because it bound him to one part of the country for six weeks,” said Giles Dilnot, the editor of ConservativeHome and a former political adviser who covered Farage for years for the BBC.

“He made that decision in anger and you never make good strategic decisions when you are angry. Then he had to take a break because of the understandable toll the byelection and all that went before it this year would have taken.”

Dilnot suggested two other issues that will have caused worries in Reform ranks. First, despite Reform consistently attacking the Tories, signs of a knockout blow do not seem to have materialised. Second, the centralised way in which Farage has always run his political projects may now be taking a toll.

“Over the 15 years it’s always the case he is both the biggest asset and biggest weakness of any party he has led. Everything is centralised, he falls out with people and voters can also be very polarised,” said Dilnot.

Sign up to First Edition

Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

after newsletter promotion

Recent polls have indicated that the surge in support for Reform has stalled, with the party failing to break out beyond core supporters and signs that Farage himself might even be a drag on its further growth.

A poll released last week by More in Common put the party at 23% – four percentage points behind Labour and Reform’s worst performance in 18 months. Labour also now leads Reform for the first time since the general election in Ipsos polling – 28% to 25%.

Nearly two-thirds of the public (65%) do not believe Farage is ready to be prime minister, according to Ipsos, while nearly three-quarters backed continuing the standards investigation even before the Clacton result.

Aside from struggling to shake off questions about the £5m, there was yet another reminder last week of another drag – namely Reform having to look over its shoulder at the siren call to its voters from Rupert Lowe’s hard-right Restore Britain party.

The latter was a factor in a much-watched byelection last Thursday on Dover district council, where Reform had swept the board during Kent local elections last year, but where Farage’s party was narrowly pipped by the Greens after Restore polled 10%.

Nonsense, say Reform sources, pointing to new policies and attention-grabbing moves by councils such as Kent, which announced plans to “protect” communities from immigrants.

“We’re coming out of this summer with a plethora of policies, our councils are getting on with it and at conference there will be more headlines, a proper fringe discussing ideas and a business engagement programme which is a major step up from last year,” said one.

Reform says it will use the conference at the Birmingham NEC to set out the first 100 days of what a government led by it would do. One of the biggest questions will be whether any dissent emerges.

Defence spending is an insatiable beast. John Healey is right to tame it

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 12:10:52 GMT

The MoD grossly overspends then claims poverty. It’s high time it was treated as just one part of a progressive government

Nowhere was the confidence of the prime minister, Andy Burnham, shown as clearly as in his appointment of chancellor. There were weeks of speculation that this appointment was a choice between the energy secretary, Ed Miliband, and the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, with their contrasting political economies.

It has been a hallmark of Burnham’s politics that he and his team do not get involved in briefing wars, so it was only when former defence secretary John Healey appeared in Downing Street together with Mahmood that it was clear that the prime minister had cut the Gordian knot, reassuring the markets with a cool, calm political operator with extensive Treasury experience as chancellor. Healey’s two years in defence meant that he would know both sides of the argument when it came to one of the biggest questions of the forthcoming budget: how to meet the bold new Nato defence spending targets without derailing the social ambitions of the Burnham government.

Just last week, it was revealed that the question of getting the right balance of the competing demands of defence, social care, council housing and devolution would be deferred to a spending review next year, and that this October’s budget would be a low-key, continuity affair. That’s a good thing, because the facts about the Ministry of Defence are stark – the stridency of its claims of underfunding are only matched by its record of overspending. The National Audit Office has a series of reports detailing the failures of the MoD’s control of spending.

When I was a special adviser in the MoD during the Gordon Brown government, there was a saying that if you wanted to know what was going on in procurement you just needed to speak to BAE Systems. It was a sardonic acknowledgment of the extent of producer capture by the UK defence industries. Now, there are more elevated phrases like “sovereign capability” or references to seemingly objective measures like percentages of GDP – “3% by the next parliament and 3.5% by 2035”. But they all mean the same thing: like the Cyclops in The Odyssey, the military industrial complex is hungry.

This is one of the strongest arguments for the appointment of Wes Streeting as defence secretary. He has, it seems, tamed the NHS appetite for overspending. The Institute for Fiscal Studies reported last week that “last year the NHS saw no spending top up for frontline services from the Treasury reserve or capital budgets for the first time since 2013-14”.

Of course, geopolitics looms over the defence spending question. The godfather – in all meanings – of the Hague investment plan, which committed the US’s Nato allies to higher defence spending, was President Trump, despite his repeated threats to the territorial integrity of members of that alliance. Keir Starmer decided that a mixture of flattery in the form of a second royal visit, and subservience – embarrassedly picking up the president’s dropped papers – was the right formula. The problem is that going along with a bully just reinforces their behaviour.

The more appropriate political response is being modelled by Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney. He sketched out a new emerging world order in a speech at Davos in January, and most Canadians support his stance since his resolute response to US trade talks and Trump’s attempted “renaming” of Lake Ontario. This led Carney to float the possibility of a deepening partnership between Canada and the European Union – an arrangement that could set a precedent for the UK to realign with the EU without rerunning the entire Brexit debate.

Political entrepreneurship on that level is already being demonstrated by Miliband, now foreign secretary, who has chosen to take the UK seat on the World Bank rather than delegating it to a junior minister. That shows an intent to shape rather than respond to the emerging international situation, and should give space for the prime minister to deal with a pressing domestic agenda.

The question that is rarely addressed in the defence debate is what kind of country we are fighting for. With his mantra of “growth in every postcode”, fixing social care, devolving power and building council houses, Burnham has laid out his programme. Simply setting out his stall has greatly increased Labour’s support. Now he has to build that better Britain – a socially democratic one in which defence spending is taken seriously but doesn’t prevent other societal needs from being fulfilled.

Of course, in politics, one of the huge advantages of having a positive vision of what you are for is that you can go negative on your opponents. Here, defence can be a huge wedge for Burnham. On the right, both the Conservative party and Reform UK were so eager to support Trump that they wanted the UK to commit to the quagmire of the Iran war. They should never be allowed to forget that they put US interests above the UK’s. On the centre-left the attack lines are easy, too. The SNP wants to be a member of an imaginary non-nuclear Nato and never address the challenge of Russian infractions into Scottish waters and airspace. Likewise, the Greens are split on whether to be in Nato and have no idea of why the UK should have defence forces.

All in all, defence is returning to the right space in UK politics. Neither an unfeasible demand on resources, nor a neglected backwater, but a positive tool for a progressive government.

John McTernan was political secretary to PM Tony Blair and is now a political strategist for Burson Global

Rise of Chicken Shop Date highlights how YouTube turned the tables on TV

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 12:00:25 GMT

Amelia Dimoldenberg says publicists ignored her interview show for years but she can now be picky over A-list guests

Just a decade ago, Amelia Dimoldenberg found it impossible to drum up any mainstream celebrities to come on her mock date YouTube show, in which she chats awkwardly with guests over chicken and chips.

Even persuading a local actor connected with her London youth club to come on took years of prodding. Managers of A-listers with movies or albums to push instead battled to claim a spot on the hallowed cushions of the primetime TV chatshow sofa.

Yet after those early years of rejection, Dimoldenberg has said that she has reached a watershed moment. Such is the influence of her Chicken Shop Date show, she says it now ranks alongside Graham Norton’s chatshow or BBC Radio 1 for celebrities seeking media cut-through.

“When I started the show in 2014, no publicist and no manager would let their talent come on a YouTube show – that was just insane,” she told the Edinburgh TV festival. “I would be banging down the doors, it was just so challenging. Now it’s so fascinating because it’s the opposite.

“If your publicist is coming to you and you’ve got a movie out, or you’ve got an album rollout campaign, now I do think one of the first things up there on the list of things to do would be to come on Chicken Shop Date.

“That has always been the ambition – my ambition – to make it as important as going on Graham Norton or going on Greg James, Radio 1, for example. So I’ve achieved that goal.”

Dimoldenberg’s rise is a prime example of how digital platforms have radically reshaped the media world, with viewers across all ages switching to YouTube, especially under-35s.

Dimoldenberg has shared the ketchup with Ed Sheeran, Charli xcx and Jennifer Lawrence, although Lawrence got Dimoldenberg’s name wrong. Even Paul McCartney turned up for a date in a vegan chicken shop this year, declining Dimoldenberg’s suggestion that he adopt a pet otter.

Dimoldenberg initially focused on interviewing figures from the UK rap and grime scene when she launched Chicken Shop Date in 2014. She secured her first big name, the actor Daniel Kaluuya, because he was a fan of the show.

Her interviews have repeatedly gone viral since then, thanks to Louis Theroux rapping or the chemistry between Dimoldenberg and the actor Andrew Garfield. “I didn’t realise fully how much the audience would catch on to how obsessed he is with me,” she said.

She is increasingly picky over guests and rejects anyone who wants to be on the show only as part of a “press run” publicising their latest project.

It marks a shift in the media hierarchy and underlines YouTube’s muscle. The platform’s rise has become so all-consuming in the TV world that Pedro Pina, YouTube’s head for Europe, the Middle East and Africa, was invited to give the keynote MacTaggart lecture at the Edinburgh TV festival last week, the industry’s most important get-together of the year.

Pina used the speech to insist YouTube was “not the villain” about to destroy the TV industry, though he made clear the age of monopoly for TV networks was over.

Sure enough, the temptation of having total creative control – as well as scooping up the ads, sponsors and brand deals that can follow – is now enticing more established media names to try their luck on YouTube.

The presenter Holly Willoughby launched her YouTube channel over the summer, amassing 22,000 subscribers so far. Amol Rajan will finish as a presenter of BBC Radio 4’s Today programme this week and launch a YouTube show, The Amol Rajan Connection. The road from TV personality to YouTuber is already well established in the US.

Yet in a media world that continues to converge, Dimoldenberg is moving in the other direction, seeking success in conventional movies and television. She is writing a teen drama for the BBC, similar to the show Skins, which ran for seven series on E4.

She is also writing a Hollywood romcom, in which she will star as a journalist who finds romance with a celebrity after interviewing them. Other than the chicken, it is a plot that sounds close to home.

“It’s a character that I’ve been playing half my life, so I feel like I know it very well,” she said. “It’s definitely just an exaggeration of who I am.”

The London office, the empty boxes and the £1bn tax loophole

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 12:00:25 GMT

Exclusive: How a court case over an unoccupied office block could end a widely used tax avoidance scheme

From the outside, the seven-storey building at 2 America Square looks like any other office block in the heart of London’s financial district.

Located about half a mile from Tower Bridge, one might expect it to be a hive of commercial activity, teeming with employees holding important meetings. However, much of the property is home not to staff vying for their next bonus, but to stacks of nondescript black boxes arranged in neat lines.

The building, leased by a Virgin Islands-based company called 48th Street Holdings Ltd, has found itself at the centre of a court case that has finally signalled the end of a tax avoidance scheme believed to have cost local authorities more than £1bn.

For almost two decades, companies in England have been exploiting a legal loophole to avoid paying business rates on unoccupied commercial buildings.

The controversial practice dates back to 2008, when the last Labour government changed business rates rules. This meant occupiers of vacant buildings no longer qualified for a 50% discount on the levy.

However, they were entitled to claim a three-month rate holiday at the end of each tenancy – and the “box shifting” scheme was born.

With commercial property owners facing higher bills, a lucrative “rate mitigation” industry emerged. Historically, this typically involved boxes being moved into the empty space at the end of the three months and back out after just six weeks. The building then became unoccupied again and the clock was reset, allowing the owner to claim another three-month rate-free period.

This cycle continued, designed to cut the rates owed by up to 67%, until a new long-term tenant could be found. It has been costing one London council an estimated £35m a year since the pandemic, when the number of claims for empty property relief doubled.

However, last month a landmark ruling by three court of appeal judges looks to have sounded the death knell for box shifting. They ruled that the scheme “cannot amount to beneficial occupation”.

The case was brought by the City of London Corporation against 48th Street Holding Ltd and a second company, Principled Offsite Logistics Ltd (POLL), which provides “rate mitigation” services.

48th Street paid £27.6m for a lease on the office block in 2019 before it brought in POLL to save £111,475.30 in rates across a series of three-month periods in 2022 and 2023.

POLL describes itself as “the largest and most reliable” provider of “empty business rates mitigation” in the UK and is jointly owned by a Labour councillor from North Hertfordshire.

It claimed by 2021 to have already saved its clients “£500m” in rates and that “every council in the UK now totally recognises Principled as being robust in every way”.

That bold claim followed a significant high court win in 2018, when POLL defeated a challenge from Trafford council. The judge in that case accepted that “the purpose of the occupation is not to store goods; it is, so to speak, to plant the occupier’s flag” and that “the motive … is rates avoidance for the landlord”, but added “the morality of that is neither here nor there”.

When the case against POLL and 48th Street came before the high court last year, Charles Bagot KC, sitting as a deputy high court judge, also ruled against the City of London.

“I agree with POLL that if legislation produces clear tramlines and someone organises themselves to fall within them, then it is not for the court to get involved in moral judgments,” he said. “If the government does not like the position, it can amend it.” He concluded that “the RMS [rate mitigation scheme] is effective”.

However, last month the court of appeal overturned that decision, with Lady Justice Falk ruling: “In my judgment, ‘occupation’ for, in effect, the sake of it, and which has no use, value or benefit other than rate saving, does not amount to occupation for the purpose of the statutory scheme.”

A City of London Corporation spokesperson said: “We welcome the court of appeal’s decision, which represents a significant victory for local authorities across England.

“This landmark ruling closes one of the most widely used tax avoidance schemes in the country and helps safeguard revenues that support essential public services.

“We are proud that the City of London Corporation has led the way nationally in pursuing this case.

“For more than a decade, councils across the country have seen hundreds of millions of pounds of public revenue lost through artificial business rates avoidance schemes and we believe the decision restores fairness, protects money that funds vital local services, and provides greater certainty for councils, ratepayers and property owners alike.”

after newsletter promotion

A government spokesperson said: “We recognise concerns about the misuse of Empty Property Relief, which exists to support genuine property owners between tenants.

“Business rates avoidance is unacceptable and we are taking the necessary action to address this, and make sure that businesses are paying the tax they owe.”

It is unclear what action the government is planning, but there are calls for a general anti-avoidance rule to control the rate mitigation industry.

POLL is not the only business offering box shifting. The same scheme was even used by Public Health England at its future headquarters in Harlow in 2018. The resulting £2.5m dispute with Harlow district council ended up in the high court, where PHE won.

It remains to be seen how councils and their rate mitigation opponents will respond.

One rating expert said that the total cost to councils of box shifting could have topped £1.5bn, and some of that money should now be reclaimed as a deterrent.

Under the terms of POLL’s contracts with clients, its success fees are refundable in the event the scheme fails. The latest accounts show it has just over £500,000 in net assets.

POLL did not respond to a request for comment and its website went down this week, replaced with a message which read: “This account has been suspended”.

The company’s founder, Steven Dawson, died in 2024 and the POLL was acquired in a management buyout by two of its own executives. One of them is a Labour councillor, Sarah Lucas, who, according to her LinkedIn profile, has been POLL’s director of finance since 2018.

Lucas was elected to North Hertfordshire council in 2024, two months after she took 50% ownership of POLL, and she serves as vice-chair of the council’s finance, audit and risk committee.

The Guardian understands that POLL’s application for permission to appeal to the supreme court was refused by the court of appeal this week but an option remains for it to apply to the supreme court directly.

The rules on empty property relief changed in 2024 and buildings now need to be occupied for 13 weeks instead of six in order for the three-month holiday to apply. According to one recent judgment, this makes box shifting schemes “less attractive but still effective”.

There are still a range of variants of rates mitigation on offer. One involves placing Bluetooth boxes in the offices to broadcast adverts. Another uses charitable exhibitions to claim not only empty property relief but also the extra rates relief available for charities.

Some schemes install snail or mushroom farms to claim agricultural reliefs, while others involve opening faith rooms to cut rates.

Elversberg and ‘miracle village’ prove that Bundesliga fairytales still exist

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 11:52:41 GMT

German football has long insisted there is more to their elite league than a title race. Now they have a story that shows the world that surprise and wonder does live here too

Friday night was no first day fun for VfB Stuttgart as they got first-hand proof of what the rest of the Bundesliga feared: that Bayern Munich are perhaps mightier than ever. The curtain-raiser, though, didn’t actually set the tone for the the weekend. German football has long insisted there is more to their elite league than a title race, and now they have a story that shows the world that surprise and wonder does indeed live here too.

Bayer Leverkusen arrived into their opening fixture of the campaign thinking their season might contain greater certainty than the last one, a more tranquil voyage after being blown off course by almost €300m of player sales and the ill-fated appointment of Erik ten Hag. Enter SV Elversberg, Bundesliga first-timers and representatives of – a “miracle village” as Bild put it – Spiesen-Elversberg, a town with a population of just over 13,000, situated 15km north-east of Saarbrücken, 30 minutes’ drive from the French border.

The miracle got big enough for all to see it on the Bundesliga’s inaugural Saturday afternoon. Seventy minutes into their top-flight debut and the locals gathered in the Ursapharm Arena – currently under a renovation programme to bring it up to a modest 15,000 capacity, with journalists covering the game from a temporary steel gantry on top of scaffolding and accordingly given a safety briefing beforehand – were pinching themselves. Vincent Wagner’s team led 3-0, courtesy of two goals in the space of 60 seconds in the opening 10 minutes, and then a third 25 seconds after half-time.

New Leverkusen coach Carles Martínez, who looked increasingly exasperated on the touchline as the game went on, threw a host of forwards on to salvage the game, and Patrick Schick and Christian Kofané both scored to reduce the arrears, but it wasn’t enough. A town with no train station and no town hall was now home to a team not only with a first-day Bundesliga win (and no team from Saarland had won a top-flight game since 1993 when FC Saarbrücken beat – you guessed it – Leverkusen), but a victory over the 2024 champions, no less. Even arriving in the same division was akin to a “moon landing”, Wagner had said before the game, continuing to say staying up would be their “mission to Mars”. August results may be notoriously fickle and this may seem like years ago by November, but the win was no fluke.

And make no mistake, Leverkusen were shook from minute one. Elversberg pressed and rattled them, with the visitors’ new captain Edmund Tapsoba looking more the Bundesliga debutant, prone as Lukas Petkov opened the scoring and then turning over the ball almost from kick-off, as Cole Campbell swept into the area to bludgeon in a quickfire second.

The Bulgarian midfielder Petkov had led from the front in the promotion campaign, scoring 13 and creating another six to pick up the slack after top scorer Younes Ebnoutalib left for Eintracht Frankfurt in the winter break. True to form, Petkov also created David Mokwa’s goal at the start of the second half, which turned out to be the difference with a delicious delivery from the right. Yet Campbell is really indicative of the step up. Bought from Borussia Dortmund for €6m in the summer, the 20-year-old from Houston has been rated for a while without truly making a dent in the top tier, either at BVB or on loan at Hoffenheim. He started here – as much of his team did – like a man on a mission, and having laid out a record fee, Elversberg need this to work too.

This spend needs to be put in perspective, of course. When Strasbourg full-back Guéla Doué (elder brother of Desiré) completes his move to the BayArena on Monday, it will be the fourth time this summer that Die Werkself have spent in excess of €20m on a player. Leverkusen, and their coach, had no excuses. After an encouraging pre-season, they were beset by many of the old problems that undercut their Champions League hopes last season. Mark Flekken, their refreshingly blunt goalkeeper, could have been talking in March or May when he told the media: “I can’t even offer an explanation right now.”

On the other side, it was all joy. Flekken’s opposite number Nicolas Kristof, whose brilliant save from Jonas Hofmann in stoppage time shut down Leverkusen’s last hope of taking something from the game, was one of two players in the lineup who has been at the club since they were in the regional fourth tier, winning promotion to the 3. Liga in 2022, at the end of his debut season at the club. It is already a fairytale. If they can build on their start as they build that main stand, it would be a story for the Bundesliga ages.

Bayern Munich 5-1 Stuttgart, Union Berlin 3-3 Eintracht, Leipzig 3-0 Mönchengladbach, Mainz 0-0 Paderborn, Elversberg 3-2 Leverkusen, Cologne 3-2 Hoffenheim, Dortmund 2-0 Hamburg, Freiburg 4-1 Werder Bremen, Augsburg 3-0 Schalke

Bayern’s opening night brutality had been, as so often in the past, aided and abetted by their visitors Stuttgart, who tend to play in their normal front-foot style against the champions and are accordingly ripped to shreds even in games (like this one) in which they have good spells. Michael Olise was on the scoresheet but Harry Kane didn’t even need to score, while Ismaël Saibari offered enterprise and two assists from the bench. Vincent Kompany’s team are frightening.

Still, Dortmund had taken hope from their second half in last week’s Super Cup and were very attractive in a one-sided first half against Hamburg, a departure from previous Niko Kovac teams. But although they cruised to a 2-0 win there was a huge blow, with new boy Giannis Konstantelias rupturing his ACL on his full debut, minutes after scoring the second. BVB now have to consider free agent replacements, with both Jadon Sancho and Reiss Nelson among the names circulating.

Saïd El Mala, who nearly ended up at BVB, instead wore the FC Köln No 10 shirt for the first time and helped to inspire a comeback win against Hoffenheim, scoring a first equaliser before new signing Thijs Dallinga struck two memorable goals in a 3-2 victory.

Elversberg’s aforementioned former star Ebnoutalib had an explosive start to the campaign, hitting a hat-trick at Union Berlin. It was an afternoon of vindication for the Moroccan striker, who scored on his Frankfurt debut against Dortmund in January and was then injured shortly after. “It’s good for my mind,” Ebnoutalib said after the game, even though an injury-time Tim Skarke equaliser snared Union a point after they had trailed 3-1 (and debutant Eintracht goalkeeper Noah Atubolu had needed to perform excellently to keep them at bay that long).

Schalke’s return to the top flight started brightly at Augsburg, with Finn Dahmen keeping them at bay in the early stages before Michael Gregoritsch punctured his former club’s hopes with the opener, and it was virtually one-way traffic from there, ending with 10 men and a 3-0 loss. Still, they could be Werder Bremen, given a 4-1 Sunday kicking at Freiburg the day after their star man Jens Stage was confirmed as out injured until the new year.

Do you have a bespoke ‘dirty zone’?

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 10:00:22 GMT

Apparently a dedicated mud room will make you less stressed. But I have a very different approach

I was excited to learn that the latest interiors essential, according to the Washington Post, is a “dirty zone”. I’m ahead of the curve – I’ve already got a dirty zone by each main door (and also one directly outside the back door, where, rudely, a mystery animal has defecated). The fridge drawers are dirty zones thanks to the windfall apples I thought I would cook, but predictably left to liquefy. There’s a dirty zone next to the washing machine and a mildewy one inside it. There’s the festering compost bin I’m too chicken to tackle post-heatwave, plus the cupboard under the stairs, which we don’t talk about. Good luck finding a clean zone, basically.

Does this make me kinda chic? Unfortunately not: the Post is actually preaching the benefits of confining the sordid ephemera of life to carefully delineated and hidden areas: storage benches, monogrammed totes or even a “mud room” (for coats, shoes, skis, lacrosse sticks and dog-washing sinks – I think posh Britons call it a boot room). A 2021 study in the Netherlands found that participants who did chores in chaotic environments had higher levels of the stress marker salivary alpha-amylase. I always wonder what’s brewing in my mouth as I fall over piles of filthy shoes yet again while running to answer the door.

This dirty zone system sounds nice, but deeply, decadently unrealistic. A mud room, rather than various rooms containing some mud, surely isn’t something most people have. If you do, apparently you’ll also want a $115 (£85) petitgrain and neroli reed diffuser, to help mask the smell. One expert consulted by the Post suggested green as a mud room colour scheme, to coordinate harmoniously with your brown delivery boxes “if you’re a heavy Amazon shopper”, which has a real last-days-of-Rome ring to it.

If you don’t have a muted green, neroli-scented mud room, don’t despair – mud is good for you. A 2022 study in Finland found that exposure to muddy environments improved immune system regulation and decreased levels of harmful bacteria in the microbiomes of nursery-age children. My home may be one big, sprawling dirty zone, but I probably have an awe-inspiringly powerful immune system – and that’s a real chic must-have.

Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

More and more undergrads are living at home. That’s a crying shame – here’s why

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 10:00:22 GMT

Spiralling rental costs have made living with parents the only option for some students. That fails to prepare them for the realities of adult life

If the headlines are to be believed, no one should want to be a student in England any more. And yet this September and October, a record number of school leavers will begin their journey at university, unwilling to let rising costs, a regressive loan system and dimming graduate job prospects blot out the promise of the best years of their lives. The burden now placed on today’s students has grown so heavy, though, that it is reshaping people’s experience of higher education: new data from the university admissions service Ucas shows a marked rise in the number of students planning to live at home with their parents, rather than moving away to study.

It’s first worth stressing that this new arrangement is not, for the most part, a voluntary one. That’s clear in the gap between those “choosing” to stay at home and those who have no choice at all: among students from England’s poorest neighbourhoods, more than half now expect to live at home while studying, compared with just under a fifth from the least-deprived areas.

The student rental market is the main culprit – it is now forcing many teenagers to fork out more than £10,000 a year just for basic accommodation, even in cities outside London. Since the liberalisation of housing regulations in the 1980s (alongside an influx of wealthy international students), private landlords have been given free rein to jack up prices while housing standards worsen, with damp, rat-infested accommodation now becoming a normalised part of the student experience. A recent study by the National Union of Students found that an appalling 84% of students reported significant issues with their housing, with almost half living with mould, despite the extortionate costs many are now paying. It’s no surprise, then, that many of my peers feel they have no option but to stay at home.

This may seem like an easy solution, but it, too, comes with its personal costs. A lack of personal space as well as family conflict can mean worsening mental health for some students who stay at home. Many will also inevitably miss out on the life skills a person only learns when living independently. Then there’s also the very real risk of being excluded from the cultural and social highs of university life – the joys that make it worth persevering through gruelling deadlines and exam schedules. That trade-off is evident in those around me who have already made the reluctant retreat to study from home: all have struggled with isolation, and some have dropped out of university entirely. With graduate prospects collapsing, it’s the lifelong friendships built on campuses and in student accommodation that count more than ever in the university experience. Take that away and replace it with an hour-long commute from your childhood bedroom, and you begin to wonder if any part of getting a degree is really worth it.

Meanwhile, students on difficult terms with their parents are left in an impossible position, forced to cough up eye-watering sums simply to maintain a healthy distance from them. In this respect, particularly for those who have experienced restrictive upbringings, the freedom to explore adult life at university remains an invaluable part of discovering our real selves. Crippling costs therefore make what should be the most liberating chapter of our lives so far instead feel like trading one set of restrictions for another.

It has always been fashionable for older generations to bemoan the laziness of “today’s youth”. Yet how can anyone expect a generation to properly grow up while being denied the hallmarks of adult life? Stuck under a parent’s roof at university, and denied the economic mobility that comes with a graduate job once they leave, my generation is being condemned to live out its own twisted Peter Pan fairytale.

Luckily, it’s not all doom and despair. The recent Renters’ Rights Act has provided much needed breathing room for students, shifting the needle back in favour of tenants over Britain’s landlords for the first time in decades. Certainly, the ability to cut our tenancy short has been a gamechanger over the summer; previously, we had to keep paying rent for rooms we couldn’t stay in. But students will need more than just tweaks to their current arrangements; we need rent controls, a shift out of the private rental market, and investment into affordable, purpose-built complexes designed for university life.

There is one silver lining to all this: earlier this year the UK’s biggest student landlord warned that profits could slide because of lower room occupancy, which could be exacerbated as students choose to study from home, so the tower of cards is looking awfully close to coming crashing down. Perhaps if this model has finally run out of road, then students’ housing needs can finally be released from the grip of profiteers.

OnlyFans and AI training: why gen Z doesn’t care where our money comes from

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 09:00:22 GMT

With traditional goals such as stability and home ownership feeling out of reach, young people are focused on the present

By now, we all know the shape of financial nihilism: the throw-your-money-at-anything reaction to the dissolution of the slow, linear path to wealth; the prediction markets, meme stocks, cryptocurrencies and microluxuries growing in its place. We’re left in an economic no man’s land. But financial nihilism only describes where we put our money. What about how we earn it in the first place?

The modern economy has long relied on our need for stable employment – to pay the mortgage, to keep our kids fed, or, for some, to chase prestige and power – to generate the work ethic that keeps the wheel of production turning. None of this is going well for young people. Our jobs are insecure, we can’t afford houses, we’re deferring having kids (if we have them at all), and only 6% of us say a leadership position is our primary career goal. Hope is one of the economy’s most productive inputs, powering our willingness to endure long hours. When the production function of income – the mechanism that turns hard work into a stable salary, then a mortgage, then a pension – breaks down, so does our relationship with the input. I call this production nihilism: my generation’s growing indifference to the kinds of work we’re willing to participate in, and where we’re willing to earn.

“Normal people are asleep. Good,” a young woman running her craft business at night-time tells the camera in Shopify’s latest commercial. Partially thanks to all-in-one e-commerce platforms like Shopify, many of us have mastered the art of polyworking. These are jobs our high school career advisers could hardly have imagined – platforms such as Mercor, where white-collar workers train LLMs to do their job; “YouTube empires”; the much-covered millions being made by young women on OnlyFans; non-sexualized escorts. Some are supplementary, some are enough to eventually become a primary source of income. Americans seem to be coming around to the idea of “portfolio careers”, with more than half calling them more desirable than traditional careers for a future workforce.

Take away the feasibility of long-term goals and our willingness to wait for “the good life” collapses. So we redirect our motivation to grind and save into channels that pay out sooner – cash, yes, but also autonomy, flexibility or a sense of identity. Fifty-seven per cent of gen Z report having a side hustle, well over double the boomer rate. Day jobs start to function as financial anchors, paying the rent while our side gigs do the identity work. After all, “writer” plays far better on a Hinge profile than “analyst”.

With no solid formula for our futures, more of us are experimenting with what it means to interact with the economy at all. The cultural counterpart to this economic logic is a series of attitude shifts to work, nervously cataloged as trends: the gen Z stare, or faked productivity. I recently wrote about the slow death of the prestige career, where – thanks to AI – companies no longer require a robust team of entry-level workers to scale.

We’re living through a transition in our economic relationship with the future. The cultural theorist Lauren Berlant described how an “anticipatory present” kept people bound to an economic system: enduring the short term in the hope for a promised version of the long term. Profoundly unable to imagine – let alone attain – a prosperous future, young people may be among the first generations to name this for what it is: foreclosed. When the promise of a future stops working, we “maxx” for the present, extracting value as quickly as possible with whatever assets late-stage capitalism permits us to spend. It’s the other side of the “little treat” economy.

Neoliberalism, the system that raised us, offers a convenient way forward: everything can be commodified if we try hard enough. When western society was first learning this lesson, France’s artists gave voice to the unease of their postwar consumer boom. The film-maker Jean-Luc Godard’s Two or Three Things I Know About Her follows Juliette, a Paris housewife, as she prostitutes herself to keep up with the lifestyle being aggressively marketed to her. She decides to sell her afternoons, her time, her body. It’s a precursor, in many ways, to the gig economy of platform capitalism: Juliette optimizes any assets at her disposal to enjoy the present moment.

The New Wave tried to warn us against the relentless tide of commodification. But where Godard and his contemporaries channelled their anxiety through women as objects, gen Z reclaims Juliette’s image – not as a helpless, bored object, but as subject. We are agents of our own relationship with the economy. Less despairing, less passive, less accepting: gen Z’s nihilism feels distinctly active. Production nihilism leans into a new definition of work, forcibly detaching us from the neoliberal “good life” fantasy that’s clearly stopped delivering. Nietzsche described nihilism of this kind as a process of clearing away dead values. Which is what production nihilism does: it detaches us from the neoliberal “good life” fantasy that’s clearly stopped delivering. Refusing to accept the current economic system as the endpoint of our search for meaning, we improvise a new set of values as we go.

But is there real agency here? There’s an idea circulating in Silicon Valley: that “high-agency” individuals – those who think for themselves and act without being told – will be the ones to survive the coming AI disruption. This isn’t really agency. It’s the anticipatory bind Berlant warned us about, another story about how to succeed in an economy where fewer of us will realistically be able to. No wonder we’ve stopped caring about where our income comes from, when its source no longer determines where we end up.

Alice Lassman is an economist who writes The Intimacy Economy, a Substack and forthcoming book on the economics of connection, care and relationships

The hill I will die on: No self-respecting adult should use the term ‘picky bits’

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 07:00:18 GMT

It’s the Boaty McBoatface of dinner time. Britons, resist the supermarkets’ cutesy branding and have some dignity

It’s a bittersweet time of year. The season of tiny shorts is giving way to wondering whether the trousers you last wore in May still fit. I’ve already seen Christmas tat in The Works; only Sainsbury’s winter-spiced bleach is the greater festive harbinger of mortality. At least we’ve hopefully seen the end of the heatwaves. And, with it, the scourge of the phrase “picky bits”.

For the blissfully uninitiated, picky bits is apparently the new national name for spending £8 on three trays of pastry-wrapped “exotic” confections in a tragic facsimile of the delicious, high-quality deli items our European neighbours enjoy every day of their goddamn lives. Every summer, the ranges get more off their nuts: who knew your picnic needed Turkish grilled pepperoncini and dressed salsa verde chickpeas? (It doesn’t.)

Before brands such as M&S, Waitrose and the Co-op leapt on the cutesy phrase as a way of bankrupting you for sticks of cheese wrapped in ham (and loads of plastic), picky bits had more innocent origins as one of the many terms that Britons use for slapping tomatoes, coleslaw and crisps on the table and letting everyone choose their own dinner.

Its potentially infinite variety demands almost as many names. Back when Twitter was fun, discussions of regional – or just family – difference like this knocked hours off British productivity levels. You call it a picky tea? Table dinner? Lovely. My friend’s mum calls it, quite wonderfully, “a cold collation”. Mine calls it “salad”, despite the sad bistro leaves (served in bag, obviously) being the last thing anyone wants, compared to the salami and dips. Salad cream, however, is crucial. I love linguistic quirks such as this. You call a roll a breadcake, a barm, a cob? Delightful!

That is, until brands get on board. Suddenly, endearing domestic chatter becomes mortifying when shouted from a 4ft-tall poster at the train station. Removed from the context of the family’s novelty salt and pepper shakers and a sibling squabble over the last sausage roll, picky bits feels – as the New York Times once wrote in a canonical 1994 report about Mr Blobby – like “a metaphor for a nation gone soft in the head”.

Every time I see the phrase in public life it makes me want to do civil disobedience. It’s the Boaty McBoatface of dinner time, exposing our once-repressed nation’s surprisingly twee core and total disregard for shame. Sure, my own personal lexicon is full of embarrassing nonsense, but you’re never going to see [REDACTED] on a billboard overhanging the A4.

Also, most of these supermarket picky bits taste incredibly underwhelming. Have some self-respect and tear a rotisserie chicken apart with your bare hands next time you go to the park.

The Nepal floods seem a world away – but make no mistake, climate breakdown will affect us all

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 05:00:17 GMT

Richer countries might have more resources to deal with catastrophe, but this problem grips the entire planet, however much leaders may want to deny it

Climate breakdown is happening on one Earth, but two different worlds. In one, its impacts increasingly encroach on everyday life; longer periods of discomfort and shorter periods of sharp pain. Endless, hotter summers, and within them sudden wildfires, evacuations, homes burned to cinders in a matter of hours. In another, catastrophe. This summer has been a snapshot of that split-screen. The hottest day on record in parts of Europe, and a wave of water, mud and ice in Nepal that so far has claimed more than 750 lives. Thousands of people are still missing.

The difference is also one of resources. The climate crisis has an economic cost, but some places can absorb it better than others. Responses to this summer of wildfires in Europe included a rapid scrambling by the French government to provide everything from tax breaks for businesses affected by the fires to relocation costs and aid to rebuild homes. The UK government had deployed almost £100m before the summer to strengthen wildfire resilience.

Entire industries exist to absorb the impact, undergirded by sophisticated technology, disposable income and evolved sectors. Wildfire insurance in the US is being powered by AI, which spits out numbers to estimate risk based on location and construction material. Outside North America and Europe, there is little of that buffer. The result is asymmetry. While developed countries will still be stressed as events triggered by climate breakdown become more regular and chronic, and they are still not immune to globalised outcomes – rising food costs, droughts, water shortages – what they experience and how disruptive that will be are far removed from other parts of the world.

The difference in scale and resources is colossal. What is needed to rebuild Nepal’s flood damage may constitute up to a 10th of its entire economy – something like $5bn, and that’s not even factoring in all the technical foreign assistance, equipment, expertise and labour required. Also colossal is the difference in exposure to the obliterative effects of events.

Take the death of coral reefs, and how that disproportionately affects coastal populations. Across the Caribbean, coral bleaching caused by rising ocean acidification and temperatures not only dramatically reduces marine life, which is a source of food and income for entire populations – 90% of Jamaica’s economic income is generated alongside its coasts – but also increases the scale and intensity of storms. Coral reefs are a sort of natural storm barrier, absorbing the force of sea waves and buffering coastal areas from flooding. The intersection between these geographical and economic features means countries in the Caribbean are being pummelled on the weather front (climate breakdown also increases the power of hurricanes through warming ocean water), as well as having their incomes drastically reduced and therefore their ability to bounce back.

Then there is the heat. Temperatures are not just jumping far above the average in Europe but also in warmer areas where the base temperatures are already high. Last week, a Harper’s Index summary of estimated heat-related mortality in India showed some staggering numbers: 3,400 excess deaths “caused by a single day of extreme heat”; 30,000 deaths “caused by five consecutive days of extreme heat”. In April of this year, all 50 of the world’s hottest cities were in a single country, India, something which according to the air-quality monitoring platform AQI “has no modern precedent across global weather data”.

This is another double whammy for poor communities without access to shelter or cooling systems of unlimited fresh water. These are the so-called climate breakdown hotspots, identified as “areas where strong physical and ecological effects of climate change come together with large numbers of vulnerable and poor people and communities”. Few places on Earth demonstrate this category more vividly than Sudan. A country already in the grip of war and food insecurity is now succumbing to the delayed rains caused by the El Niño climate pattern, cracking the dry earth and draining the Nile. The risk of famine stalks populations that are already acutely hungry.

And what is felt asymmetrically has been caused in that way too. These poorer, more vulnerable countries are paying the price for the emissions caused by wealthy countries, and not even being extended the full, remedial support from the coffers of those nations that accumulated the wealth generated by industries that contributed to climate breakdown and global heating. We are not just battling complacency, or indifference to the importance of climate justice, but a political climate that has in recent years, led by Donald Trump’s second term, seen its own collapse.

Look closer and the problem isn’t only historical failure but a casual disregard, an adventurism that launches wars and stresses economies with buffers already damaged by the climate crisis. The Iran war in combination with El Niño is a weather and politics collaboration that has hiked fertiliser costs on the one hand and choked rain on the other. More broadly, what was a generously named albeit tenuously implemented “rules-based order”, which at least had some bedrock of global cooperation and aid, has been cancelled altogether. Trump’s withdrawal from the Paris agreement set the tone, while the dismantling of USAID cut the funds that diverted billions of dollars from the rich to the developing world to help with the fallout of extreme weather and reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Here is another cascade. As the US withdraws from its commitments, sending the signal that there are no rules or duties, and indeed no problem with climate breakdown at all, pressure will rise on other countries to contribute more. They will need to figure out a way to hold together a coordinated response in the shadow of a destabilising hegemon, as well as try to foster that sense of social obligation in a time of political sociopathy.

The foolish shortsightedness of it all is that even though there is a large gap between experiences, and so a sense that glaciers and floods and famines are happening all the way over there, their knock-on effects and food supply challenges, and political and refugee crises, will affect us all. Things will get dramatically worse for the hotspots, but there is still no outrunning it all in the long term. It seems that at precisely the moment when this realisation should yoke us together in all the ways life is rapidly changing, we are all being untethered. But ultimately, whatever different spheres we inhabit, we are all still trapped on the same planet.

Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist

‘Everything’s smashed to bits’: Ukrainians turn anger on those storing weapons near their villages

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 04:00:17 GMT

As Russia hits another ammunition warehouse, killing at least 38, locals put blame on poorly placed depots

It is a day and a half since a Russian jet-powered drone smashed into an ammunition dump in Myla, a village 15 miles outside central Kyiv. Volodymyr, 61, a security guard, leads visitors from his family’s badly damaged home, its roof blown off, back windows shattered, through the garden towards the impact site 300 metres away.

The garden, like so many in Ukraine’s villages and suburbs, is a sizeable allotment. But today the greenhouse is shattered, a vegetable patch is blackened and crisp underfoot. Several metres of grapevine have been destroyed. Even so, Volodymyr finds two surviving bunches to hand to the Guardian.

It is a remarkable moment of generosity, though his family now has no electricity and no water after Thursday night’s extended bombing. The death toll rose by one on Sunday, to 38, and four more people are still missing in an episode that has swiftly raised questions about why ammunition was stored so close to people’s homes.

In the yard before the garden, Vira, 65, knows who is at fault. “Those who set up the depot here are to blame. There are people here, this is a village. You can’t keep something like that here,” she says. She and her son Serhii hid for hours in a small bunker by the side of the house waiting out what witnesses said were 30 or 50 explosions that went on for about six hours after the initial strike at 8pm.

Serhii says they had no idea ammunition was stored in their village. “I thought it was humanitarian aid that was stored there.” Now the family is presented with a cleanup that will be costly and difficult while starting with next to nothing. He is charging his phone from a car battery via a converter. It is all the power they have.

A missile shell from a Grad rocket launcher was found on their property once the explosions subsided, Serhii adds, as well as “several mines and cluster munitions”. They have been removed by the cleanup team, although a burnt-out box of bullets, freshly discovered in another part of the semi-collapsed ceiling, has not and sits by the front door awaiting a further collection.

Volodymyr’s tour continues out back. A grass line, effectively a track, has been marked out through the wood beyond the garden, between blackened patches where fires burned. There is smouldering, even flames in places, more bullets and boxes of bullets, then, on the right, unmistakably, a detonated anti-tank mine.

Finally, the woods open out, revealing a warehouse site, large parts of which are bombed out, an open area of destruction. A sulphurous smell endures, and periodically explosions can be heard, though they may be controlled detonations. Clear-up work by the emergency services is in the process of being halted at lunchtime because there is another drone threat above.

Volodymyr was on guard duty at a lumber yard close to the ammunition store on the night of the bombing. He survived the initial strike unscathed, and headed back home promptly, but feels a guard’s need to return. “I’ve been coming back and forth for two days to see these ashes,” he says.

Thirty of the dead were from a care home close to the ammunition store, the location of which is now subject of a criminal inquiry by Ukraine’s intelligence service. But it is not the first attack of its kind in recent weeks. There have been other Russian bombings of poorly placed ammunition dumps, as Moscow aggressively targets warehouse sites at a time when Ukraine is doing similar.

The fact this has happened recently in Ukraine is not lost on Liudmyla, whose adult daughter was in the house a couple of doors down when the Shahed drone hit. The home is also heavily damaged, windows facing the warehouse blown in, and Liudmyla recalls that a similar incident happened in early July, on the edge of Kyiv.

“Look at what’s going on here. Everything’s smashed to bits right here. Vyshneve [the scene of the previous incident, nine miles south-east] wasn’t enough for them, and there was more somewhere else too. No, they’ve dumped all this right by people’s vegetable gardens, right on their doorsteps,” she says, warning that munitions are still strewn around, not yet cleared up.

Nine people were killed after a munitions store was hit at Vyshneve, and 280 homes damaged. Two people have been detained on suspicion of allowing weapons to be stored in an inappropriate place after the episode, but as the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said on Saturday, similar has happened again.

It is a dismal repetition at a time when Kyiv is already coming under increased attack from Moscow, the harm to civilians from attacks on food stores and logistics warehouses increasing. When Liudmyla is pressed to say who is at fault for the deaths and destruction at Myla, she offers a double answer.

“Putin! Who else? And those who set up the depot here.”

Forbidden planet: was Pluto’s 2006 demotion a big mistake?

The Guardian Mon, 31 Aug 2026 04:00:16 GMT

Since it was stripped of planetary status, Pluto’s defenders have been fighting the decision – and they’re only getting more passionate

Twenty years ago, Pluto got demoted. After a vote by the International Astronomical Union (IAU) in August 2006, Pluto was relegated from major planet to dwarf planet status. Our solar system dropped from nine planets to eight. At the time, many scientists were unhappy with the decision. Two decades on, the debate is, if anything, even more polarised.

“The definition of a planet they created, you can’t use it at all,” says Philip Metzger, the director of the Stephen W Hawking Centre for Microgravity Research and Education at the University of Central Florida. “It makes the definition of a planet completely non-useful in science.”

Metzger is one of a number of scientists and lay people who consider Pluto’s demotion a big mistake.

For some, Pluto’s downgraded status is the source of their affection for the ex-planet. “Pluto represents the underdog that so many people root for, the small kid on the block that is being picked on,” says Kevin Schindler, historian at the Lowell Observatory in Arizona, where Pluto was discovered in 1930.

For others, the IAU’s decision, and the way it was taken, is central to the debate. “My being involved with advocating for Pluto started on the day of the vote,” says writer, actor and amateur astronomer Laurel Kornfeld. “I was like: wait a minute, this is wrong.” When we meet on Zoom she is wearing a T-shirt that says: “Pluto Resistance, 20 years: 2006-2026.”

The campaign to reinstate Pluto – with its passionate advocates, ongoing debates, occasional protests and petitions – seems to be largely confined to the US. “It is more of an issue in the United States,” says Metzger. “This was the one we discovered.” So, the planet’s demotion was a source of wounded pride? “I’ll admit there was some of that – among the public, not the scientists.”

More recently, the campaign has taken on a populist tinge, with Trump’s Nasa administrator, Jared Isaacman, telling a congressional committee in April that he was in favour of a rethink. “I am very much in the camp of Make Pluto a Planet Again,” he said.

The event that sparked the IAU’s 2006 vote was the discovery of a distant celestial body that would come to be called Eris. Eris was out in the Kuiper Belt, beyond Neptune – where Pluto also resides. It was roughly the same size as Pluto (less volume, but more mass). If Pluto was a planet, the argument went, then so was Eris. And if Eris wasn’t a planet, how could Pluto continue to be one?

Eris and Pluto were by no means alone in the Kuiper Belt. Other smaller bodies were discovered around the same time, including Haumea, Makemake and Sedna. Were these also planets? There were likely many more similar objects still to be found. How would schoolchildren manage a planetary roster that might number in the hundreds?

In search of a solution, the IAU came up with a three-point definition of a planet: it must orbit the Sun; it must have sufficient mass to pull itself into a round shape; and it must have “cleared its neighbourhood” – meaning it must gravitationally dominate the area in which it orbits. Nothing beyond Neptune that we knew about qualified; Pluto was out.

It was the last point in particular that upset a lot of Pluto advocates, because a body’s ability to clear its neighbourhood depends a lot on the neighbourhood. “One of the biggest flaws with the IAU definition is that you can have the same object in two different orbits,” says Kornfeld. “In one, it’s considered a planet, and in the other, it’s not considered a planet.” If the Earth were towed out to Pluto’s position, the planetary scientist Alan Stern argued, it wouldn’t be able to clear its zone either, and would no longer meet the IAU definition of a planet.

“You could even have small asteroids, that are too small to be round, clearing an orbit if they’re close to a star,” says Metzger. “It just goes to show that orbit clearing isn’t really that meaningful of a category.”

To its detractors, the IAU definition seemed crafted with a specific intent. “A reason was invented to exclude Pluto,” says Kornfeld.

Pluto’s demotion created two opposing scientific teams: the so-called geophysical camp, which believes the physical properties of a celestial body should count toward its planethood; and the dynamicists, who are more concerned with the position a body occupies, its surroundings and its direction of travel. You could characterise the split as planetary scientists v astronomers. Many planetary scientists, including Metzger, simply do not use the IAU definition.

When the New Horizons spacecraft made its flyby of Pluto in 2015, the geophysical camp seized what it saw as an advantage. Pluto definitely had the geophysical makings of a planet, they maintained. It had mountains, evidence of recent geological activity, and water ice hills floating on frozen nitrogen. It might even be able to support life. How could that not be a planet?

Those agitating for Pluto’s planetary status do not, by and large, recognise any problems stemming from reinstatement. They welcome a definition broad enough to take in hundreds of new planets, as taxing as that might be for children and their wallcharts. “The more the merrier,” says Paul Byrne, associate professor of earth, environmental and planetary sciences at Washington University in St Louis. “There are 1,025 official Pokémon species, and I’ve never heard a kid say that’s too many.”

Those against Pluto’s reinstatement say the problem isn’t with a larger number of planets, per se – but with a primarily geophysical definition that would encompass, among other bodies, planetary moons, including our moon.

“I have no problem with having a larger number of planets,” says the astronomer Mike Brown, over email. “My argument is simply that we decided long ago that the moon is not a planet and that also precludes Pluto.” Brown is often described as The Man Who Killed Pluto, because he led the team that discovered Eris back in 2005, setting the whole de-planetisation in motion. It’s a title he leans into: he even wrote a book called How I Killed Pluto and Why It Had It Coming.

Brown often says that the moon is bigger than Pluto; it’s round and has a complex geophysical history, and would certainly meet the criteria for a planet if you excluded any requirement concerning orbit. What he’s saying is: if Pluto’s a planet, so is the moon.

“I don’t have an issue with calling the moon a planet,” says Byrne. “Because I can be a brother and a husband at the same time, and it doesn’t require that I be one or the other. And so I don’t see why the moon can’t be a satellite and a planet.”

For the outsider, this debate can often seem mired in political, even procedural questions, with Plutonians contending that the IAU vote was incorrectly conducted and therefore void. “You could make the argument that they never officially voted on a planet because they didn’t follow the procedure that was required,” says Metzger.

Brown denies there was anything political about the decision. “The only people who complain about the voting procedure were the ones who didn’t like the outcome.”

So the question remains: why does any of this matter?

“It was almost like a coup,” says Kornfeld. “And as a result, kids are learning less. They’re learning eight planets, and that’s it.”

For Metzger, the planetary definition excluding Pluto is based on an outmoded notion of the solar system. “They were creating a reactionary view towards an orderly cosmos, rather than the more modern scientific view where it’s chaotic,” he says. “The second problem was that I think they misread the room. The public of today is not the public of the 1800s. They’re perfectly happy understanding a dynamic, chaotic cosmos, and we missed the opportunity to teach that.”

Pluto’s nature has always been elusive. In 1915, the astronomer Percival Lowell published calculations based on peculiarities in the orbits of Uranus and Neptune, predicting the existence of a new, ninth planet, which he called Planet X, with a mass somewhere between Earth’s and Neptune’s. In 1930, the long search for Planet X bore fruit: the new body, discovered at the observatory that bore Lowell’s name, was christened Pluto.

Gradually, however, it became clear that whatever Pluto was, it wasn’t Planet X. It didn’t seem anywhere near large enough to account for irregularities in Neptune’s orbit. Scientists offered theories to explain why Pluto looked so small, but the truth was, it was small – even smaller than the moon. Only in 1992 did we learn that Lowell’s calculations were based on an overestimation of Neptune’s mass. There was no Planet X.

Pluto’s reputation as an underdog, the picked-on kid, may stem from the 2006 vote, but one could argue it was punching above its weight for years. How would they have voted on Pluto’s planetary status if they had known the truth in 1930? And will it take another vote to satisfy Pluto’s defenders?

“People have locked in,” says Metzger. “We would have a less useful vote today than we did back in the 2006 timeframe. So we don’t want another vote. What we want is for people to recognise that voting was a mistake, and we’re not going to do that any more. We’re going to go back to the scientific method.”

Justice Dept. Issues Grand Jury Subpoena to Comey Confidant

The New York Times August 31, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The subpoena of Daniel C. Richman is the latest move in a persistent campaign to go after James B. Comey, one of President Trump’s most reviled political adversaries who has already been indicted twice.

By Alan Feuer

Federal prosecutors have issued a grand jury subpoena demanding testimony from Daniel C. Richman, a close confidant of James B. Comey, the former F. B. I. director and one of President Trump’s most reviled political adversaries, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The subpoena, issued by prosecutors in the U. S. attorney’s office for the Southern District of Florida, appears to be connected to the so-called grand conspiracy case that has sought to implicate Mr. Comey and other federal officials who have investigated Mr. Trump in an overarching plot to deprive him of his rights. It was a small but significant escalation of the Florida case and the latest move in a persistent campaign to go after Mr. Comey in particular who has already been indicted twice in separate cases in Virginia and North Carolina.

It remained unclear what sort of testimony the prosecutors in Florida want from Mr. Richman, a law professor at Columbia University who once served as an adviser to Mr. Comey at the F. B. I. But he has found himself caught up in two previous investigations of his friend and former boss.

One of the inquiries — which ended without charges — sought to determine whether Mr. Comey had used Mr. Richman as a conduit to leak information to the news media about sensitive investigations conducted when he ran the F. B. I. The other resulted in an indictment last September accusing Mr. Comey of lying to Congress about some of the same matters covered in the leak investigation.

The Justice Department did not respond to an email seeking comment on the subpoena.

The inquiry in Florida is the third time Mr. Richman has been called to provide information about Mr. Comey. The investigation is being led by Joseph diGenova, a Trump loyalist who has convened a grand jury in the Federal District Court in Fort Pierce overseen by one of the president’s friendliest appointees to the bench, Judge Aileen M. Cannon. It has targeted other former officials who have triggered the president’s ire — chief among them, John O. Brennan, a onetime C. I. A. director.

The grand conspiracy case is arguably the most far-fetched of the Justice Department’s serial efforts to pursue Mr. Trump’s political opponents. Under Mr. diGenova’s leadership, prosecutors have tried for months to connect disparate inquiries into Mr. Trump — including the investigation into ties between Russia and his 2016 presidential campaign and the later inquiry into his mishandling of classified documents — as a single, long-running scheme to damage his political prospects.

Mr. Comey first ran afoul of the president when he oversaw the early stages of the Russia investigation and was ultimately fired by Mr. Trump in May 2017. That move led to the appointment of a special counsel, Robert S. Mueller III, who continued the inquiry but eventually determined that charges could not be brought against a sitting president.

When prosecutors in Virginia filed their first indictment against Mr. Comey, they relied heavily on a trove of text messages and emails between him and Mr. Richman. Those communications, they claimed, proved that Mr. Richman had served as an intermediary funneling information to journalists on behalf of Mr. Comey.

That first case was dismissed in its entirety in November after a federal judge determined that the inexperienced prosecutor ordered by Mr. Trump to bring the charges had been improperly appointed to her post. Mr. Richman quickly complicated the Justice Department’s efforts to bring a new indictment involving similar accusations by persuading a federal judge that investigators, in a glaring misstep, had improperly obtained his communications with Mr. Comey in the first place.

Five months after the initial charges were dismissed, the Justice Department brought a second indictment against Mr. Comey, accusing him of threatening to kill Mr. Trump by posting a photograph of seashells arranged on a beach in North Carolina spelling out a message reading, “86 47.”

Prosecutors claim that “86” is a mafia term meaning to kill someone and that “47” was a reference to Mr. Trump’s role as the nation’s 47th president. But lawyers for Mr. Comey have scoffed at the idea that the photo was a real threat against the president, adding that prosecutors have been unable to come up with any evidence that Mr. Comey meant to harm Mr. Trump.

Alan Feuer is a reporter for The Times who covers the effects President Trump has had on the courts, the Justice Department and the broader rule of law.

6 Takeaways From the GTA VI Extended Look

Wired August 27, 2026

It’s safe to say Grand Theft Auto VI is the most anticipated game ever. Thirteen years after the last entry in the series, rampant fervor and speculation about what features the game will include have ratcheted up. Today, Rockstar Games divulged more details through an exclusive livestream event on Netflix called Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look. The spectacle was a 26-minute-long collection of gameplay, cutscenes, and game mechanics.

And boy, does this sure look like a GTA game. The trailer featured Lucia and Jason, the two main characters, driving around Vice City, GTA’s fictional version of Miami. It highlighted all kinds of violence and shenanigans your characters can engage in, and it looks good doing it.

The livestream follows a week of gameplay leaks and story spoilers by the hacker group Cyberleek, which Rockstar called “heartbreaking.” A bevy of other details about the game emerged just a day before the event in a story published by the British magazine Dazed. The piece chronicles the extraordinary level of detail and effort Rockstar has put into GTA VI, including how players control the characters and the unprecedented realism that Rockstar put into its satirical sandbox version of Miami.

It’s bound to be a massive game; today’s reveal shows just how much of a monster it will be. Here are the big takeaways from the livestream.

GTA VI is gorgeous. The cityscapes, nightclubs, and lush natural parks shown all seem vibrant and awash in color.

There is a noticeable difference between cutscenes and gameplay, though, as the gameplay clips looked a little flatter and more desaturated than the cinematic cutscenes. That’s kind of a nitpick, though it’s worth noting that in the very first scene—in the dark basement of a crack house—the lighting is so dim it washes out the features of several Black characters around the table.

The player can control two characters, Jason and Lucia, a Bonnie-and-Clyde-esque couple who seem to be working out some lingering tension in their relationship as they go about their various criminal activities.

The voice acting for the main characters and other non-playable characters (NPCs) feels tightly written, though that’s based on the select clips Rockstar showed. According to Dazed, the relationship between the characters can change over time, and the player’s actions can affect how that plays out. Keep that in mind if you’re hoping for a particular ending.

GTA VI offers a plethora of options for changing the two main characters’ appearances. Eating too much or too little food affects their weight. Working out can make them swole. The Extended Look also showed off characters eating and working out in minigames. It was a feature in 2004’s GTA San Andreas and in a smaller way in GTA V. Now, that reactivity will be much more fully realized in GTA VI.

There’s also an array of clothes you can equip your characters with, which Rockstar has apparently coordinated with real-life fashion designers to put in the game. Some of these, however, may only come with the $100 Ultimate Edition that people are very mad about.

The NPCs in the game appear much more responsive and interactive than in prior games. According to Dazed, Rockstar has an entire studio in Los Angeles dedicated to working on NPC pedestrian behavior alone.

In the Extended Look, gameplay segments with car chases pointedly avoided streamrolling over pedestrians. But NPCs wore yoga outfits, rode scooters, and seemed to have more personality than the cut-and-paste crowds of past games.

Driving seems greatly improved. When driving, you have a minimap that looks like an actual GPS map guiding you where to go. A car chase saw the main characters running from the police. The player can switch between Lucia and Jason and choose to either drive or shoot at the pursuers. Shooting out tires can cause a car to flip, crash into the sidewalk, and cause environmental destruction.

At one point, a character also body-slams a cop through a wall, which hints at potentially more destructive environments indoors as well. GTA games have been iffy about destructible environments before, though. Sometimes in GTA V you can easily crash through a large light pole but then get instantly stopped by a volleyball net. So we’ll see how reactive everything gets.

Vice City and the surrounding areas seem absolutely massive. It’s also fully Florida, allowing your characters to fanboat around the Everglades, kayak on the rivers, or scuba dive and jet ski in the Gulf.

One scene from the trailer shows Lucia accidentally kidnapping a livestreaming influencer, then carrying him along through a car chase from the police. Many of the characters use phones and communicate via text. It’s clear that GTA VI has some satirical takes on social media, but we’ll see how relevant it feels in a constantly shifting era.

A dog is in at least one scene of the game. Can you pet it? Yes. Yes, you can.

In 2023, Rockstar bought the modding marketplace Cfx and reworked it into an official place to share and purchase user-created mods for the game. That service, along with GTA Online’s Rockstar Mission Creator, which lets users make custom levels and modes, indicates that Rockstar has long realized that GTA is fertile ground for user creativity.

The Extended Look didn’t show anything suggesting it would advance those user-creation capabilities, but that’s likely because the game is being released as a single-player title before any multiplayer elements are added.
